entries.heading: Rev. W. Riland Bedford
paras: Cricket was being played in Rectory Park and Sutton Park as far back as 1837 according to the Club’s minute book of 1897. However, in which it stated that Rev. William Riland Bedford (1794 – 1843) had an early association with cricket. Nevertheless, on his death the Rector of Sutton Coldfield was Dr. Richard Williamson (1844 to 1850), whose nephew was the Rev. W.K. Riland Bedford. This suggests that cricket was being played in Rectory Park from 1837 or maybe before.  1837 is ten years before the Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club was formed in 1847.

entries.heading: The Rev W.K. Riland Bedford
paras: The Rev W.K. Riland Bedford’s (12 July 1826 – 23 January 1905) whose first marriage was on 18 Sept. 1851 to, Maria Amy, youngest daughter of Joseph Houson, who died in 1890 of Southwell, Nottinghamshire. His second marriage was in 1900 to Margaret, daughter of Denis Browne. He had by his first wife seven sons and three daughters. Five of his sons were all cricketers, and it was largely due to his own, his sons, and his gardener's efforts, that the pitches were laid and the ground converted into an area suitable for the game.
R.S. Sadler
R.S. Sadler became the Hon, secretary.

entries.heading: Rev. J.H. Gibbon
paras: Rev J.H. Gibbon came into the parish church as curate and was a decided acquisition.  He has played in the Harrow and Oxford teams, and arrived with a reputation as a “stone-wall” batsman, but he “forsook his style in country cricket”

entries.heading: A.L. Crockford
paras: A.L. Crockford joined the club, who later became one of the club’s outstanding personalities and a fine cricketer.  His sons, L.C. and E.B. followed, but more will be heard of them in due course.

entries.heading: Rev.G.F. Hough
paras: The Rev G.F. Hough was elected Hon secretary and treasurer.  He had come to Sutton two years earlier as tutor to the young sons of A. Lloyd at Moor Hall and later succeeded the Rev. Gibbon as curate.
Hough took a major part in the management of the club over the following five years and as a cricketer he was described as a “fast bumpy bowler with a rather doubtful action".

entries.heading: R.S. Sadler
paras: R.S. Sadler took over the treasurer roll later in the season.

entries.heading: Ges Roadley
paras: A professional, Ges Roadley was engaged to bowl at the nets at a salary of 30 shillings a week and the boy of BVGS are allowed to use the ground for 4 guineas for the season.

entries.heading: A.L. Crockford
paras: A.L. Crockford joined the club, who later became one of the club’s outstanding personalities and a fine cricketer.  His sons, L.C. and E.B. followed, but more will be heard of them in due course.

entries.heading: Rev. G.F. Hough
paras: Now as Chairman the Rev. G.F. Hough proposed that an annual subscription of 5 shillings should be made, which was seconded by Mr Sheldon.  However, Mr Dowler proposed an amendment, seconded by Mr Butcher that the annual subscription should be 10 shillings and 6 pence. The amendment was carried by 12 votes to 2.

entries.heading: Mr Dowler
paras: There was some considerable discussion on Club Colours, and it was agreed that the colours which had formerly been used by the club should be again adopted and Mr. Dowler had to obtain a sample of such colours and lay the same before some future committee meeting.

entries.heading: Mr Payton
paras: Mr. Payton proposed that the opening match of Married v Singles be replaced with the “1st Xl play against the Next sixteen” on the 30th April. This was agreed
3 New Members in 1881
F.G. Clarke; H. James; W.J. Watson; & J.H. Haigh.

entries.heading: Membership
paras: After nearly two years away from the Town the Rev. W.C.R. Bedford returned as curate, and resumed his activities with the club and D.T. Jeffreys; Mr. Pryse; Rev. A. Foster; B. Smith; & G. Mae Kean, joined the club.
Three of the Rev. W.C.R. Bedford brothers H.E.R, A.E.R. and C.Y.R. were in the side and other members included.
Rev. Lloyd Wood, Rev. P.G. Mainwaring, H.E. Wilson, F.W. Simkin, A.L. Wentworth Crockford, F. Colmore, C.H. Ware, W.W. Bagot, H.M. Eddowes and Herbert Addenbrooke (both in the Repton School Xl).

These men constituted a good team and during this and the following year only one defeat was suffered.  The success of the side depended upon the three fast bowlers, A.L. Crockford, Colmore, and Ware, the latter also a forceful batsman.  Squire Bagot and W.C.R. Bedford (slow) also took a lot of wickets, and assisted in making the attack well above club cricket average. paras: An account was rendered by a Mr. Atkins (believed to be Landlord of the Boot public house) for payment by the Committee for liquor supplied.  The Committee denied their liability and the Hon Sec was instructed to write to that effect.  There was further reference to this in the minutes so presumable the club did not pay.

entries.heading: J. Woodward
paras: The Club Secretary had been in contact with his counterpart in the Warwickshire County Cricket Club seeking a professional bowler, after some negotiation a J. Woodward was engaged as the Club’s Professional Bowler on Monday evenings from 6p.m. too dark during the months of May and June and on Thursdays from 5 p.m. till dark for 12 shillings and 6 pence a week including his rail fare and any other expenses, with the Club having the option to engage him in July and August which they did so.

entries.heading: C. Harlow
paras: C. Harlow, playing for Harborne 2nd scored 101 not out and took 7 for 14 against Sutton 2nd Xl

entries.heading: A.L. Crockford
paras: A.L. Crockford, who had been promoted to the Aldermanic Bench, was requested to watch the club's interests in view of negotiations connected with the Rectory Park.

entries.heading: E. B. Crockford
paras: E.B. Crockford on his debut for the club with the second eleven had impressive bowling figures - 9 overs, 7 maidens, 2 runs, 1 wicket

entries.heading: Rev. W.C.R. Bedford
paras: Tribute was paid to the Rev W.C.R. Bedford who had so worthily followed as President in the footsteps of his father for the services he had rendered to the club.

W.R.C. was presented with a photograph of the cricket ground and an album containing views in Rectory Park.  It may have been noticed that little has been written of the playing activities over the first sixty years, the reason being at the historians have not succeeded in unearthing many of these, because no strict control was kept over the Minute and Score books.  From here onwards fairly comprehensive records have been kept.

entries.heading: Dr. A H. Evans
paras: Dr. A H. Evans, a nephew of George Elliott, the novelist, and who was subsequently knighted, and in later years became President of the club, was in his prime.  He was a good wicketkeeper and a powerful hitter.  It is reported that he once hit a ball into Rectory Road, a mighty hit even if the road was slightly nearer than it is today.

C.Y.R. Bedford had been elected captain and H.M. Eddowes, a prominent local solicitor, Hon secretary.

entries.heading: W. Ansell and E. Ansell
paras: W. Ansell and E. Ansell were elected as playing members at the AGM on 28th January having moved recently from Bromsgrove as their brewery business was in Aston.  Incidentally the Club sold Ansell Bitter until 2009, however at the 5th May 1888 the Club decided that a liquor license is not required as refreshments and drinks for match days will be ordered from the Boot Hotel.

entries.heading: New Members

entries.heading: A.L. Crockford
paras: The first century to be made at the Rectory Park is credited to A.L. Crockford, who was run out for 117 against Birmingham Gas.  Sutton scored 300 runs and the scorebook records that the visitors did not bat.  Until the following year there was no law on declarations and consequently a side had to be dismissed before opponents could bat. However, the ground was now scythed one or twice a season.

H.E.R. Bedford,

H.E.R. Bedford, playing for Warwickshire at Birmingham opened the innings with Richards (A Professional) against Yorkshire. Set to make 212 runs for victory, the pair put on over 100 runs for the first wicket, of which Bedford made 28, Richards went on to make 120 not out and Warwickshire won by 5 wickets.  Richards was the recipient of a collection of over £20 and a further £5 donated by a Birmingham gentleman to any Warwickshire’s professional making 100 runs.

entries.heading: Golden Jubilee
paras: The Jubilee, the fiftieth year since the formation of the club, was celebrated by a match on May 2nd between the Captain's and the Secretary's elevens.  The occasion was marked by a presentation by the captain, O.H. Stone, to the founder members present, the Rev W.K. Riland Bedford and Henry Addenbrooke.

entries.heading: George Sharp
paras: From 1907 to 1914 George Sharp was the skipper and it was during part of this period that his son Norman, a school boy, took over the history of SCCC and became the 2nd team’s scorer.

entries.heading: Second Xl Personalities
paras: Little, so far, has been said about the junior elevens, so perhaps a brief resume, may not be out of place.  The writer (Norman Sharp) has very little knowledge of the happenings during the earlier part of this period. 1901 to 1914.

Personalities one remembers were P.A. Grove; J.H. Cornwell; E.J. Hallmark; Bert Cornwell; W.J. Saunders; T. Etchells; E.J. Tabb; among the batsmen, and F.E. Abbott; R.H. Griffiths; H.R. Yardley; A.J. Lilly; and G. Saunders as bowlers.  With a strong first eleven over this period, it was natural that there were a number of good players in the second team, and, in fact the two teams met in an annual encounter, in which the second team usually performed very creditably.

entries.heading: C. Lowe
paras: A character of the period was C. Lowe.  He was not a good cricketer but one of those people upon whom the game depends so much.  He loved his cricket and played until he was over seventy and his long beard was reminiscent of W.G. Grace. He never aspired above the "A" or “B” teams, and was happiest when trundling up his round arm slows.  Upon ceasing to play he remained in the game as “A” team umpire and was a great "asset" to that side for invariably he gave his decisions in favour of Sutton.  When at square leg he produced a camp stool from his pocket where he took a disinterested view of the game.

entries.heading: W.L. Mortimore
paras: W.L. Mortimore, who had played with Aston Unity in the Birmingham League for 34 years, joined the club. Though his best years as a cricketer had passed, he enjoyed his game and continued to play for many years and was still an extremely useful bowler for the second team and regularly obtained his 50 wickets a season. He also rendered good administrative service as Hon treasurer, as manager of Lloyds Bank, he was well suited.

entries.heading: R.E. Yates
paras: R.E. Yates after leading the first team most successfully for six -years relinquished the captaincy in favour of J.B. Russell.

entries.heading: J.B. Russell
paras: John Russell was one of the great personalities in the club's history, and a most likeably character.  A powerful and hard-hitting batsman, the pavilion windows, to the delight of spectators, suffered considerable damage from his bat. Reference to his wicket keeping has already been made, but special mention must here be made of his leg side work which bore the stamp of an artist.

On occasions he was a useful change bowler and with other keepers capable of deputizing he would sometimes take off the pads and went on to bowl, he was also an exceptionally good skipper, always getting the best out of his team, and down on any slackness in the field. As captain of Staffordshire, he “kept” for many years to that great bowler Sidney Barnes.

entries.heading: C.A.F. Fiddian- Green
paras: In 1913 C.A.F. Fiddian-Green, who, just after the war played a prominent part for Cambridge University and Warwickshire, and for England at hockey, played a few games for the second eleven.

entries.heading: J.B. Russell

entries.heading: F.B. Crockford and R. Evans

entries.heading: F.B. Clark
paras: F.B. Clark was again in brilliant form with the ball and took 89 wickets for under 10 runs each.  He would almost certainly have been the first Sutton player to obtain 100 wickets in a season but for the outbreak of the war which caused the cancellation of the last four matches from 1st August 1914. Against Yardley he took all ten wickets for 35 runs.

entries.heading: H. Lott
paras: The Sutton Club was and is still a great supporter of the County Cricket Club and had H. Lott as their representative on the County Cricket Committee at the outbreak of what became the Great War or W.W.1.

entries.heading: Mr. W. Yeo
paras: Mr. Yeo was engaged as the new Professional & Groundsman from 19th April 1920 for a wage of £3-10s-0d per week. It was recommended by the Committee that members should support Mr. Yeo as much as possible by buying their Cricket equipment through him.

entries.heading: A Boy
paras: It was agreed that a sum of £4 be voted for payment of “Boy” at the beginning of the season to assist the professional in his duties as groundsman.

entries.heading: H. Lott
paras: Horace Lott resigned from the Committee and a letter of thanks would was sent by the secretary expressing the Club’s thanks for his many years of service he had devoted to the Club.

entries.heading: E.B. Crockford
paras: A letter received from the Warwickshire County Cricket Club suggesting that Mr. E.B. Crockford be appointed by them as a country representative and not as a SCCC member.  It was decided that the Club would accept this suggestion.

entries.heading: Mr. J. Nasmith
paras: Mr. J. Nasmith offered a bat to the first member of the Club under the age of 21, who makes the first 50 in the season.

entries.heading: Mr. J. Garland
paras: Mr. J. Garland had been secured as umpire for the first team.  No umpires had been secured for the other teams.

entries.heading: F.B. Clark
paras: Including Wednesday games F.B. Clark scored 886 runs and took 66 wickets.

entries.heading: E.B. Crockford
paras: E.B. Crockford scored 456 runs, including a century and took 64 wickets.

entries.heading: Mr. W. Yeo
paras: The professional and groundsman Yeo, took 65 wickets.

entries.heading: E.W. Norton of Harborne
paras: The match played at Rectory Park is particularly noteworthy, in that E.W. Norton, Harborne's googly bowler, secured all ten Sutton wickets for 35 runs whilst his father W. Norton contributed 50 not out towards Harborne's victory.
Batting first Sutton were dismissed for 72 runs of which Yeo “the Pro” scored 35 runs & the schoolmaster J. Manton, made 37, in a partnership of 57. Harborne defeated Sutton by 8 wickets.

entries.heading: During the season 12 new members joined the Club as follows: -

D.L. Hobbis 	- C/o Lloyds Bank.		Eric Baker	-   The Cot, Jordan Road.

1921 AGM

entries.heading: L.C. Crockford
paras: L.C. Crockford had captained the first team for the first two years after the war, but at the annual general meeting held on the 14th March 1921 elected J.B. Russell, who had held the office at the outbreak of war, was re-elected, with E.B. Crockford as deputy captain.

entries.heading: Mr. L.C. Crockford
paras: The purchase of the Cricket Ground in Rectory Park was discussed and Mr. L.C. Crockford said that he would hold “a watching Brief” for the cricket club.

entries.heading: J.B. Russell, E.B. Crockford
paras: It was a grand summer for the 1st Xl batsmen as all matches everywhere were on the hard wickets, with Russell and E.B. Crockford both averaged 39 with Russell making 145 not out at Ashford.
J. Manton, N. Sharp, G.L. Miller, H. Lott, & L.R. Martin & F.H. Beardshaw.
Six other 1st team players all averages of over 20.

entries.heading: F.H. Beardshaw
paras: F.H. Beardshaw, although a 1st Team Player he never to date made a century, although he had made 99 against Ashfield. It would appear that Ashford was a favourite ground for Sutton batsmen.

entries.heading: George Duckworth
paras: The first match of the 1921 season was played at the County Ground against Sparkhill Belvedere and resulted in a tie of 120 runs each.  George Duckworth, in later years the England and Lancashire wicketkeeper, was behind the stumps for Belvedere.  He was never a tall man, but in that game he seemed to be enveloped behind a pair of pads nearly as big as himself.

entries.heading: George and Norman Sharp
paras: For a father and son to open the innings is always a rare occasion in cricket.  Against Bromsgrove, at the Rectory Park, George and Norman Sharp did so, the older man scoring the most runs.

entries.heading: C. and D. Swift
paras: In a footnote. It was noted that During the 2nd World War;  C. and D. Swift opened the batting for Sutton.

entries.heading: G.H. Miller and E.R. Eardley
paras: In a 2nd eleven match against Aston Unity 2nd, Sutton’s 9th wickets, G.H. Miller and E.R. Eardley, were un-separated in a partnership of 143, after the first eight wickets had fallen for 77.

entries.heading: Norman Marsh
paras: The AGM was held on the 13th March 1922 in the Town Hall with the Rev. Cannon Bernard and 31 members of the Club in attendance the treasurer reported that the Club had a surplus balance of £23-8s-5d for the year ending December 1921.  With a fee of 10 Guineas having being agreed at the February meeting with both the Early Closing Cricket Club and Four Oaks College; so, the Clubs financial position looked good.

entries.heading: Mr. Sidney
paras: There had been discussions at previous meetings over the last two cricket seasons concerning Mr. W. Yoe, who was employed as the groundsman. However, the position was clarified at the 20th March 1922 committee meeting, when Mr. Sidney stated that he was prepared to take over the duties of groundsman to the club for a consideration of £4 per week and a benefit similar to that given to the last groundsman.  The Committee decided to employ Sidney and the Secretary would set out an agreement as dictated by Sidney.

entries.heading: Mr. J. Garland
paras: “Garland’s Benefit – It was decided that a collection on the ground during whit week and a subscription list be opened during that period, the proceeds which were to be devoted to Garland who was the 1st Team umpire. All teams other would have to find their own umpires.

entries.heading: A.F. Leighton
paras: A.F. Leighton joined Sutton in 1922 from league cricket and soon proved himself to be a decided acquisition to the side.  Not only had he played hockey many times for England he had also played cricket for Cambridge University and Hertfordshire before taking up a business appointment in Walsall.  He was a fine batsman, amazingly quick on his feet, and a good medium pace off spin bowler.  With Norman  Sharp as his opening partner for many years they developed an excellent understanding of quick singles.

entries.heading: C.C. Windle
paras: A magnificent innings of 96 by C.C. Windle followed by a brilliant display behind the stumps gave great promise of a fine future for this young cricketer but an untimely death the following winter was a shock to all his friends.

entries.heading: G.L. Miller
paras: Gordon Miller, a young cricketer from Malvern College and a Corinthian footballer, was another attractive batsman and a very fine cover -point.

entries.heading: C.E. Francis
paras: C. E Francis was developing fast as a batsman and excellent fielder and before long was to become one of the leading batsmen, a good spirit pervaded the cub and every encouragement was being given to the younger players.

entries.heading: F. H. Beardshaw
paras: The only century made in 1922 was by F H Beardshaw against Knowle and Dorridge, and with N Sharp in the same match, participated in a first wicket stand of 164.

entries.heading: New Members – 1922
paras: H.J. Partington, C.H. Smith, P. Terry, J. Parsons, R.T. Janury and J. Avery joined the Club during the season.

entries.heading: Norman Marsh
paras: Norman March as treasurer reported to the meeting of the 26th March 23 that the Club had made a loss of £9-6s-6d on the year ending December 1922.  It was agreed that Honorary Members should be invited to join the Club for a minimum subscription of ½ Guinea, and that such members should have seat reserved for them in the Pavilion Enclosure for the season.

entries.heading: Mr Sidney
paras: It was agreed that Mr. Sidney should be engaged as groundsman for the ensuring season at a wage (which Sidney had proposed in a letter to the secretary) of 5 shillings a week to a £3-15s-0d a week for the season, which was accepted with a rider made by Mr. Crockford that a subscription list for Sidney’s benefit should be displayed in the pavilion for member to contribute as they wished, similar to the agreement made the previous season.

At the 19th December 1923 General Meeting the Treasurer announced that Sidney’s benefit amounted to £22-9s-4d and that Mr. Sidney wished the treasurer to convey his thanks to the Club for their amble contributions.  It is noted that in the 10th March 1924 Mr. Sidney agreed to a further reduction to a weekly wage of £3-10s-0d from 14th April to 13 September 1924.

entries.heading: Mr Cox
paras: The committee again appointed Mr. Garland as the 1st Team umpire and that a Mr. Cox would carry out the same duties for the Second Team, a fee of 7s-6d being paid to Mr. Cox for each match.  The money for the expenses of the umpire and scorers should be collected by the captains of each team each week.

entries.heading: Mr. Edward Ansell
paras: Mr. Edward Ansell presented the Club with half a dozen tubs for flowers.  He had arranged to cut in half some old beer barrels from his Aston Brewery.

entries.heading: Mr. Marsh
paras: The committee meeting of the 25th May 1923 agreed that the Mr. Marsh the Treasurer should arrange with the London Joint City and Midland Bank in Sutton Coldfield for an overdraft up to £50 so that he himself should not be in debt through the expenses of the Club until the members had paid up their subscriptions.

entries.heading: J.B. Russell
paras: Russell score two centuries with a season’s average of 34. However, at Wolverhampton the home team in the last over of the day won with 5 wickets to spare. Sutton scored 284, with Russell with a fast century with 122 runs but a fast century by E W Page. However, in a game against Ashfield's who were bowled out for 191 for Sutton to win by eight wickets with Russell scoring 101

entries.heading: A.F. Leighton
paras: In a victory at Olton where the home side scored 188 and lost by eight wickets to Sutton with Leighton  was 102 not out and a season’s averaged of 49

entries.heading: E.B. Crockford
paras: Crockford scored 130 runs away at Leamington and total of 584 runs for the season with an average of 53.
Norman Sharp
Sharp also scored a century.

entries.heading: D. Foster & J and C. Fletcher
paras: The committee elected Mr. D. Foster as a Holiday Member of the Club also Mr. J. Fletcher was elected a Holiday Member of the Club along with Mr. C. Fletcher (Senior)

entries.heading: George Sharp
paras: At the Annual General Meeting George Sharp was presented with an arm chair in appreciation of his eight years as Hon secretary.  He had done a lot of valuable work for the club particularly during the war period when it had been chiefly through his efforts that the ground had been kept in a fit state for cricket upon the cessation of hostilities.  He captained the Second eleven from 1907 to 1921, excluding the war years when there was no 2nd X1.  Upon his retirement from business his major hobby was on the ground where he made a number of constructive improvements including the making and erection of the pavilion railings, which were not replaced until over thirty years later.  Before this wooden fence was erected the pavilion was enclosed by the iron railings put round when the pavilion was built.  Two years later George Sharp was honoured with Life Membership of the club

entries.heading: A.F. Leighton
paras: Leighton's 85 not out in a total of 119 for 5 in defeating Coventry & N.W. at Coventry, there was nothing of particular note in connection with the matches played during the season. It was a season largely ruined by rain which prevented a ball being bowled until the middle of May.

entries.heading: G. Sharp and F Styles
paras: The Rectory Road frontage of the park was being developed for building and as houses went up the appearance of the ground was completely spoiled.  G. Sharp and F Styles planted hawthorn hedges and silver birch trees along the far boundary in order to maintain the rural atmosphere of the ground. Trees and hedges have now grown up in the gardens of those houses, and nowadays they can hardly be seen.

entries.heading: Geo Sharp, Francis and Broadley
paras: A Pavilion Fund was set up to meet the necessary money being spent and to do this by means of a balloting for prizes (Tombola) organised by Geo Sharp, Francis and Broadley, which made a profit £40.

entries.heading: Canon Barnard
paras: Canon Barnard made an application for use of the ground for his Sunday-School Children on Friday 13th June, which was accepted.

entries.heading: Mr Sidney
paras: Several complaints had been made regarding Mr. Sidney not being in attendance on the ground when it was considered by members that his presence was required, acknowledging that Sidney had taken a wage reduction it was felt that he must be in attendance on the ground two evenings a week – Tuesdays and Thursdays.

entries.heading: Garland & Sidney
paras: Both Garland, 1st team umpire and Sidney, groundsman would receive benefits: -

entries.heading: Mr. Garland on 4th July against Wolverhampton
paras: Mr. Sidney’s benefit would be on Monday 3rd August against Moseley Ashfield.

entries.heading: Mr R. Sidney
paras: Mr R. Sidney, son of W. Sidney was offered 2 Guineas a week to be responsible for locking up the Pavilion and for general security of the premises after all members had left the ground each night.

entries.heading: Mr. Showell
paras: There was also a problem with the horse as Mr. Showell had on two occasions left the Club’s horse untethered when he was collecting his own animal from Rectory Park.

entries.heading: Geo Sharp, H.L. Mortimore and the Secretary
paras: A sub-committee of Geo Sharp, H.L. Mortimore and the Secretary were appointed to obtain estimates for the re-thatching of the Pavilion

entries.heading: Norman Sharp
paras: Against Chester Road C.C, Sutton won by ten wickets in a Wednesday match, A.J. Terry (81) and N. Sharp (101 not out) put on 184 for the first wicket.
Sutton scored 272 for 5 against Kings Heath at the Rectory Park mainly due to N. Sharp obtaining 152 in 140 minutes, out of 253 scored whilst he was at the wicket.

entries.heading: R. Sidney and F. Law
paras: At Ashfield, Sutton was facing defeat with eight wickets down for 92 when R. Sidney and F. Law came together and added 75 for the ninth wicket to enable Sutton to win.

entries.heading: J. Nasmith
paras: The death of John Nasmith was a loss to the club.  Though not a cricketer of renown, he had, since joining the club in the war years, played an important part in the administration, particularly as Hon. team secretary, and he was always keen to give every encouragement to the younger generation.

entries.heading: New Members
paras: During the last four seasons a number of new cricketers had joined the Club: - including Messer L Wilkes, H.J. Partington, C.H. Smith, P. Terry, J. Parsons, G. Cowfe, J. Radford, H. Startin, C.G. Walker, Mr. Abrams, M.C. Butcher, Mr. Lyndopp, Mr. James, Mr. Roper, C.H. Bailie, F. Law, H.R. Wheatley, J.P. Griffith, A.P. Cawdle, G. Hasell, N.R. Oldaker, F. Styles, C.H. Smith, K.W.C. Dobson, and R. Stanley,

entries.heading: R.T. Janney & F.H. Beardshaw
paras: Two matches during the season are worthy of special mention.  Leamington the home side scored 148 and after a disastrous start eight Sutton wickets were down for 80 runs. The match seemed virtually over but R.T.  Janney, who joined Beardshaw, had other ideas.  Janney, putting a dead bat to everything, stayed whilst Beardshaw did the scoring.  The score crept up amid tense excitement until the winning hit was made.  Janney scored only six runs but played a hero's part whilst his partner collected 71 not out.

entries.heading: Norman Sharp
paras: In reply to the visitors Coventry & N.W. declared with their score at 219 for 5. W.R.P. Hayward and N. Sharp put on 88 for the first wicket in quick time.  The score was then taken to 147 by Sharp and Francis after the innings had been in progress only 75 minutes.  Sharp was out for 85, and Francis with the assistance of Russell and R. Sidney hit off the required runs with 5 wickets and 15 minutes to spare.

entries.heading: Leighton and N. Sharp
paras: Centuries were scored by A.F. Leighton and N. Sharp during the season.
1927 & J.H. Yates

J. Hartley Yates resigned and so brought to an end a long association with the club.  For many years he had been a regular first team player alongside his brother R.E. Yates, but since the war his connection had been that of a vice president.

entries.heading: D.G. Foster and R.M. Wilkinson
paras: New members elected in this year were D.G. Foster and R.M. Wilkinson, both of whom played important roles in the club in the years to follow.

entries.heading: N. Marsh
paras: It was in the early part of this year that Norman Marsh passed away very suddenly and at a comparatively early age.  At the time of his death, he was the Hon treasurer of the club. Norman at the 8th March General Meeting reported that the thatching of the Pavilion had been placed a fee agreed at 30 Guineas, with the work being completed by Mid-April before the playing season commenced.

Norman was not outstanding as a cricketer, though he made useful contributions with the second team.  He is remembered mainly for his work for the club over his 23 years membership, and for eight years as Hon treasurer.  The pavilion clock, to which nearly all members subscribed, was erected in his memory.  (The clock was replaced in 1956 by an electric one, and "retired" to the lower ground).

entries.heading: George Sharp
paras: The garden in the pavilion enclosure was made and planted with flowers by G Sharp in the early part of the season.

entries.heading: A.F. Leighton
paras: A.F. Leighton was elected captain of the first team, in succession to E.B. Crockford, and proved to be a keen and astute skipper.

entries.heading: F. Hawkins
paras: Mr. Hawkins was appointed as Groundsman at a wage of £2-15s-0d per week for 21 weeks, and he indicated that he would be happy to be appointed for the 1928 season without any benefit, but Mr. Garland 1st team umpire would have a benefit on Whit Monday as in previous years.

entries.heading: F.B. Clark and R. Sidney
paras: F.B. Clark and R. Sidney scored 143 without being parted for the sixth wicket against Sparkhill, thereby establishing a club record for this wicket.

entries.heading: J.B. Russell and N. Sharp
paras: Against Stratford upon Avon who was dismissed for 199, J.B. Russell and N. Sharp put on 140 for the first wicket and laid the foundation for Sutton to win in the last over.

entries.heading: Rev Canon C.W. Barnard
paras: The Rev. Canon C.W. Barnard, although he had retired from the rector-ship a year or two earlier and made his home at Leamington, was re-elected President. He had, however, not long to live, and passed away a few months later.  He was a president well worthy of the honour, a genial and generous personality, and whilst living at the Rectory rarely missed attending a home a match.  His death was a severe loss.

entries.heading: M.K. Foster
paras: Maurice K. Foster (One of the famous brotherhoods of Worcestershire) who had recently relinquished the captaincy of Worcestershire, joined the club, but unfortunately his appearances were few. A magnificent quick scoring batsman, he played a memorable innings at Tettenhall. Sutton were left with two hours batting against Wolverhampton's declaration of 207 for 5, and opened with M.K. Foster and N. Sharp. In sixty-five minutes, the partnership had realised 142 and Foster had reached his century in 56 minutes.  He went on to score 128 in seventy-five minutes, and the match was won comfortably by Sutton.

entries.heading: E.H.  Walters and N. Sharp
paras: E.H.  Walters and N. Sharp scored 149 for the third wicket against Coventry & N.W., and the same pair also made 120 for the same wicket against Aston Unity.

entries.heading: N. Sharp
paras: N Sharp, in six successive innings scored 632 runs, including four centuries. The scores were 80 (Wrekin College), 104 (Barnt Green), 129 not out (Stratford upon Avon), 126 (Ashfield), 81(Sparkhill), and 112 (Coventry & N W, in 90 min).  In 21 innings in the season, he made 1053 runs, and this was the first occasion a club member had scored A thousand runs.

entries.heading: H.L. Mortimore
paras: H.L. Mortimore, in the concluding match of the season, and playing for his old club Aston Unity, completed fifty years of playing club cricket.  He joined Unity in 1878 and for twenty-five years was a regular first team player.  The last sixteen he played for Sutton, mostly second eleven, and at sixty-nine years of age was still an off-spin bowler to be respected. During his career he probably took over two thousand wickets, and that of course was in Saturday games only, for Sunday play had not yet commenced.  Nor was he a mean performer with the bat.

entries.heading: F.B. Clark
paras: F.B. Clark, one of the best all round players in the history of the club, during the season completed ten thousand runs and one thousand wickets in club cricket.  Joining the club in 1907 he played most of his cricket with Sutton, and represented Staffordshire on many occasions.  He was a stylish batsman with beautiful strokes in front of the wicket, and one of the best bowlers of his time in club cricket, as a seam bowler.  His best ball, which had many good batsmen floundering, was his late in-swinger.

entries.heading: The 1st Team
paras: It not often you see a Cricket Club with such a pedigree – If you are not county standard or better you are unlikely to play in Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club’s 1st team.
The side in batting order was: -
M.K. Foster (England & Worcestershire),
N. Sharp (Warwickshire),
F.B. Clark Staffordshire),
T. Walters (Warwickshire),
E.B. Crockford (Warwickshire),
A.F. Leighton (Hertfordshire),
D.G. Foster (Warwickshire),
C.E. Francis,
J.B. Russell (Staffordshire),
R. Sidney,

entries.heading: P.I. Terry
paras: Twenty-four matches were played during the season, eleven were won and two lost.

entries.heading: Sir A.H. Evans
paras: Sir Alfred H. Evans succeeded the Rev. Canon Barnard as President.  He had first become a member in 1870 and reference to his qualities as a hard-hitting batsman and wicketkeeper have already been made.  He was knighted for his services to the Royal Town in which he had lived for most of his life.  Though now ageing, he would be seen on most Saturday afternoons, walking to the Rectory Park during the summer months and he maintained his interest in the game to the end of his life.  He was no lover of motor cars (after they arrived) and in the days he practiced as a doctor he visited his patients on foot or in his pony and trap.

entries.heading: W. Leonard
paras: W. Leonard became the groundsman in 1928 and was reengaged, for the 1929 season. He was highly respected and continued to serve the club satisfactorily from March to October annually until 1939.

entries.heading: T.B. Russell, G. Sharp & F.B. Clark
paras: In the spring water, was laid on to the pavilion by connecting up to the mains in Rectory Road.  Naturally, considerable benefits were derived, including a shower bath.  T.B. Russell supplied the pipes and G. Sharp and F.B. Clark supervised the work and the total cost was £35.  Prior to this date water had to be brought up each Saturday from Sidney's cottage (Riland Road entrance) and water for the ground was ladled from the pool at the south west corner (behind the existing score box).
1st Xl
Some high scores were compiled during the season, and on at least five occasions Sutton passed the 250 mark.
At Leamington a record fourth wicket partnership was established by A.F. Leighton and C.E. Francis, of 172, the former making 108 and the latter 94.
A few weeks later Leighton and N. Sharp in a day match at Wolverhampton had a first wicket partnership of 120 in seventy minutes, and by the luncheon interval 165 for 3 was on the score board.
F.B. Clark made a century against Ashfield,
N. Sharp against F. Broadbents Birmingham League Xl was out with his score at 99, his partner having run "one Short" in the earlier part of his innings.
Leighton and	P. Richardson scored 118 in an unfinished partnership for the sixth wicket against Knowle & Dorridge.
Barnt Green was dismissed for 19 runs at Sutton when F.B. Clark took 3 wickets for 11 runs, including the "hat trick".
In the return match at Barnt Green rain delayed the start until late afternoon and after getting the home side out for 87, Sutton knocked off the runs in thirty-seven minutes.
Against Olton, A.F. Leighton did the "hat trick",

It will have been noted that at around this period Sutton were the fortunate possessors of four fine all round cricketers, E.B. Crockford, F.B. Clark, A.F. Leighton, and D.G. Foster, all of whom played county cricket. Not only were they good batsmen, but also, they were all bowlers of a high standard for club cricket, Crockford was a slow medium seam bowler, Clark fast medium seam, Foster fast, and Leighton seam and off spin, medium pace.

entries.heading: Paul & A.J. Terry
paras: Paul Terry joined the club in 1922, and played mostly for the second team in this period before gaining a regular first eleven place.  He took an enormous number of wickets for the second team, but more will be said about him later.
A.J. Terry, elder brother of Paul, first played as a schoolboy in 1915.  He was a very useful batsman and wicketkeeper for the team.

entries.heading: F.H. Beardshaw
paras: F.H. Beardshaw, joined the Club after many years in the league, and his activities with Sutton commenced at an age when many are considering retirement from the game.  Though slightly built he wielded his bat to very good effect and scored many runs for the first team, until he felt the club would benefit more by his retirement to the second eleven.  He skippered the side with skill for two years. As a bowler (slow) he used his knowledge of the game to good effect to obtain many victims.

entries.heading: Leslie B. Miles
paras: Leslie B. Miles was another good batsman and captain.

entries.heading: L.R. Martin
paras: L.R. Martin was a batsman of a high order but unfortunately his services were lost to the club upon his taking up a business appointment abroad.

entries.heading: H.P. Gardner
paras: H.P. Gardner, a popular personality and a good batsman, and a wicketkeeper of a high standard would surely have established a place for himself in the first team but for the fact that the club already possessed at least two other first-class keepers.

entries.heading: W.P. Richardson
paras: There were a number of other good second eleven cricketers during this era, particularly E.A. Avery and W.P. Richardson.

entries.heading: R. Sidney
paras: Of the bowlers, R. Sidney (son of W.H. Sidney, for many years groundsman) showed excellent promise, and later gained a regular first team place.

entries.heading: C.H. Miller
paras: C.H. Miller was a fast bowler of no mean ability and a brilliant fielder.

entries.heading: G.B.O. Stone
paras: G.B.O. Stone (son, of G.H. Stone) was a good left arm bowler and an efficient Hon secretary for a period.

entries.heading: FRANK STYLES
paras: Frank Styles was a great worker in this respect.  His genial personality and his slow bowling with his entertaining antics, also considerably assisted the team in its struggle against the severe handicaps to the enjoyment of the game.  It was he, too, who was mainly responsible for the erection of the pavilion on the lower ground in 1933.

entries.heading: R.T. Janney
paras: After three years excellent service as Hon Secretary, R.T. (Bob) Janney retired from this office.

entries.heading: E.H. Walters
paras: His place was taken by E.H. (Ted) Walters, son of R.S. Walters, who had served the club so well in former times.  Ted proved himself to be a keen and industrious official and retained the office until he joined the forces in 1940.
Ted first became a member in 1922 and to his first season played with the "A" team, but it was not long before he obtained a regular position in the first eleven.
At Oundle School he was a stylish batsman and very good wicketkeeper, and represented the Rest of the Public Schools against the Lords Schools in the annual fixture at Lords.
During his career with Sutton, he was a prolific run getter, but as a wicketkeeper, good though he was, he generally had to play second fiddle to J.B. Russell.

entries.heading: D.G. FOSTER
paras: Derek G. Foster (no relation of M.K.) was another young cricketer at this time and later brought considerable distinction to the club.  A product of Shrewsbury School he was a fast bowler and forcing batsman.   As a bowler he made full use of his great height and proved himself to be an outstanding bowler both for Sutton and Warwickshire, for whom he had a number of creditable performances including a "hat trick" against Glamorgan and a brilliant piece of sustained bowling against Surrey in whose side both Hobbs and Sandham were playing.

Derek also represented the Gentlemen against the Players.  A curious analogy was that in this season he headed the Warwickshire bowling averages yet in his seven games for Sutton he was fourth, but was top of the batting with an average of 35.  Though his batting generally lacked stability he was nevertheless a forceful batsman and played some exceedingly good innings.
As a slip fielder there have probably been very few better and he ranked closely to Walter Hammond who was generally considered one of the world's best.

Foster was also a powerful thrower of the ball and is mentioned in “Wisden” as having thrown the cricket ball 133 yards (the record by R. Percival in 1834 is 140 yds. 2 ft.).  He also holds the Danish record of 120.1 meters (approx. 130 yds.) made at Copenhagen in 1930.

entries.heading: E.H. Walters and C. Howl
paras: Some interesting cricket was played during the season with the batting again very strong.  At Wolverhampton, E.H. Walters and C. Howl made a stand of 139 for the third wicket to enable Sutton to close the innings at 286 for 7,

entries.heading: N. Sharp and D.H. Twiss
paras: Cnturies were scored during the season by N. Sharp and D.H. Twiss.  However, four of the last five matches were ruined by the weather, not a ball was bowled.

entries.heading: E.H. Walters
paras: E.H. Walters succeeded A.F. Leighton as captain, and with a strong side at his disposal the first team won nine of the seventeen matches.  Only one defeat was suffered and that by Olton who rubbed it in by dismissing Sutton for 26, L.J. Morris taking six wickets for five runs.

entries.heading: R.F. BARNES
paras: R. Frank Barnes. who had met with considerable success at Bromsgrove School, had joined the club the previous season and became a decided acquisition to the club.  During his first year he did very well with the second team and performed creditably in the current season with the first.
During the next ten years he was to have some excellent matches both with bat and ball.
He also made a name for himself in the world of hockey reaching the final England trial in 1939, but for the intervention of the Second World War, must surely represented his country.

entries.heading: H.P. Gardner & F. Styles
paras: H.P. Gardner led the second eleven successfully, as also did F. Styles the “A” team.

entries.heading: J. GARLAND
paras: Jack Garland passed away.  For about the past twenty-five years he had been the first eleven umpire and earned a high regard throughout the Midlands for his abilities in that respect.
At one time he was the Aston Villa trainer and the useful knowledge gained in that capacity served the members of the club in good stead for minor injuries sustained.

entries.heading: H.E. ROBINSON
paras: Jack was succeeded by H.E. Robinson, who from boyhood days, had always been a keen enthusiast and with particular interest in the Sutton club.  He had always lived close to the ground and as a small boy made himself useful by putting up the numbers and doing other little jobs, until he graduated to first team scorer.

It was a bit of an experiment when he was first given the job of umpiring but he soon established himself as a very efficient umpire and it was not long before he was invited to stand in minor counties matches.

He moved south at the outbreak of war and remained there ever since, and is highly regarded as an umpire and authority on the game in the Home Counties.  But for an accident in which he lost his right arm he would probably have been a useful cricketer.
He “stood” regularly in C.C.C. matches, umpired at Lord’s in 1954 and refereed the England v Scotland Schoolboys Football International at Wembley.

entries.heading: C. Howl and E.A. Avery
paras: One of the outstanding features of the season was a fifth wicket partnership by C. Howl and E.A. Avery against Olton at Rectory Park. They became associated after four wickets had fallen quickly, and before they were parted Avery had made 70 and Howl 100 not out.

entries.heading: D.G. FOSTER
paras: D. G. Foster performed the "hat trick" against Cannock,

entries.heading: F.B. Clark
paras: At Lichfield, F.B. Clark took 9 for 38, and obtained 65 wickets in the season.

entries.heading: R.F. BARNES
paras: R.F. Barnes, in a second eleven match took 5 for 13, and made 79 runs.

entries.heading: A.F. LEIGHTON
paras: At the end of the season A.F. Leighton decided to retire from the game.  He was a fine all-round sportsman and during his eleven years with the club made nearly four thousand runs and took about two hundred wickets.

entries.heading: J.B. Russell and E.B. Crockford
paras: J.B. Russell and E.B. Crockford did not play many games in the 1933 season, and it proved to be their last, though the latter did play on a few occasions in the following year. Both these men will always retain a special niche of their own as outstanding characters in the history of the club.

It would not be out of place to mention once again, that Russell was a fine skipper, a powerful forcing batsman, and a first-class wicketkeeper, and his genial personality will always be remembered by those who had the privilege to know him.

entries.heading: E.B. CROCKFORD
paras: Though some of the deeds of E.B. Crockford (Tom to his friends) have been given earlier, the chapter of his career cannot be closed without special mention of his outstanding qualities as a sportsman.  At all ball games he possessed the touch of genius.

At hockey he was capped on nearly twenty occasions by England, and but for the First World War, would undoubtedly have had more.  He did play in the Great Britain and Ireland team in the 1920 Olympic Game in Antwerp where he won a Gold Medal
At billiards and snooker, he was Midlands’s amateur champion on a number of occasions, Tennis, Football, and other games he took easily in his stride, but here we are concerned more with his cricket.

entries.heading: E. B. Crockford
paras: It is doubtful if a more natural and attractive stroke player has ever played for the club, he had all the shots "in the book", and though he made many runs he would no doubt have made many more if he had approached the game in a more serious vein than was his wont.
He generally opened the bowling with his slow medium deliveries, and was a brilliant fielder in any position.

entries.heading: C.E. FRANCIS
paras: Another first team player to retire was C.E. Francis.  He had been a regular member of the side since 1921 and was a more than useful batsman and fielder, but with an array of outstanding club cricketers during his career he did not have the same opportunities that might have him greater opportunities with a weaker side.  He, also, was a Warwickshire hockey player.

entries.heading: C. da L Innis
paras: Against Stafford at Sutton, the home side had the assistance of C. da L Innis, a West Indian Test cricketer, who was studying at Oxford.  During the season he had on occasions assisted the West Indies touring side.  In the match in question, he played a faultless innings of 100 not out and with N. Sharp (102) made a second wicket stand of 191.

entries.heading: C. Howl, N. Sharp & R.F. Barnes
paras: C. Howl and N. Sharp had a number of good opening partnerships during the season, whilst a brilliant innings of 94 not out by R.F. Barnes, at Wolverhampton, enabled Sutton to declare with 243 for 4 on the board.

entries.heading: Brevet Colonel L. C. Crockford, M.C., T.D. (retired)
paras: Brevet Colonel L. C. Crockford was born in Vesey Road, Wylde Green on July 4th 1887 – the year of Queen Victoria’s Jubilee.  His father was Arthur L. Crockford solicitor practicing in 71 Temple Row Birmingham, a member of the Town Council, and subsequently Mayor of the Royal Borough of Sutton Coldfield.
Leslie was educated at King Edward’s High School, Rugby School, and Cambridge University, and joined the profession of a solicitor in his father’s business.

He served in the Rugby School Cadet Corps, which was then affiliated to the 2nd Vll (now the 7th Battalion) The Royal Warwickshire Regiment, from 1902-1906, when he joined the Cambridge University Rifle Corps.   Here he very soon attracted the attention of the Adjutant, who

subsequently recommended him very strongly for a commission in the then newly formed Territorial Army.  He was gazetted second lieutenant in the 9th Bt. The Royal Warwickshire Regiment on Nov. 14th, 1908, and was posted to “Q" Company, then commanded by Captain P. G, Danielson.  Promoted lieutenant in 1912, he mobilized with his Battalion on the outbreak of War in August, 1914, and proceeded to France in March 1915.  He was very soon selected to act as assistant staff captain, in which he was attached to the brigade staff.

On June 1st, 1916, he was promoted captain, and on August 18th greatly distinguished himself at the battle of Ovillers (Somme), for which he was awarded the Military Cross.  Single handed front behind a bomb stop, with two men loading for him, he poured such fire into the flank of the enemy that he was very largely instrumental in bringing about their surrender.

entries.heading: The 6th Battalion “THE ANTELOPE”
paras: On Feb. 6th, 1917, Leslie was appointed staff captain to the 143rd (Warwickshire) Brigade, and on June 27th, 1918, brigade major, in which capacities he was present at the operations, on the Somme, in the Ypres Salient, and in Italy.  He obtained a brevet majority on June 3rd, 1918.
On Oct. 9th, 1918, he was appointed temporary major and D.A.Q.M.G. to the British Forces in Italy, which position he held until his return to England.
He was twice mentioned in dispatches and awarded the Italian Military Cross (Croce de Guerra).

On the reconstruction of the Territorial Army after the War, he rejoined his old unit and resumed command of his former company, which included (since the introduction of the double company system in 1914) Q " Company, in which he served before the War.
He was promoted to the substantive rank of major on Jan. 19th, 1921, and awarded the Territorial Decoration in 1924.
On Feb. 16th, 1928, he succeeded to the command of the 6th Battalion, on the retirement of Colonel J. L. Mellor, was promoted lieutenant-colonel, and on Feb. 16th, 1932, appointed brevet colonel.

His cheerful disposition won for him the affection of all ranks, and one of the nicest tributes that can be paid to him is to place on record that wherever he went, he was popular not only with the officers of the staff on which he was serving, but also retained his popularity with all the regimental officers with whom he came into contact.

This popularity persists until the present day, so that the severance of his connection with the Battalion in which he has served for well-nigh 25 years is cause for the unfeigned, regret of all who have ever served with him, either side of the war, retiring in 1933 as one of the founder members of the Territorial Army.
Leslie played his cricket at Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club alongside his father, Arthur Crockford and his younger brother, Eric Bertram Crockford.

entries.heading: R.F. Barnes had by this time fully established himself
paras: G.E. Richardson, a young cricketer of great promise as a batsman and wicketkeeper, unfortunately only had a short stay before going to Scotland.
H.M. Wilkinson had been doing exceedingly well for several years with the second team and came into the first Xl,
L.W. Stevenson, who was primarily a batsman but developing well as a medium pace seam bowler.
K. Mendl was also another useful bowler and very hard-hitting batsman.

entries.heading: D.G. Foster
paras: D.C. Foster, in his second year as captain, was able to play more regularly than in the previous year, when in fact, through an injured foot, he was unable to play at all.

entries.heading: Granville and Jerrim
paras: There were some high scoring games during the season, including a game at home against Leamington, the Sutton side in 125 minutes, ran up a score of 251 for 5.  Leamington, in reply, obtained the runs in exactly the same time for the loss of two wickets, thanks largely to a fine second wicket partnership of 226 by Granville and Jerrim, the former scoring 134 not out.

entries.heading: Barnes, Walters, Foster and Howl
paras: At Knowle, Sutton amassed the huge total of 297 for 4. Howl and Foster were associated in a second wicket partnership of 121, and Barnes and Walters 117 for the fifth wicket.  Knowle & Dorridge replied with 259 for 5, and altogether there were 556 runs scored in less than five hours cricket.

entries.heading: D.G. Foster & C Howl
paras: A first wicket partnership by D.G. Foster and C. Howl against Stafford at the Rectory Park realised 179 runs in eighty minutes, with Foster obtaining 125 of them.

entries.heading: R.E.S. Wyatt
paras: At Coventry, R.E.S. Wyatt, who was to captain England against Australia in the final Test at the Oval a few days later, skippered Coventry & N.W. on this occasion.  On a spinners wicket Wyatt won the toss and put Sutton in to bat and largely thanks to Tom Greening Sutton were dismissed for 23.  Tom was undoubtedly the best left arm spin bowler in club cricket over a long period, and combined with his captain's (J. Morton) field placing he was a difficult bowler to play on any wicket.

entries.heading: N. Sharp
paras: After Kings Heath had declared at 238 for 8, N. Sharp scored 108 not out of Sutton's 135 for 3, whilst only 18 runs were made from the bat of the other Sutton batsmen.

entries.heading: C. Howl & N. Sharp
paras: Due chiefly to an opening stand of 157 by Howl and Sharp, Wolverhampton were defeated by nine wickets at Sutton.

entries.heading: R.F. Barnes
paras: In the drawn return match against Wolverhampton R.F. Barnes scored a brilliant 101 not out.

entries.heading: Free Foresters
paras: After a long absence from the ground of their birth the Free Foresters fixture was renewed with a two-day fixture in July.  They brought a strong side including about six players with first class cricket experience.   Against the weak attack of the home side, they recorded the highest score made on the Rectory Park ground, 364, and defeated the home club by an innings and 17 runs.

entries.heading: F.B. CLARK
paras: This was F.B. Clark's last season. At the end he quietly retired from active participation after twenty-eight years continuous service, apart from the war years.  He had a brilliant playing career, one cannot say he was a “natural” cricketer he attained his greatness by making a devoted study of the game and by the practice and perseverance in what he learned, and was always a most regular attender at the nets.  He was one of the finest all-round cricketers in the history of the club.  He aimed at the top in every activity in which he was interested by making this characteristic study of the job in hand, and it is of interest that he obtained an ice-skating gold medal (at a considerably advanced age for this sport) and also reached the top at ball room dancing.

entries.heading: FREE FORESTERS
paras: An excellent game with the Free Foresters in June ended in a closely drawn match. Though the Sutton side was not very representative of the members they scored 256 and 207 for 6 declared, to which the Foresters replied with 272 and l83 for 5, thus falling short by seven runs.
Peter Cranmer (Captain of WCCC after WW2) batted exceedingly well for the Foresters with innings of 104 and 57 not out.

In the evening of the first day, the Mayor, Councilor W.A. Perry, entertained the players and officials to dinner at the Masonic Hall.  A special guest at the function was the Rev A.E.R. Bedford, who had returned to the district as Vicar of Boldmere after a long period as Vicar of Morley in Derbyshire.

entries.heading: A.G.K. BROWN
paras: Arthur Godfrey Kilner Brown of 146 Rectory Road a 1936 a gold Olympian played in June1937 played for the Sutton Club & Ground side against the school.  Looking through the club’s old scorebooks and press cuttings it appears that Godfrey played a limited number of games for Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club during the 1933 - 1939 period taking a few wickets and getting some runs

entries.heading: H.E. Robinson
paras: H.E. Robinson used to lock up the pavilion on week days and he relates a story of one dark night he came to the ground for this purpose when a ghostly figure fled past him.  He gave chase, and though no mean runner himself, he soon realised he was losing ground.  Finally, he managed to head off the figure by taking a short cut, when he discovered it was Godfrey Brown doing his training in Rectory Park.

entries.heading: Sir A.H. Evans
paras: Alfred Evans, president of the club since his election in 1929, passed away during the year, at the age of 88. His death after a record membership period of sixty-six years severed the link between the present and the earlier years of the club. A fine cricketer in his prime as a forceful batsman and good wicketkeeper, he had rendered a great service to the club, and even nearly up to the time of his death had rarely missed seeing at least part of a match at Rectory Park.  He was a local doctor of medicine, a pillar of the church, and in 1891 was Mayor of the town.  He received his knighthood for services to the town.

entries.heading: R.S. Walters
paras: R.S. Walters who had had forty-six years association with the club was honoured with Life Membership.  In thanking the members, he indulged in some reminiscences.  After modestly admitting his abilities as a wicketkeeper, he said that when he was Hon treasurer his duties were combined with those of groundsman.  The construction of the area now known as the lower ground was his responsibility, and in those days the ground was mown only once a year, for the Trinity Monday sports. The batsmen frequently ran sixes for balls hit into the long grass, where often as not the ball disappeared down a rabbit hole, and the Rectory Park at that time was overrun with the pest.  There was also a deep watercourse between the two grounds which ran into the pool in the south west corner. Before the ravine was filled in it was quite a common experience for a visiting fielder, unused to the ground, to disappear into the ravine after heavy rain.

entries.heading: G.V. Swift
paras: G.V. Swift was elected captain of the 1st team.  He was in his day an outstanding wicketkeeper.

entries.heading: FREE FORESTERS
paras: An interesting two-day fixture with the Free Foresters ended in a drawn game, Sutton scoring 244 and 227 for 6 dec., to which the Foresters replied with 238 and 181 for 5.

entries.heading: D.G. Foster
paras: At Knowle & Dorridge both sides lost seven wickets for less than 100 runs, yet in both instances the eighth wickets added more than 70.  D.G. Foster, batting number 10 for Sutton, made 81 not out in forty-four minutes.

entries.heading: Roy Baker
paras: Roy Baker in a hurricane innings against Stafford hit 6 sixes & 9 fours in a score of 89.

entries.heading: W. Bigwood
paras: Alderman Wilfred Bigwood M.C. was elected President in succession to Sir Alfred Evans.  Though never having played for the club he was nevertheless, a useful cricketer with Barnt Green in his younger days.  He was a prominent personality in the town and greatly interested in its many activities.

entries.heading: C. Howl
paras: Clifford Howl was elected captain and with the material at his disposal at low ebb (at least for Sutton) he led the side with great skill and initiative and his shrewd knowledge of the game enabled ten matches to be won. It is of particular interest that no games were left unfinished, probably a unique record for senior club cricket in the Midlands, at least in modern times.

entries.heading: N.F. Prosser
paras: N.F. Prosser made a fine maiden century at Stratford upon Avon and assisted by E.H. Walters (87 not out) they had an unfinished partnership of about 200 runs for the fifth wicket.  (NB. The actual partnership figure has not been ascertained; it is not indicated in the score book)

entries.heading: C. Howl
paras: C. Howl was re-elected captain at the Annual General Meeting before the 1939 season commenced.

entries.heading: F. Styles and D.H. Twiss
paras: D.H. Twiss was appointed Hon treasurer in succession to Frank Styles, who had for the past ten years looked after the financial side of the club's affairs:  During his period of office F Styles had initiated and collected many of the early records incorporated in this survey.  D.H. Twiss carried on, but due to the war he was unable to proceed very far.  The meeting passed a unanimous vote of thanks to F. Styles for the services he had rendered to the club, and also to D.H. Twiss for the efficient way he had carried out his sometimes-exasperating duties as Hon team secretary for the past four years.

entries.heading: REV. A.E.R. Bedford
paras: The last remaining link with the Founder, the Rev. A.E.R. Bedford, passed away during the year, though, subsequently, the connection was renewed when two of the grandsons of the Rev. W.K.R. Bedford were elected vice presidents, and incidentally they were the sons of A.E.R.

entries.heading: H.L. MORTIMORE
paras: H.L. Mortimore, who had had a long and glorious "innings" in the game also died during the year.  With Hitler marching and taking over various parts of Europe the season opened on a somber note.  Would there be war before the cricket season was over?  As all know, Britain declared war on Germany on the 3rd of September, and cricket was brought to an abrupt end and the last three fixtures were cancelled.

entries.heading: Roy Baker
paras: In a drawn game at Tettenhall, Sutton was faring badly against Wolverhampton's declaration of 214 for 7, when Roy Baker arrived at the wicket.  In forty-three minutes, he scored 97 by brilliant forcing cricket, before being caught on the boundary off a hit which almost gave him what would surely have been one of the fastest centuries on record.

entries.heading: At Olton, the following week he scored 71 runs in thirty minutes
paras: After serving in the forces throughout the war, Baker took up a business appointment in the North of England and played a considerable amount of cricket for Northumberland.

entries.heading: Sharp and Farmer
paras: The Whit Monday game with Ashfield was memorable. Sutton declared at 245 for 8 (Sharp 95 not out and Farmer 41 not out shared a ninth wicket partnership of 67) and Ashfield knocked off the runs without losing a wicket.

John Hacking and John Brownsdon both made centuries and recorded the highest partnership on the Rectory Park ground 246, which beat by three runs the partnership of Spencer and Hiatt for Stratford upon Avon in 1933.

entries.heading: R.F. BARNES
paras: R.F. Barnes had a good season with both the bat and the ball, though, as is often the case with reliable men, he did not frequently hit the headlines with spectacular performances. Apart from his cricket, his genial personality and modest nature were much missed when he was unable to return to Sutton after the war.

entries.heading: P.I. TERRY
paras: For the past few years Paul Terry had been a tower of strength to the bowling of the first team.  Slow and left arm over the wicket, he caused the downfall of many good batsmen, particularly with the "Chinaman".  His most noteworthy performances were 8 for 31 against Olton in 1936, 6 for 10 against Kings Heath, and 6 for 20 at Stafford.
A little Information on the 2nd & "A" TEAMS  1930 - 1939.

entries.heading: H.P. Gardner
paras: During the period 1930 – 1934 the Second Eleven was led by H.P. Gardner, a very successful and popular captain and was a very able batsman and wicketkeeper.

entries.heading: F.H. BEARDSHAW
paras: F.H.  Beardshaw took over the captaincy of the 2nd team for three years 1935 -37. As mentioned previously, his best days were spent in league cricket but he was still a good all-round cricketer and possessed a sound knowledge of the game.  Though still worthy of a 1st Xl place he put the interests of the club before those of himself and by his captaincy was able to impart his experience to the younger members.

entries.heading: R.M. WILKINSON
paras: R.M. Wilkinson captained the side 2nd team in 1938 and 1939.  A good all-round cricketer, but he never quite established himself as a regular first eleven player. Although he had many fine games with both teams.  His highest score was 116 against Knowle & Dorridge in 1932, and in the following year he took 6 Ashfield wickets for 20 in a first eleven match.

entries.heading: A.J. TERRY
paras: A.J. Terry was a capable batsman and wicketkeeper over a long period for the second team, and a most entertaining member of the side.

entries.heading: D.H. TWISS
paras: Throughout the 1930’s with the second and “A” teams H. Twiss was an outstanding batsman who made a lot of runs.  Unorthodox, in his style, he was nevertheless a difficult batsman to dislodge, and he made several centuries.  He was also a keen and reliable worker for the club.

entries.heading: P.I. TERRY
paras: Before P.I. Terry, became a regular first team player, was often a devastating bowler for the second team.

entries.heading: R. SIDNEY
paras: P. Sidney (son of W H Sidney, groundsman, coach, and player for many years) gave great promise in his youth but did not develop quite as anticipated; but all the same he was a good pace bowler and a batsman who could turn a game by his forceful batting, and he had a number of seasons in the first eleven.

Other players to assist the second eleven during the period under review, all with considerable success, were: - W.P. Richardson; G.T. Jones; G.I. Richardson; G.B. Tuckwell; P.D. Sadler; S.W. and H.W. Homer.

entries.heading: Jim Terry, V.A. Beardshaw and R. Sidney
paras: Against Stafford 2nd in 1932, Sutton 2nd was struggling, when Jim Terry joined V.A. Beardshaw (son of F H) the score was 93 for 7, but these two added 53 for the eighth wicket, and this was followed by an unfinished partnership of 88 for the ninth wicket by Beardshaw and R. Sidney.

entries.heading: Paul Terry and E.F. Miles
paras: The 2nd Xl in the 1933 season Paul Terry and E.F. Miles took the score from 96 for 8 to 169 for 9.

entries.heading: D.H. Twiss and J.R. Sparkes
paras: In 1936 D.H. Twiss and J.R. Sparkes were associated in a large stand for the second wicket against Cheadle Royal, a touring side.  The visitors made 185, Sutton lost their first wicket before a run was scored, and then Twiss and Sparkes proceeded to 165 at which point the game came to an end with their partnership unbroken.

Against the Midland Bank, Sutton, having scored 152, looked set for a comfortable victory when the visitors were 118 for 9 although the first pair had given them a good start by putting on 80 for the opening partnership, but the last wicket added 37 to win the match.

entries.heading: F. Styles & the “A” Team
paras: Frank Styles was the outstanding character in the "A" team during the decade. Skippering the side for a number of years was not an easy task in those days. The senior elevens had first call on replacements for players crying off, and the third team was frequently three or four men short an hour or two before the match was due to start. Styles often had to run round the district after his bank closed in order to complete his team.  There are not many records of the “A” team cricket in those days but it was known they had rather a lean time, largely because they never had a settled side.

entries.heading: O.H. Grove & W.P. Richardson
paras: O.H. Grove also captained the “A” team for a period and some valuable work for the club amongst the junior members, as also did W.P. Richardson.

entries.heading: JOHN I HAVE LEFT THIS IN ALTHOUGH YOU MAY HAVE COVERED BELOW
paras: The following article, I believe published in the Sutton Coldfield News in 1961 concerning the demolition of the Rectory in Rectory Park in 1936 which I have scanned into this history of SCCCC without changing any of the wording or the English – Peter Bell, the Club’s Historian
“Ghosts” Of The Town’s Past Enshrined In Old Rectory

This is the last picture ever taken of Sutton Coldfield's Old Rectory, just as demolition was about to begin. The timely picture was taken by Mr. W. Strange, then the " News " reporter in the town, now living in retirement at Rugby.
How many readers remember the old Sutton Coldfield Rectory? It stood on a site near the parish church of Holy Trinity for 235 years until demolished just a quarter of a century ago.

Its disappearance in 1936 was deeply deplored, as the disappearance of older buildings in the Royal Town is still deplored today. but one writer at the time pointed out that "one salutary result, if only one." of its disappearance was that Rectory Road would "properly run" towards the present Rectory, opposite its Coleshill Street end, and not away towards a lone. forgotten and nameless old house hidden by giant elms."

This writer recalled that in a day when Sutton Coldfield was sometimes Sutton Colefield, and Birmingham was not yet "Brum." when seven miles of leafy lanes separated them, the new young Rector of Sutton Coldfield John Riland, decided it was time to build a new Rectory. It may have been that he saw before him a long line of Rilands and Riland Bedfords. and wished to consolidate the family interests with those of the fine old parish church; or it may have been that the existing Rectory —described in a volume of 1671 as equal to the best of the residences in the place, not excepting even New Hall — had grown a little loose in the joints.

Whatever the reason, John Riland, without cost to his parishioners, contracted in 1701 for building, a new Parsonage house 45 feet long, 35feet deep and 23 feet high, at a cost of £239 11s 9d.—the price including a tall wall around the front court.

The original wall disappeared a hundred years ago when a new wing was added to the Rectory; and now the Rectory and wing are fast disappearing beneath the demolisher’s hammer to make building land, and in a few weeks will be no more. "He wrote: "The Rector of Sutton, some years ago, moved to a smaller house beside the church, and since then the old Rectory has been a somewhat pathetic hybrid."

Referring to the demolition then in, progress, he wrote: "It may be doubted if the muscular demolishers or the white-flannelled cricketers who repair to the still lovely and leafy old Rectory Park on these summer evenings, realise what memoried ghosts may stalk in the skeleton of the rose-hued brick, so gaunt, now amid its tall elms and weed-stocked garden.Its ,tenants in the far off days were no mere passive parsons, content with the half-mile walk to the church and i an occasional amble round the parish, or a horse canter to Lichfield. Some of them, and in particular this progressive John Riland, were keenly political, and there is no knowing what highly seasoned talk flowed across the oak-panelled dining parlour of the new Rectory, nor what lordly personages rode across their parks and the parson's rich glebe lands to its elegant Queen Anne porch. For John Riland was I a stout Jacobite."

How stout may be gauged from a book, he adds. "Three Hundred Years of a Family Living," published in 1889 by the Rev. W. K. Riland Bedford, wherein it is related that hand-writing, strongly suspect of being John Riland's left a revealing marginal note opposite a passage in an old volume in the Rectory library. The passage ran : "Henry I, surnamed Beauclark for his learning. was wont to say that an unlearned king was a 'crowned asse" The marginal comment in about the year when George I was crowned ran: If so what of our King George.?”

entries.heading: Jacobite
paras: But there are stronger reasons even than that for believing that Rector John Riland was not enamoured of the Hanoverian succession, continued the article. Most of the neighbouring country gentlemen favoured the Jacobite  cause, and it is narrated in the Rev.W. K. Riland Bedford’s book (which, incidentally is a delightfully written piece of local history, and may be seen at the Birmingham Reference Library that they were wont to meet and toast the cause in a club at Coleshill, where Dr Kettlewell , the celebrated non-juror, for some time was Vicar.

There was naturally much excitement, therefore, when the even more celebrated Dr. Sacheverell, after his suspension in 1709 for a violently political sermon in St. Paul's Cathedral came to live at New Hall, Sutton—a countryside well known to him, since once he had been the handsome curate of Cannock. He contracted life-long friendships in the district during the years that followed, and although he made a spectacular "come-back" by being appointed to the prosperous living of St. Andrew's, Holborn, London, in 1713. he was so far from forgetting his old friends that he agreed to preach in Sutton Coldfield Church on October 20, 1714—the Sunday before the Coronation of George 1.

entries.heading: Rectory plot?
paras: This could have been no piece of chance kindliness towards old friends on his part: it must have been the culmination of a "plot" probably hatched in that charming and sedate new rectory at Sutton; for over 200 Birmingham Jacobites attended the service and heard his eloquence en masse.

“The consequences appeared a day or two afterwards,” recorded Dr. Tindal,”a scandalous riot and attack on the dissenting places of worship in the town of Birmingham." None may say whether, by then, Dr. Sacheverell had returned to Holborn, or was still sipping his port at Sutton Coldfield Rectory, but it is a pretty piece of Sutton history, and as one watches the gaps appearing in the
old Rectory House it is curious to reflect how for more than two centuries these old walls have kept their ghosts so close-penned.

entries.heading: Apothecary
paras: The John Riland who was its author, was very popular in the district. His father, also John Riland, had been appointed Rector of St. Martin's, Birmingham. at a moment in the history of that parish when it had fallen, according to Hutton, into a sad state owing to the ministrations of "a broken apothecary and a man of very inferior calibre in all respects."

The younger John was appointed Rector of Sutton in 1689. He must have found it a pleasant enough s and quite lucrative living, judging by a venerable and yellowing document written in ink, now preserved in Birmingham Library.

This is a "Terrier of the house, outhouses, barnes, gleab lanes and tithes and other profits belonging to the Rector of the Rectory and Parish Church of Sutton Coldfield, and by Mr. John Riland, Rector, and Thomas Gold and John Veasey, Churchwardens, according to the book of articles given them by the Rt. Rev. Father in God, William II' Lord Bishop of Coventrie and Lichfield, at his visitation, held in the
Parish Church of Coleshill, on August 4, 1698."

entries.heading: Beautiful hand
paras: It is a fascinating bit of work in beautiful handwriting. It names al fields in the Rectory glebes—such charming names as Blabb's Close, Gilbert's Close, Calves' Close—and all the still surviving though differently spelled outposts of the parish —“Many and the Wild." Beyond the it Wood." “-Wormley," and the "Fee of Wiginshill"—and all the land-owning and farming parisioners with, in each case, the exact amount of tithes and dues they had to pay.

The amounts range down to such small sums as twopence. There are some minute directions as to assessment—thus “the tenth of all corne is paid to the Rector, except the corne which grows in the Fee of Wiginshill, of which two-thirds are paid to the Rector and the other third to the Improprietor of Curdworth; also, “everie tenth fleece of woll as it falls from the sheep, and according to ancient custom, the is one fleece due to the Rector out of seven and two out of seventeene.”  The above is how it was recorded – not my bad spelling
HI  JOHN  Back to the names
Largely due to the delayed call up to the forces or a number of the older members Sutton were able to field two teams in 1940, and some very enjoyable cricket resulted.

entries.heading: D.G. Foster
paras: A exciting game with Olton ended in a TIE with both sides scores of 87 all out. D.G. Foster making 47 not out.

entries.heading: N. Sharp and D.H. Twiss
paras: Against Kings Heath, Sutton declared at 245 for 2, E.F. Twiss (55 not out) and N. Sharp (115 not out) being associated in an unfinished stand for the third wicket of 152.  Sharp batted through the innings for the second successive week.

entries.heading: A.J. Terry & R.M. Wilkinson
paras: Most of the previous season's officers were in charge of the club during this year except that A.J. Terry had taken over the 2nd X1 captaincy from R.M. Wilkinson.

entries.heading: GEORGE SHARP
paras: George Sharp died in February of this year.  In 1904, business reasons brought him from Derby to Sutton, and during his thirty-seven years with the club he rendered many services.  As a cricketer he was a good batsman and useful slow bowler.  He played very little first team cricket but captained the 2nd X1 from 1907 to 1921, apart from the war years when there was only one team.  He was Hon secretary for eight years and fixture secretary for fourteen, but perhaps his greatest work for the club was performed during the First World War when he made himself mainly responsible for maintaining the existence of the club and the ground.  Upon his retirement from business, he devoted much of his spare time to the improvement of the amenities, including, amongst other things, the enlargement of the pavilion enclosure and the erection of the wooden fence, and the making of flower beds.  In 1926 he was honoured with Life Membership.

The war had taken a more serious turn and many more members had joined the forces, and enemy bombers were frequent visitors.  By the commencement of the season it was known that it would be difficult to raise even one team as most of the members who were left were either doing war work on Saturdays or were engaged on Civil Defence duties.
