However, thirteen matches were played, mostly against local clubs or war time units, none of which call for any serious comment.
There were no official meetings of the club held between April 1940 and March 1942, and the club merely carried on “On a hand to mouth basis”.
No information

entries.heading: Frank Styles
paras: Frank Styles, who had done so much for the club during the past decade retired from business in the early days of the war and moved to his residence at Borth y Gest in his beloved Snowdonia.  His house was temporarily taken over by evacuee children and during this period he took up residence at a cottage on the shores of Nant Gwynant.  It was here that the writer visited him one sunny summer afternoon.  All seemed so peaceful after the turmoil of life in the Midlands, and the remark had no sooner been made when there was a terrific burst of machine gun fire across the lake, and the peaceful afternoon was at an end. It transpired that Commandos were undergoing their training.  Upon his departure from Sutton, Frank Styles was honoured with Life Membership.

entries.heading: Paul Terry and L.W. Stevenson
paras: The cricket during the period produced little worthy of mention.  No big scores were made largely on account of the uncut outfield and the wickets which were of an inferior standard through lack of preparation.  Paul Terry and L.W. Stevenson were two bowlers well above the average of war time cricket, and both of them took a lot of wickets, a factor which enabled more games to be won than lost

entries.heading: N. Sharp, Wilkinson, Stevenson & Thompson
paras: There was a match at the County Ground in 1944 with the SCCC played against the Castle Bromwich Aero Factory.  C.B.A.F batted first on a good wicket to the bowling of Stevenson and Wilkinson.  For the first forty minutes runs came freely at a run a minute.

With no recognised change bowlers in the side Norman Sharp went on to turn his arm over.  In his third over N. Kilner, late Warwickshire’s opening batsman was caught for 38 of the 45 runs for the first wicket. The next seven wickets fell to Sharp (all bowled) for no runs in three overs, and with Stevenson taking two at the other end, C.B.A.F. were all out for 52. Until the last pair, who added five runs, nine wickets had fallen whilst two runs were scored.
Sharp's full analysis was eight for ten.  Sutton won comfortably. Wilkinson going on to score 75 not out and with C.B. Thompson added 85 for the seventh wicket without being separated.

entries.heading: N. Sharp & Swift
paras: In a match against the Royal Air Force (Sutton) G.V. Swift and N. Sharp made 102 for the second wicket, and as the outfield was long grass no boundaries were scored and every run had to be run.

entries.heading: L.W. Stevenson, P.Terry & Sharp
paras: In May 45 and the war over, L.W. Stevenson relinquished the secretarial-ship which he had held throughout the war years in favour of P. Terry, who accomplished a tremendous amount of work both in his official capacity and on the ground, and he was ably assisted by N. Sharp and a few others.  By the end of the season considerable progress had been made though there was still a long way to go.

entries.heading: E.H. Walters
paras: There were several prominent pre-war members who did not return in an active capacity.  One of these was E.H. (Ted) Walters, one of the outstanding members in the period between the two wars.  Not only was he a fine batsman and wicketkeeper he also rendered wonderful service to the club in an administrative capacity as Hon secretary for eleven years, a period of service only equaled, to date, by William Fowler in the last century.  Mention should be made, however, that Walters did play a few times during this season.

entries.heading: D.G. Foster
paras: Derek C.T. Foster was another personality who was unable to play again after the war.  In a parachute jump he was injured and it left him unfit to resume.  His great abilities as a cricketer were very much missed.

entries.heading: R.F. Barnes
paras: Frank Barnes, too, was sadly missed when he went to reside in Worcestershire.

entries.heading: C. Hawkins, B.T. Wood, F.E. Whitfield, F.L. Bindon, and N. Dainty
paras: During the war the Civil Defence services in the Sutton area formed a cricket side and played a number of games against the club, and when the organisation disbanded after the cessation of hostilities a number of their members joined Sutton, and some played important parts in the club in subsequent years.  Amongst these were C. Hawkins, B.T. Wood, F.E. Whitfield, F.L. Bindon, and N. Dainty.

entries.heading: N. Dainty, P.I. Terry, L.W. Stevenson, P.P. Ashcroft, &B.T. Wood
paras: Of the seventeen matches played by the first team nine were won.  The batting strength was of a low standard, but the bowling was extremely good and the success of the side depended almost entirely on this department.  At a time when most of the best cricketers were still in the forces the club was very fortunate to possess such a varied and good attack in N. Dainty (fast left arm), P.I. Terry (slow left arm), L.W. Stevenson (right arm seamer), and P.P. Ashcroft (right arm “seamer” & off spinner), with B.T. Wood supplying the slow right arm spinners.

Norman Dainty had a particularly good match against Ashfield.  He participated in a ninth wicket stand with P. Terry of nearly 50 enabling Sutton to total 107.  He followed this by taking 7 wickets for 6 runs and was mainly instrumental in dismissing Ashfield for 28.
B.T. Wood, against Kynoch C.C., performed the "hat trick".

entries.heading: Clifford Howl
paras: During the winter the pavilion was re-thatched in straw at a cost of £40 which was generously paid for by Clifford Howl.

entries.heading: T. Nicholas & W.H. Sidney
paras: T. Nicholas was engaged as groundsman, and though he had little expert knowledge he was a good worker, and W.H. Sidney, now getting on in years and unable to do as much as in the past, was paid to help him and to give him advice.

entries.heading: Paul Terry and E.B. Crockford
paras: After considerable negotiations in which Paul Terry and E.B. Crockford played important parts) a twenty-one-year lease was granted by the Sutton Corporation, one, behind the scenes A.E. Terry also rendered invaluable services. Through his influence, too, the Corporation purchased two ex-army huts which were erected on the ground and for which the club paid an annual rental.  One hut was used for the storage of the ground equipment and the other replaced the old tea room which had disintegrated during the war.

entries.heading: Peter Cranmer, Tom Pritchard and Eric Hollies
paras: The first match of the season was against almost the full Warwickshire County Cricket Club led by Peter Cranmer.  In sustaining a heavy defeat, the out of practice Sutton team had no answer to the pace of Tom Pritchard and the spin of Eric Hollies.

entries.heading: Roy Strivens
paras: In the 1st season of Sunday cricket, the 1st XL at Avery's. Roy Strivens, a very good all-round cricketer who had played for the Erdington club in pre-war days, performed the “hat trick”, and later made a fine 112 runs not out in a closely fought draw game at Pickwick.

entries.heading: Paul Terry
paras: P. Terry, in his first over at Pickwick, and bowling first change, dismissed the first three batsmen for a "hat trick”.  He followed this up with two more wickets in the next over, all at a cost of no runs. His final figures were 7 for 29. “The author does not know if Strivens & Terry played in the same match at Pickwick.”

entries.heading: George Swift
paras: The name of George Swift has not appeared on these pages many times for the reason that his performances both on and off the field were more of a reliable than of a spectacular nature.  Playing his earlier cricket in the London area he came to Sutton in 1936 after a few years with Coventry & N W.  He was a splendid wicketkeeper doing all his work in such an unostentatious manner that his brilliance often passed unnoticed, and he was a very useful batsman too.  He was one of the few who helped to keep the club together during the war, and in the post war period of rebuilding he performed his part and gave maximum support to the money raising efforts as every good club man should.  During the current season he played in fourteen first team matches and throughout the season conceded only nine byes and obtained nearly thirty victims, a remarkable achievement in any cricket.
It is of interest that throughout the present century (20th), at least, the club has always been fortunate to have wicketkeepers of first-class ability.

entries.heading: Alec Warren
paras: The Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club had allowed their ground to be used for the playing of the final of the Sutton Coldfield Youth Clubs an inter club competition. In the 1946 the league winners were “The Royal Youth Club” and their captain Alec Warren, was presented with the league trophy.

entries.heading: Roddy Wilson
paras: Roddy Wilson played cricket in his early youth, who turned to umpiring when he was stricken with Polio while in Junior school. This meant he had to walk with callipers on both legs and with the aid of sticks. He umpired at the Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club in the 1950 & 60’s before umpiring in the Minor Counties League which was followed by two seasons umpiring in the 1st class game. I Peter, the writer of the Club’s history was a Member of the MCC and met up with Roddy when he was umpiring a 1st class game at Lords in July – August 1977 and I was I was based in Wembley.  Roddy died while on holiday in France on 24th August 2001 at the age of 69. So, he would have been born around 1932, and in 1946 he would be 14 years of age.

entries.heading: THE CENTENARY YEAR & COMMITTEE
paras: Before and during the early part of the season an extra effort was made by the members to complete the major repairs necessary in readiness for the season that was to become memorable.  A full report by the captain in the Centenary year appears in the Minute
The officers elected at the Annual General Meeting were: -
President, Ald. Wilfred Bigwood MC. J.P.
Hon Sec P.I. Terry,
Joint Hon Treasurers, A.B. Heywood and B. Cooke,
Captain 1st Xl, N. Sharp,          Captain 2nd Xl B.T. Wood.

entries.heading: M. R. Strivens
paras: M. R. Strivens was proving a decided acquisition particularly as a batsman, and though a useful bowler he had little opportunity of displaying his ability, for the side contained a good variety of bowling.

entries.heading: L.W. Stevenson
paras: L.W. Stevenson had a fine season with the ball in taking 86 wickets for 12.1 runs during the season, including 15 for 90 in the two-day fixture with the Free Foresters, and though he made quite a lot of runs he was not fulfilling the early expectations anticipated of him as a batsman.

entries.heading: P. Ashcroft and V.G. Gabriel
paras: A first wicket partnership of 131 by P. Ashcroft and V.G. Gabriel was the outstanding feature of the game at Leamington.  There was an exciting finish at Knowle & Dorridge where the last batsman came in with four runs required and one ball to go to pass Sutton’s total of 200.  Having a “go” he was stumped.

entries.heading: C. Howl
paras: Clifford Howl retired as a player at the end of the season.  He did not commence to play the game until he was in his twenties, and for many years played in the star-studded Wolverhampton eleven, and where by sheer practice and determination he attained his Staffordshire County cap.

Leaving the Wolverhampton club, he joined Sutton in 1930, and played many fine innings for the club of his adoption, and rendered many excellent services too.  Though not a polished batsman he made a lot of runs and had many good opening partnerships with N. Sharp as his opening partner in the ten years prior to the war.  He was still a good cricketer upon his retirement at over sixty years of age.
Restart here

entries.heading: Free Foresters
paras: In the two-day match with the Free Foresters the visitors were Captained by E.H. Riland Bedford, grandson of the founder of both clubs, and the side also included his brother Peter Bedford. N. Sharp and W.E. Houghton put on 108 for the first wicket, until C H Palmer, who later captained England was given the ball.  He promptly took six wickets, but a stand by M.R. Strivens and E.H. Walters raised the score to 199 for 6 declared, thanks to L.W. Stevenson's fine bowling the Foresters were all out for 83 and followed on making 126 in their second innings. Sutton won comfortably by nine wickets. On the Thursday evening the teams were entertained to Dinner at the Royal Hotel, and this was followed by a club dance at the Town Hall.

entries.heading: W. Bigwood
paras: At the Centenary Dance in 1947 the president, W. Bigwood, had been presented with one of the balls used in the Centenary match against the Free Foresters.

entries.heading: Olton
paras: It was a miserable day on the Saturday with Olton as visitors.  Play started at 12.30 pm, but with the players in and out of the pavilion all afternoon the Olton innings was not closed until 6.5pm at 115 for 7.

Another delay followed and Sutton was left with 55 minutes batting.  Sutton obtained the runs in another exciting finish on the stroke of time and with seven wickets in hand, J.H. Odell making 57 in thirty minutes, a grand climax to the week's cricket.

entries.heading: The End of 100 Years of History
paras: And so, we come to the end of the first hundred years of the Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club. The writer has endeavored" to chronicle the principal events in its history, but obviously, with limited information of the earlier years, these records must be incomplete.

It would have been a proud day for the Rev. W.K. Riland Bedford and his family, had they been alive to appreciate the results of their pioneer work, and to know that the two clubs of their foundation, the Free Foresters and Sutton Coldfield, as well as many members of both, had become famed throughout the world of cricket.
2nd Xl

There is not much to say about Second Eleven cricket during this short post war period.  It was largely a case of rebuilding and bringing along some of the younger members, which they did, and D. Norton, V.G. Gabriel, and G.A. Pritchett were later to play important roles in the club.  The same can be said of the "A" team except that their cricket was not particularly good, for the lower ground had not recovered from the neglect during the war.

The commencement of the second century brought with it new hopes aid promises of better things.  The ground, though still under standard, was rapidly improving from the war years through the efforts of the members, whilst the playing strength was also getting steadily better.  Some clubs had recovered earlier than Sutton and at about this time one or two of the old established fixtures were in danger of being discontinued by the opposition.  Fortunately, the club survived the threats, for a renewal of the fixtures would have been a major problem once the club had regained its feet.

entries.heading: Officers
paras: S Wilfred Bigwood was re-elected president, and with Paul Terry continuing his untiring work as Hon secretary, B. Cooke, Hon treasurer, and N. Sharp, captain.  It was generally conceded that the interests of the club were in capable hands. But there was a lot of reconstruction yet to be done.

Primarily the financial position had to be improved, for without this no organisation can flourish or progress. A successful sweepstake followed by a December dance in the Town Hall helped to improve matters, and further repairs to the property, long overdue, were put in hand to a limited amount.

entries.heading: T. Nicholas
paras: T. Nicholas was re-engaged as groundsman and because of the shortage of this type of labour, and the easy money obtainable in industry; it became necessary to retain him throughout the winter months. This was naturally a severe strain on the resources of the club. Until this time, it had always been possible to discontinue the groundman’s services for five months of the year.

entries.heading: N. Sharp
paras: The other ball used in the 1947 match with the Free Forresters was suitably mounted and presented to the captain Norman Sharp at the Annual General Meeting of 1948.

entries.heading: F.H.R. and P.R. Bedford
paras: At the AGM in 1948 an important addition to the historical records took place. There was a presentation to the Club an etching of the founder, W.K.R. Bedford by his grandsons, F.H.R. and P.R. Bedford. The etching was executed by C. W. Ashmore in 1894, who resident in Clifton Road, Sutton Coldfield. Written on back of etching was the following details: - No. 8 cut. mt oval. 1 in Oak & Gilt. Paid 3/9. This etching is still proudly displayed in the Pavilion lounge in the center above the BAR.

entries.heading: W. Bigwood
paras: The sudden death of the President, Alderman Wilfred Bigwood in the early part of the year (1948) in Germany, was not only a great loss to the club but also to the town he had served so well for many years.  Amongst his many activities he had been Mayor, an Alderman of the Warwickshire County Council, Colonel of the Home guard during the War, and a leading personality in many of the town's activities.  He did not play cricket for Sutton, but was a feared opponent in the days when he played for Barnt Green CC.

entries.heading: A.E. Terry
paras: Alderman Arthur E Terry was unanimously elected as his successor.  Like his predecessor he was a leading citizen in the Royal Town, had occupied the Mayoral Chair, and had taken a leading part in most Civic matters and many sporting organizations and was still doing so. A few years after this date he was accorded the highest honour the Town can bestow. He was elected a Freeman of the Borough.  But it was not because of his great influence in the town that he was accorded the honour of presidency. It was by virtue of his long association with Sutton cricket as a player, administrator, and sportsman, and by his lovable and genial personality, that his election became almost automatic, After a period with Four Oak All Saints, he joined Sutton in 1914, and was a good medium pace bowler and a capable batsman, but more than anything, he loved his cricket, Two of his sons Jim and Paul, were playing leading roles in the activities of the club at the time of his election.

entries.heading: I.H. Hobbs
paras: Ivor Hobbs, son of Sir J B Hobbs, became a member, and though very popular, he did not compare favorably, as a cricketer, with his illustrious father.

entries.heading: Sharp & Strivens
paras: Only N. Sharp completed the season with an average exceeding 20, but against Olton he and M.R. Strivens partnered in a record (to date) stand of 162, for the third wicket.

entries.heading: L.W. Stevenson, P.I. Terry, and P.P. Ashcroft
paras: It was the bowling of L.W. Stevenson, P.I. Terry, and P.P. Ashcroft that enabled the team to make a fight of a number of matches. Ashcroft, in particular, had excellent performances with 8 for 17 against Kings Heath, and 7 for 18 against Ashfield.

entries.heading: Sharp
paras: Sometimes the unexpected happens at all games. One such incident occurred against Aldridge at Rectory Park when N. Sharp, who was never considered a bowler of any merit, took 9 for 35.  Sutton had declared at the moderate score of 158 for 7.  Aldridge had reached 50 without loss but were behind the clock.  At such times it is the captain’s privilege to toss a few up.  Sharp did just this and the first six batsmen “holed out” in quick succession. Having had the longest spell of bowling in his career, the openers were re-introduced into the attack, but without success, with ten minutes remaining Sharp again took the ball and secured three more victims before time was called with the Aldridge score at 95 for 9.

entries.heading: B.H. King
paras: At Stratford upon Avon, in a Sunday game, B.H. King, a fifteen-year-old schoolboy at Bishop Vesey's, performed the "hat trick".

entries.heading: B.T. Wood
paras: The second eleven, under B.T. Wood's captaincy, met with greater success than the senior team. Wood was well supported by R.M. Wilkinson, A.J. Terry, C. Hawkins, and N.C. Heath, whilst V.G. Gabriel, rapidly rising to the top was available occasionally and in fact scored a century against Olton 2nd.

entries.heading: Wilfred Jones
paras: The "A" team, led by that keen and enthusiastic personality Wilfred Jones, had their most successful season for many years.  The success was attributable almost entirely to the ability of the captain with both bat and ball, and to his shining example in the field.

entries.heading: N Sharp
paras: The Midlands Club Cricket Conference which had been inaugurated in 1947 was now getting into its stride and fulfilling a long-needed want and service to clubs in the area.  W. Leslie Jones, whose initiative was the main spring of the organization, became the first Hon secretary, and indeed; the brains and organizer in chief for many years to follow. The club was honoured in having N. Sharp on the founder committee, and he was later honoured with both the Chairmanship and the Presidency of the Conference.

entries.heading: R.T. Janney
paras: R.T. (Bob) Janney took over the “A” side captaincy. Although, some twenty years earlier Janney had been an excellent Hon secretary and captain of the 2nd eleven and a most consistent bowler.

entries.heading: Nicholas
paras: The bar, too, started in a very small way at the top end of the main pavilion.  At that time there was only one small window at that end, and except at the height of the summer, it was an extremely dark corner.  At first candles and then a paraffin lamp provided the illumination. The bar was generally supervised by Nicholas, the groundsman, and the stocks consisted mainly of a few cases of bottled beer, followed later by a small barrel.

Owing to the after effects of the war spirits were in short supply at that time, but occasionally the brewery gave a small quota, and these were generally stored away until the annual dance. Though the bar made little money for the club, it served a most useful purpose not only in bringing together the members of the club, but also the improvement and cementation of relations with visiting clubs.

entries.heading: W.B. Price & Peter Tansley
paras: Off the square there was no satisfactory piece of turf sufficiently good for members’ net practice. As a result, a concrete wicket was laid on the lower side of the main ground in the spring. W.B. Price, Peter Tansley, and a few others put in a lot of hard labour in its construction, but, unfortunately, after the initial enthusiasm, it was found that members preferred the less true turf on which to practice, and the concrete subsequently became a "white elephant" and was later demolished.

entries.heading: D.H. Twiss & G.Y. Wilkes
paras: The return of D.H. Twiss, a pre-war stalwart of the 2nd Xl added strength to the batting. G.Y. Wilkes, too, returned after a long absence playing with other clubs, and one cannot help thinking that his early departure from the club was largely due to the lack of opportunities to which he was entitled.

entries.heading: P.E.S. Bowerbank
paras: Another new member was P.E.S. Bowerbank, a fine all-round cricketer who had previously represented both his native Devonshire and Suffolk.

entries.heading: R.M. Evans
paras: R. Marsh Evans retired in his capacity as Hon auditor, though he continued as a Vice President. For many years he was a useful left arm bowler with the first team and always a reliable number eleven in the batting order.  In both respects his opportunities would probably have been greater had he not been a player when both the batting and bowling strengths been of a high order.  He also played hockey for Warwickshire.

entries.heading: F.E Whitfield
paras: F.E Whitfield was elected Chairman of the Committee.  Prior to 1940 he had played for the, (now defunct) Chester Road C.C. at one time one of the leading Midland clubs.  He became a member of Sutton after the war and was a good opening batsman.  As a worker he rendered excellent services to the club particularly in the social sphere where he helped to raise a lot of money at the time it was most needed.

entries.heading: N. Sharp
paras: After thirty years of first eleven cricket Norman Sharp decided to retire from the more competitive game, but continued to play for the junior elevens for a number of years. Norman Sharp scored the century, 116 runs, a record for a Sutton 3rd team against Coventry & N.W.  -   The last 86 runs came in fifty minutes

entries.heading: Pat Bowerbank finished top of the averages with 38
paras: Pat Bowerbank scored a century against Olton, and a hurricane partnership of 129 in 65 minutes was made against Notts County F.C. in a Sunday game.

entries.heading: G. Wilks
paras: G. Wilkes was runner up with an average of 28

entries.heading: P. Ashcroft
paras: The first team, again under the captaincy of P.P. Ashcroft, did not meet with great success, due largely to inconsistent batting.  Only three of the twenty-one matches on Saturdays were won, but the Sunday side won twelve out of twenty against somewhat weaker opposition.  P. Ashcroft made a lot of runs and scored a century off Knowle & Dorridge and went on to take the bowling honours with the most wickets.

entries.heading: A.H. Butler
paras: A.H. Butler (“Pinhead") off spin bowler and batsman in his 1st season with the 1st team took the bowling honours in becoming the first bowler to take a hundred wickets in a season for the club.  Until this date the bowlers leading the field were F.B. Clark with 89 wickets for 9.8 runs apiece in 1914.

entries.heading: Dudley Cockle
paras: Dudley Cockle, a slow left arm spin bowler who played for Wiltshire, was a decided acquisition.

entries.heading: J.H. Odell took 8 Tamworth wickets for 17 runs
paras: Against Bournville C.C. total of 175, Sutton were unable to obtain the one run necessary for victory, with five wickets in hand.

entries.heading: J. Frisby
paras: There was a note-worthy performance in a second team game against Birfield with J. Frisby taking 6 for 6 runs in which the Birfield's last four wickets all fell with the score at 65 ending up in a tie

entries.heading: P. Tansley
paras: P. Tansley in a 2nd team match took 6 for 11 against Shirley and 6 for 11 against Four Oaks.

entries.heading: P. Wells
paras: Peter Wells (later to become Chairman and President of the Club with a nickname of Seam) took 6 BVGS wickets for 11.

entries.heading: P.D. Hutton
paras: For the "A" team P.D. Hutton took four wickets in four balls against Knowle & Dorridge "A".

entries.heading: A.L. Evans
paras: A.L. Evans, a Cambridge "blue", a fine wicketkeeper and most attractive batsman, who also gained an England Cap at Rugby Football, joined the club.

entries.heading: R.V. Burton
paras: R.V. Burton who had recently come to the town as Deputy Town Clerk and was a useful all-round cricketer.

entries.heading: R.J. Wood
paras: During the winter months R.J. (Bob) Wood, a retired business man and a vice president of the club, showed a keen constructive interest in the club's affairs.  One of his first self-imposed jobs was the enlargement of the kitchen in the tea pavilion, and the decoration of the interior. Bob formed a "House Committee" whose functions were to consider, advise, and carry out work to the club's property, and it was largely due to the efforts of Bob Wood, who acted as Hon secretary, that much work was accomplished at minimum costs, for most of the labour was supplied by this committee

entries.heading: Trustees
paras: One of the clauses in the lease granted in 1946 was that the club must appoint three trustees.  The gentlemen appointed were Alderman Wilfred Bigwood, F.B. Clark, and Clifford Howl.  The death of W. Bigwood earlier this year left a vacancy which was graciously filled by E.H. Walters.
The Thatched Pavilion & Surrounding Buildings in 1949

entries.heading: Officers
paras: Officers elected at the Annual General Meeting were: - P.I. Terry, Hon sec; N. Sharp, Hon treasurer; R.M. Wilkinson, Hon fixture sec; W.B. Price Hon team sec; and P.F.S. Bowerbank captain 1st Xl.
For the first time fixtures were arranged for a 2nd Xl on Sundays.

entries.heading: L.W. Stevenson
paras: After nearly twenty years with the club L.W. Stevenson (Steve) moved into the Wolverhampton district, and though he retained his membership he was unable to play for Sutton and his activities were mostly confined to playing with the Greenflies C.C. on Sundays.

His departure was a sad day for Sutton cricket for not only was he a popular character he was also a good all-round cricketer, and one of the main supports during the past difficult ten years.  Primarily a batsman in his earlier days he later developed his medium pace “seamer” so effectively that he frequently kept an end going through a complete innings.  He had many excellent performances with both the bat and the ball, and for periods acted as Hon secretary and Team secretary.

entries.heading: R.J. Wood
paras: The toilet arrangements had reached a dreadful state.  Before the commencement of the new season a new brick and concrete block was erected under the supervision of Ben Wood. The cost was in the region of £150.

entries.heading: L. Pellow
paras: A new members elected was L.N. Pellow known as Les, had been a fine all-round cricketer for many years with Kynoch C.C. for he made a lot of runs and took many wickets, also representing Warwickshire 2nd on occasions. Les had always been a resident of the town and had an ambition to play with Sutton, but the demands of his works side precluded him until he was past his prime, but all the same in the years to follow he was to be of enormous value to the club.

entries.heading: Roger Coombs & George Robinson
paras: Roger Coombs, and George Robinson joined – Roger became a high-class wicket keeper and a very capable batsman

entries.heading: Harry Foster
paras: A new score box was one of the necessities, and it was originally intended to make an appeal to the vice presidents for donations, but a tactful word in the right direction by the President resulted in W. Harry Foster, late of Four Oaks and now in retirement at Eastbourne, making a most generous gesture by donating it all.  Unfortunately, he was unable to be present at the opening, and in his absence the short ceremony was performed by his son, Tony Foster.

entries.heading: Pat Bowerbank
paras: It was in this year that the club really began to find its feet again, for Pat Bowerbank had at his disposal a potential side better than any the club had had during the past twenty years.  This proved to be the case, for the team won eleven of the twenty-four Saturday matches.  The success was in no small measure due to Bowerbank himself, for he led the team excellently, and made 1,184 runs during the season (a record aggregate to this date) and took 59 wickets. Against Bournville he scored a century in seventy minutes, and against Harborne he also scored a century.

entries.heading: P. Ashcroft
paras: P. Ashcroft was top of the batting average with 31,

entries.heading: A.L. Evans
paras: A.L. Evans also made centuries against Wolverhampton and Little Aston.

entries.heading: Pat Bowerbank and G. Robinson
paras: A second wicket partnership for the 1st team was 178 runs made against Bournville by Pat Bowerbank and G. Robinson.

entries.heading: A.J. Terry & V.A. Beardshaw
paras: With the improved strength throughout the club, A.J. Terry, who was again skippering the 2nd team, was also able to show good results.  The batting was very strong with V.A. Beardshaw averaging 61 and scoring 492 runs, including a century.
and W.B. Price, N. Sharp, D. Norton, G.Y. Wilkes, and B.T. Wood, all finishing the season with averages exceeding 25.

entries.heading: D. Norton, G. Wilkes, W.B. Price, & V.A. Beardshaw
paras: D. Norton and G. Wilkes made 152 for the second wicket against Stafford 2nd,
G. Wilkes and V.A. Beardshaw 149 for the fifth wicket against Leamington 2nd.
W.B. Price made a century.

entries.heading: R.S. Hill
paras: The "A" team too, under R.S. Hill, showed great improvement in winning the majority of the games played.

entries.heading: L. Stevenson
paras: There was a remarkable finish in the Sunday match with the Greenflies.  The Greenflies, batting second, required one run to win with seven wickets in hand when the last over commenced.  Over anxiety and good fielding caused the loss of three wickets in the first five balls.  For the last ball J. Harrison, who was not out 70, was at the receiving end and was joined by L Stevenson, who had naturally decided to run at all costs.

The final ball was bowled, missed by Harrison, and through to the wicketkeeper standing back.  By the time the wicketkeepers shy had broken the wickets Stevenson had made his ground, but Harrison had not moved.  The ball was retrieved by a fielder and rolled down the pitch to the bowlers end with Stevenson charging back again.  He was beaten by a "short neck" and the game ended in a draw.

entries.heading: Mayor, Councillor Keyse
paras: 1951 was "Festival of Britain" year, a national advertising campaign throughout the country. As part of the Royal Town's contribution, a local cricket knock-out competition was inaugurated and sponsored by the Mayor, Councillor Keyse.  Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club was the first -winners of the Challenge Shield in a competition which was to grow in momentum as the years went by.

entries.heading: G.B. Tuckwell
paras: G.B. Tuckwell, who had proved himself a loyal worker for the club over the past twenty years, as well as a useful cricketer, mostly for the second eleven, was elected a vice president upon his retirement from the playing scene.

entries.heading: P.I. Terry - Life Member
paras: At the Annual General Meeting Paul Terry resigned from the Hon secretarial role, an office he had held since 1945 through a very difficult phase in history of the club.  Though he had not specifically acted in that office during the war years, it was he, nevertheless, who was mainly responsible for keeping alive the club's interests during that period, and as previously mentioned, it was through his insistency in this respect that the club was in a position to resume normal activities so soon after the war.  Not only did he lose his wife during the war, a lady who or many years looked after the club's teas, but he also had many other responsibilities and commitments.

In recognition of his services throughout the war and in the seven years that followed he was elected a Hon Life Membership, the highest honour the club can bestow.  He was also presented with an oak bureau towards which almost every member subscribed.  During his period as the Club’s secretary Paul had steered the club through some difficult times, and with the limited resources during the period most of the reconstruction work had to be carried out by the members, and Paul himself carried the biggest burden.

In recording Paul Terry's services as an administrator, his prowess in the game must not be overlooked.  As a boy he missed some important years through ill health, but on becoming a member in 1922 he soon developed into a good left arm (over) bowler with a devastating “chinaman".

During his career this ball secured for him, many wickets.  As will be seen in the club's statistics he had many fine performances with the ball but probably his most noteworthy feat was a "hat trick" against Pickwick against the first three batsmen in his first over, and followed with two more victims before a run had been scored off him.  As a batsman he more or less permanently booked the number eleven berth, more by his own wish than by virtue of his ability, for he was no mean performer as proved at Wolverhampton and Stafford when he helped to add 73 and 63, runs respectively, for the ninth wicket at a time when runs were needed.  On one occasion his captain insisted on him opening the innings and he batted right through making 19 not out.  Illness in 1952 prevented any further activities, but fortunately his wise counsel remained available.

Upon Paul Terry’s retirement he presented the club with a Ship’s Bell, later inscribed. It was stolen on 2 occasions but only recovered once and it was alleged that it was in use in a Sutton Coldfield public house.

entries.heading: V. Gabriel; A.D. Pritchett; & V.B. King
paras: The club had never previously owned a flag.  This omission was generously rectified by three vice presidents; V. Gabriel; A.D. Pritchett; and V.B. King.

entries.heading: G.A. Pritchett & V.G. Gabriel
paras: Though the 1st X1 record was not as good as the previous year, the opening pair of Pritchett and Gabriel developed a fine understanding and both made a lot of runs.  Geoff Pritchett aggregated 1,181runs in the season,
P. Bowerbank &  D. Haworth,

Pat Bowerbank also had a good season in 1952 scoring a total of 936 runs.  D. Haworth, aged 17, joined the Club direct from school, and after a short period with the "A" and 2nd X1, made the First team grade and obtained a hundred wickets with his left arm spinners.

entries.heading: K.S. Anirudhsinghi
paras: K.S. Anirudisinghi, a direct descendant of those illustrious batsmen K.S. Ranjitsinghi and K.S. Duleepsinghi, both of whom scored centuries upon their debut in Test Matches against Australia, was completing his studies locally and played for the First team throughout the season.  Though not in the same class as his ancestors as a batsman, he, nevertheless, left his mark in the history of Rectory Park cricket, by taking 9 Bromsgrove wickets for 16 runs.

entries.heading: B.T. Wood
paras: B.T. Wood, for the 2nd Xl, performed a similar feat against Ashfield 2nd with 9 wickets for 23 runs.

entries.heading: Tatler Magazine
paras: In the Tatler Magazine of 21st May 1952 the Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club 1st team featured with a with an article by S.A. Patman including a team photograph by naming the players of the players and officials in his write up who were F. Langley (scorer); T.P. Daly; G.J. Robinson; S. Cutler; L.N. Pellow; A.H. Butler; K.S. Anirudhsinge; F.L. Bindon (umpire).  B.D. Clewer; G.A. Pritchett; P.E. Bowerbank (captain); P. Ashcroft; V. Gabriel. Followed by the article.
Set high in the rolling north Warwickshire countryside the Royal town of Sutton Goldfield, chartered by Henry VIII, possesses many ancient societies, and numbered among these is the Cricket Club.

In the year 1847, the Reverend W. K. Riland Bedford, having produced six stalwart sons, all enthusiastic cricketers, circulated the local gentry and residents, "There being a want of recreation and amusement for the inhabitants of this neighbourhood, it is proposed to form a cricket club to be composed of all classes willing to join."

Thus, the club was founded and first played in Sutton Park, but upon the reverend gentleman becoming Rector in 1850, the club moved to the Rectory Glebes, later called Rectory Park. The Rector was also an ardent member of the Toxopholite Society and in 1856 inaugurated the Free Foresters Cricket Club, now known wherever the game is played. The Rectory ground was the scene of most of its early matches.

entries.heading: A Sumary of the Prominent Personalities of the Mid-Victorian Era
paras: Prominent Personalities of the mid-Victorian era were T. F. Eddowes, Dr. (later Sir) Alfred Evans, Vincent Holbeche, the Town Clerk, H. Addenbrooke, and the Rev. G. F. Hough, described as a "fast bumpy bowler with a doubtful action."

The first recorded century was achieved by A. L. Crockford, and A. H. Evans is reputed to have hit a ball into Rectory Road, though it should be pointed out that the road ran nearer the ground than at present.

When the club celebrated its Jubilee in 1897, presentations were made to the surviving founder members, the Rector and Henry Addenbrooke, when the leading players then were C. Y. R. and H. E. R. Bedford, F. A. Vaughton, R. S. Walters, T. M. Colmore and M. N. Bagot.

MANY members responded to the call in World War One and among those who made the supreme sacrifice were Arthur Lilley and Percy Grove, treasurer and secretary respectively. The club survived the war period mainly through the efforts of George Sharp, F. Styles, H. L. Mortimore, N. Marsh, A. E. Terry and J. H. Cornwall. Thereafter, under the captaincy of J. B. Russell and excellent all-rounders in F. B. Clark, E. B. Crockford and A. E. Leighton, the club had a powerful side and at one time included nine who had played in county cricket. Mention must be made of George Sharp, who gave such fine service to the club during his thirty-seven years' membership, and the family tradition is now carried on by his son, Norman, a well-known figure in Midland cricket circles.

Largely through the energy of Paul Terry, the present secretary, the club quickly overcame the difficulties of post-war cricket and celebrated its centenary in 1947 with a cricket week, when the Free Foresters, skippered by E. H. R. Bedford, the grandson of the founder, and the M.C.C., were visitors to the Rectory ground.
To-day, under the leadership of P. E. Bowerbank, the club ranks as one of the strongest in the Midlands and fields six elevens each week-end.

entries.heading: N. Sharp and R.S. Hill
paras: For many generations the "A" team had been the chopping block for the senior sides.  With every vacancy created in the 1st and 2nd teams so were the better players withdrawn from the 3rd, leaving them not only short of players but of ability as well.  In consequence they were generally unable to hold their own, even against weak opposition.

Because of this state of affairs, the club for very long periods had been unable to retain members or to attract new ones unless they were of 1st team standard, to any satisfactory degree.  There were a number of new members available this season and the elected captains of the "A" and occasional "Extra A'', N. Sharp and R.S. Hill, with a pre-conceived plan considered this a suitable opportunity to set about the task of building up third team cricket. This was the commencement of a new era for the junior sides.

The aim was for the furtherance of the interests and prosperity of the club as a whole, and the plan was fairly simple - to have balanced sides, to give all members as good a game as possible whatever their ability, to attract new members, and to give younger players the opportunity to advance, without neglecting the older ones.

For generations prior to this date the 2nd Xl had consisted mostly of men who had played together for long periods, few of whom had either the ability or the inclination for 1st team cricket, thereby creating a bottleneck for younger men to the 1st team.  They were still useful and enjoyed their cricket and could prove valuable assets in assisting to make "A" team cricket worthwhile.  It was planned too, that retiring 1st Xl players would be able to carry on a few years longer in good though less strenuous) games in the lower grade.  This plan gave a chance to youth for advancement and strength so much needed to the lower teams.  Furthermore, it was planned that the junior teams should not be denuded of players who formed the nucleus of their strength by promoting them after selection, to other teams by reason of "cry-offs".

Opposition in the early stages was both expected and experienced, but the storm was weathered, and by the end of the season some progress had been achieved, though it was not anticipated that the ultimate aims would be fully realised for several years.

The final results of the “A” teams during the season were probably the best they had ever had with thirteen out of the twenty-six matches won.   However, the objective was not to create any records, it was merely to improve the standards of cricket on the lower ground and by doing so to open up avenues to attract new members where a level would be found according to their abilities.

D.H. Twiss had a batting average of over 40, and N. Sharp and F. Wain in the middle thirties.  The bowling was shared by P. Wells (34 wickets), P. Tansley (51), and F. Henderson (32) the last named taking 8 for 8 against Marlborough C.C.
Centuries were scored during the season by Pat Bowerbank (1st Xl), D. Norton (2nd X1), and D. Twiss and N. Sharp (A Teams).

entries.heading: A.J. Terry
paras: For several years the 2nd Xl captaincy had been under the capable leadership of A.J. (Jim) Terry, but before the new season commenced, he announced his retirement from further active participation in the game.  He had first played for the club as a schoolboy as far back as 1915, and became a full member in 1919.
Apart from service in the Second World War he played regularly for the club, mostly with the 2nd team, but with occasional appearances in the first - a period of thirty-four years.

A popular and cheerful personality, he had a number of good performances both as batsman and wicketkeeper, and also rendered excellent service to the club.  He participated in the highest official first wicket partnership (to date] against Chester Road C.C. in 1925. (No scorebook details were recorded) Upon retirement he was elected a Vice President.

entries.heading: Bob Wood
paras: Bob Wood again devoted his activities towards the betterment of the amenities, by adding an annex to the tea pavilion, for the purpose of supplying teas to spectators outside the enclosure.  Year by year, these steady improvements were made possible mainly by the profits from Dances and Sweepstakes, and it is of interest to note that the annual expenditure had risen from about £150 in 1939 to £900 at the present time in 1980, the largest contributory factor being the groundsman's wages and the fact that he was now engaged all the year round as compared with only a seasonal engagement.

entries.heading: Alec Harvey
paras: Alec Harvey was engaged as the new groundsman in place of T Nicholas who had found another job.
Playing Activities

entries.heading: G.A. Pritchett
paras: Geoff  Pritchett scored 1,280 runs for the 1st team,

entries.heading: Pat Bowerbank
paras: Pat Bowerbank scored 1,225 runs and had an average on Sunday of over 50 runs

entries.heading: V.G. Gabriel
paras: V.G. Gabriel 1,151, with an average of 52 runs in Saturday games and a century to his list of achievements including 13 half centenaries

entries.heading: D. Winter
paras: D. Winter, in his first game with the Club’s 2nd Xl scored a century against Pickwick 2nd,

entries.heading: Brian Clewer
paras: Brian Clewer was the 1st team leading run getter with 1,055 runs.

entries.heading: D Norton
paras: D Norton made most of his runs with the 2nd Team 1,017 also participated in the 2nd team with five century partnerships with four being for the first wicket.

entries.heading: L. Pellow
paras: Bowling honours went to L. Pellow, with 54 and 48 wickets on Saturdays and Sundays respectively and completed the hundred wickets in 424 overs.

entries.heading: P.J. Tansley
paras: P.J. Tansley, newly promoted from the "A" team into the second Xl secured 64 wickets, with a meritorious performance against Pickwick he not only performed the "hat trick" but bowled four batsmen with five successive balls.
Miss Russell, Mrs. & Misses Mortimore, Mrs. Lott, Mrs. G. Sharp, Mrs. Shelvoke, Miss Cornwell

During the writing of this history of the Club, little mention has been made of the part the "fairer" sex play in the life of a cricket club.  In almost every cricket club they do in fact play most important roles.  They give unselfish support to their menfolk to enjoy their games, whether or not they themselves are interested in the cricket, and generally, too, they are the backbones of the catering departments.  The Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club has indeed been fortunate in this respect, and over the course of the years the ladies have been responsible for a considerable portion of the revenue providing teas to the players and officials but to the public.  The writer's memory takes him back to the early part of the century when the names of Miss Russell, Mrs. and the Misses Mortimore, Mrs. Lott, Mrs. G. Sharp, Mrs. Shelvoke, Miss Cornwell, etc. readily come to mind.

entries.heading: Mrs. N. Sharp and Mrs. A.J. Terry
paras: Between 1930 and 1940 Mrs. N. Sharp and Mrs. A.J. Terry were responsible for the teas nearly every week, with the assistance of one "washer up".
Mrs. E. Miller, Mrs. G. Thompson, Mrs. N. Sharp, Mrs. M. Wood, Mrs. E. Wood, Mrs. G. Croxford, Mrs. E Smith

Of more recent years the work has been spread out under the supervision of Mrs. E. Miller, Mrs. G. Thompson, Mrs. N. Sharp, Mrs. M. Wood, Mrs. E. Wood, Mrs. G. Croxford, Mrs. E Smith. Not only producing sandwiches they operate a cake-rota,  – produced at home and served to players and the public. With the increased facilities the work had naturally grown, as did the cash handed over to the club’s treasurer.
The ladies now function with their own committee, and it is with sincere appreciation of their efforts for so many decades that, on behalf of the male members, the thanks are here officially
recorded.

entries.heading: V.G. Gabriel
paras: In the autumn a new financial venture was introduced in the form of a "Football Pool" (weekly contributions). V.G. Gabriel put in a lot of work to ensure its success, but unfortunately, partly through lack of support by the members in general and partly through the difficulties of collection, it lasted only into the second year, but nevertheless, a sum of between f200 and £300 was raised in the short period of operation.

entries.heading: P.P. Ashcroft
paras: After eight years with the club P.P. Ashcroft left the district at the end of the year.  He was a useful all-round cricketer and had a number of good batting and bowling performances to his credit, and skippered the 1st Xl in 1949 and 1950.

entries.heading: W.B. Price
paras: One of the most important and thankless jobs in a club is that of Hon Team Secretary, and particularly so when there are so many sides to complete.  It is when players advise the team secretary at the end of the week that his job becomes most difficult and irritating, for to find replacements at that late hour is not always easy and yet to maintain balance in sides. W.B. (Bill) Price had held this office for the past four years and had performed his duties exceedingly well, for very seldom had a team been short in the field.

Prior to the war W.B. Price had been a stalwart of the Chester Road C.C. and in midweek with the Sutton Coldfield Thursday C.C., but after the disbandment of these clubs he became a most useful member and keen worker for the Sutton Coldfield C.C.  He was a good batsman, mostly with the 2nd team and for whom he scored two centuries, and a very capable wicketkeeper. In the following year he retired as a player and devoted his attention to umpiring and again proved his ability, and at the same time put something back into the game from which he had gained so much enjoyment.

entries.heading: Norman Sharp
paras: The Midlands Club Cricket Conference had now been established seven years and from about sixty founder member clubs it was now receiving the support of over three hundred.  Since formation the Chairmanship had been in the capable hands of Guy Heaton, of Harborne C.C. but upon his retirement this year the honour was conferred upon Norman Sharp.

entries.heading: Pat Bowerbank, V.G. Gabriel & G.A. Pritchett
paras: The summer of 1954 was extremely wet, and there were but few days when the game could be played under good conditions.  In all teams no fewer than forty-one matches were either cancelled or abandoned, and in these circumstances, it is somewhat surprising that some players met with success with the bat.  P Bowerbank scored 1032 runs but V.G. Gabriel narrowly missed a four-figure aggregate but he and G.A. Pritchett both scored centuries.

entries.heading: CJ. Frisby & Vince Fitzgerald
paras: Under the new team selection policy the 2nd Xl, again under the captaincy of J. Frisby, had now become a fairly young side and gave a good account of themselves with six members having batting averages of over twenty.

A noteworthy achievement was by eighteen-year-old fast bowler V. Fitzgerald who took all ten Solihull wickets for 18 runs. Only once before had a club member taken ten wickets and that was by F. B. Clark in 1914.

entries.heading: F. Henderson
paras: In the "A" teams the standard of cricket continued to improve for seven men averaged over 20 with the bat, a satisfactory performance when taking into consideration the fact that the oppositions bowling was comparatively well ahead of the batting.
F Henderson, though approaching the veteran stage took 95 wickets for about eleven runs each.

entries.heading: G.V. Swift
paras: George V Swift, who had adorned the game for about forty years, retired as a player at the end of the season.  His unassuming character and sportsmanship had earned him many friends and his departure was a loss to the game, but his election as a vice president ensured his continued interest in Sutton cricket. His qualities as a cricketer, particularly as a wicketkeeper, have already been written but there can be no harm in repeating that he ranked high amongst the many outstanding wicketkeepers that the club has traditionally possessed.

He must have been one of the best keepers in the game who throughout his career never received the county recognition and it must have been a proud moment in his life when his son, Derek was selected for Staffordshire, as a wicketkeeper.

entries.heading: B.T. Wood
paras: Another retirement this season was B.T. Wood, a 2nd Xl stalwart during the post war period. A native of Yorkshire, he was a typical product of that cricketing county, and a dour batsman, though mainly he shone as a bowler and secured many victims with cleverly controlled flight.

entries.heading: His 9 wickets for 23 against Ashfield 2nd
paras: A "hat truck" against Kynoch were the highlights amongst many fine performances.
He captained the 2nd Xl in 1947 and 1948, rendered many good services to the club, and continued his keen interest after retirement.
Report in the Stratford-upon-Avon Herald that an Organist Dies in Church

entries.heading: Obituary to Mr. H. F. Lott A.R.C.M
paras: Horace Lott was a distinguished cricketer with the Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club either side of World War One, prior to his retirement to Bearley where he played the organ at St Mary’s Church.  He was also a talented entertainer with a fine tenor voice who organised several outdoor concerts in Rectory Park.

Horace scored several centuries for Sutton 1st team, none more so than the 120 against Ashfield in 1920, when he was aged 50.  He also distinguished himself bowling leading the clubs’ averages in 1913 with 9.4 runs per wicket and scored 539 runs in the same season.

Seated in St. Mary’s Church, Bearley. on Sunday, April 15th, waiting to play the organ for a service, Mr. Horace F. Lott A.R.C.M., collapsed and died.  Mr. Lott, who would have been 75 next Monday, was prominent in musical circles.  A native of Margate, Kent, he was educated at Thanet College. Margate.  He started his musical career as a chorister in Lichfield Cathedral, where his father, the late John Browning Lott, Mus. Doc., was organist for 44 years.

A teacher of singing, Mr. Loft had studios in London, Birmingham and Leamington Spa. He was particularly well-known in Warwickshire and Worcestershire as a conductor of choral societies. and, among them the Great Alne, Tardebigge and Claverdon Societies, the Feckenham and Ashwood Bank Ladies’ Choir and the Bearley Singing Class.

entries.heading: Horace was also a Member of the MCC
paras: Although a busy man professionally, this accomplished musician found time to indulge his love of sport and for 30 years was a member of the M.C.C.  At one time he was captain of the Hastings Football Club, and he played for the Hampstead Cricket Club.  For 17 years he represented Sutton Coldfield CC. on the Warwickshire County Cricket Club Committee.
During The First World War Mr. Lott was superintendent of a Church Army hut in France, and his services and delightful tenor voice were greatly appreciated by the men.
His passing will leave a blank in the village that has been his home for the past 20 years, and where he was so; familiar a figure.

The funeral of Mr. Horace F. Lott took place at the Church of St. Mary the Virgin, Bearley, on Thursday, April 19th.  Squadron-Leader Easters, of the RAF, officiated, and in a brief address paid high tribute to Mr. Lott, who, he said. in that church led the praises of the Master whom he served.

It was in the House of God that he breathed his last.  L.A.C. Greenhough (R.A.F.), at the organ, played “O Rest in the Lord” as the cortege entered the church and the “Dead March in Saul” at the end of the service. The hymns were “Just as I am” and “Fight the good fight,” and the ‘Nunc Dimittis” was sung as the cortege passed out of church.
The chief mourners were Mrs. H. Lott, (widow), Mrs. Birse (sister-in-law), Mrs. Woods (niece) and Miss Thornton.
The bearers were Messrs. C. A. Farmer, A. Tombs, H. Washburn and T. Wheatland.
