entries.heading: V.G. Gabriel
paras: At the annual general meeting the Hon treasurer reported a surplus of nearly £200. This excellent profit was largely due to the hard work and enthusiasm of a few members, and special mention was made of V.G. Gabriel whose efforts on the "pools" had resulted in the handsome profit during the period in which they operated. Owing to lack of support by members in general this source of income had now ceased to exist,

entries.heading: George Sharp & Frank Lamb
paras: The railings surrounding the enclosure, first erected by George Sharp some thirty years earlier, were also, not surprisingly, in a poor state, and mainly through the efforts of Frank Lamb they were renewed in the early part of the season.

entries.heading: Bill Price & Hockey Club Members
paras: The pipes bringing water to the club's premises had been laid in 1929 and were now beginning to perish and cause flooding, particularly in the winter months.  Bill Price and a few assistants had re-laid a section the previous year, & and a further section was replaced by members of the Hockey Club in the spring of this year.

entries.heading: Pat Bowerbank
paras: A fairly successful season was enjoyed by the 1st X1, for whom the skipper, P. Bowerbank, passed the previous highest for the club in scoring 1445 runs with a batting average of 50.  Two centuries were included in this total, and in one of these, against Wednesbury, his score moved from 78 to 104 in the space of one over.

entries.heading: V.G. Gabriel
paras: V.G. Gabriel scored a century against Ashfield, whilst again at Olton,

entries.heading: D. Glover
paras: D. Glover was dismissed with his score on 99.

entries.heading: L. Pellow & J. Olsen
paras: The spin bowling of L. Pellow and J. Olsen again bore the brunt of the attack, the former obtaining 102 wickets and the latter performed the "hat trick" against Bromsgrove.

entries.heading: V.G. Gabriel & G.A. Pritchett
paras: At Moseley Ashfield, declaring at 241 for 2, lost to Sutton on the stroke of time by six wickets, mainly due to a third wicket partnership of 148 by G.A. Pritchett and V.G. Gabriel.

entries.heading: G.A. Pritchett
paras: A club record at that time was created by Geoff Pritchett behind the stumps.  He secured 69 victims (48 Stumped and 2l Caught) and proved of great assistance to Pellow and Olsen.

entries.heading: J. Frisby
paras: Under J. Frisby’s captaincy the 2nd Xl won a large proportion of their matches.
The batting was strong with such players as G.Y. Wilkes; D. Norton; A. Hodgson; M. Cook, and W.E. Wood, whilst with the ball, V. Fitzgerald and D Dewsbury gave excellent accounts of themselves.
M. Cook, against Leamington 2nd, scored 91 out of 134 for 9 in enabling Sutton to win by one wicket.
H. Hodgson and R. Coombs scored 161 for the second wicket against Hampton in Arden.

entries.heading: I. McCrae
paras: The third elevens continued their ascendancy with two useful Saturday sides and one on Sundays.  Ten batsmen averaged over 20, with I. McCrae the most consistent bowler and a "hat trick" to his credit.

entries.heading: F. Henderson
paras: The outstanding performance of a 3rd team player was by F. Henderson -who became only the third Sutton player in the records to take all ten wickets.  The feat was performed against Birmingham Municipal "A" for a cost of only 10 runs, and eight of his victims were bowled.

entries.heading: S. Lightfoot
paras: S. Lightfoot took four wickets in four balls against Wylde Green College Old Boys for te 3rd team.

entries.heading: Mrs. E. Miller and Mrs. M. Thompson
paras: A profit on the teas of £125 was handed over by the ladies’ tea committee at the end of the season, and the thanks of the club were again recorded to Mrs. E. Miller and Mrs. M. Thompson.

entries.heading: Miss Kathleen Grove
paras: Under the Will of the late Miss Kathleen Grove the club was bequeathed £100.  Miss Grove, though she herself did not display an apparently keen interest in the club, also left a legacy to the Warwickshire County Cricket Club.  She came from an old Sutton family whose members were closely associated with Sutton cricket, including two brothers Percy and Oswald Grove.

At the outbreak of the 1914 war the former was Hon secretary, Percy Grove  of the club and was subsequently killed in action, whilst the latter, after many years abroad, re-joined the club and skippered the "A' team for a period in the thirties.
The Crockfords', too, were related to Miss Grove. The generous legacy was most gratefully received and specifically allocated to the interior furnishing of the pavilion.

entries.heading: Frank Lamb
paras: In the spring, interior structural improvements were made to the main pavilion.  For these the club was greatly indebted to Frank Lamb who not only sacrificed many of his own week end pleasures, but also directed and carried out most of the work himself.  The work consisted of the removal of the old quarter light window panes which covered about two thirds of the length of the building, and the construction of new and larger windows along the entire length. With the general structure out of alignment it was a task that called for skilled and careful workmanship.  New main doors were also added.

entries.heading: Obituaries Herbert Strong and Jim Burrows
paras: The deaths of Herbert Strong and Jim Burrows, both respected members of a few years standing, were recorded with sorrow.  The former had upon his retirement shown a keen interest in the club's activities, and amongst numerous other self-imposed duties, he had appointed himself chief operator of the score box.  The latter had acted as 2nd Xl umpire for several years in an efficient capacity.

entries.heading: R M Wilkinson
paras: Before the season commenced a major undertaking in the form of the installation of electricity fulfilled a long-needed necessity.  The power was brought from Rectory Road by underground cable, and the cost, including accessories, was about £330.  The successful St Leger Sweepstake of the previous season which had produced a profit of £195 was specifically allocated to the scheme, and a further £50 was donated by the Sutton Coldfield Hockey Club.  The interior wirings and fittings were supervised by R M Wilkinson.

entries.heading: W.P. Richardson
paras: W.P. Richardson, after an association with the club of over twenty years, left the district.  He was a loyal member and useful cricketer, and a keen worker.
“Jenny” The Cat

There was an unusual item in the accounts: - "Cat Food".  During the previous season a stray cat had made its home in and around the pavilion and became "adopted" by the groundsman and some of the members.  It was so well looked after that it made no attempt to leave.  When kittens were on the way preparations were made for the confinement in a secluded spot near the clock and a ladder remained permanently in position inside the main pavilion in front of the door, in order for 'Jenny' to maintain contact with the outside world. Naturally, too, there was constant friction with members dogs, particularly with the repeated and regular arrival of more and more kittens.  During: - the winter months a few members formed a visiting rota and regularly kept her supplied with the best cat foods, under all weather conditions. Though many members objected to a cat for a mascot no action was taken until it became a committee issue, and she was then found a new home.

entries.heading: Norman Sharp
paras: At the Annual General Meeting Norman Sharp was elected an honorary life member and was presented with two lounge chairs by the members in appreciation of his services to the club.  His first association with the club was in 1905, at the age of four, and the year his father George Sharp, joined the club after moving from Derby. His father's performances were his main interest in the game at that time, but in 1910 he became 2nd Xl scorer for a few years.
At Bishop Vesey's G.S. he passed through the various phases before he finally became captain of the school in all its sporting activities until he left in 1919.

He played his first game for Sutton Coldfield C.C. in 1915 but did not become a full member until leaving school. After a year' graduation with the "A" and 2nd teams, he became the regular 1st X1 opening batsman for the next thirty years and subsequently continued to play in the lower elevens until 1958, afterwards he captained the Warwickshire Nursery Xl for two seasons.

During his career he scored nearly 25,000 runs in club cricket, mostly for Sutton, and was 1st X1 captain for eight years, and "A" team captain for four. He succeeded his father as fixture secretary, an office he held for eighteen years, followed by the treasurer-ship for seven. He played for Warwickshire in 1923 and represented the County at hockey for several years.

entries.heading: G. B. Thompson
paras: Before the commencement of the season G. B. Thompson made an excellent job of a kitchen extension to the tea pavilion.

entries.heading: D. Glover
paras: Dennis Glover was the outstanding batsman in the first team, who aggregated 1361 runs, including two centuries, with an average of 40.
Pat Bowerbank
Pat Bowerbank scored 1,173 runs,

entries.heading: G.A. Pritchett
paras: G. A. Pritchett (one century), and again, he had a fine season behind the stumps with 67 victims

entries.heading: Brian Clewer
paras: Brian Clewer was little short of a thousand.

entries.heading: L. Pellow
paras: Les Pellow obtained a hundred wickets for the first team
J. Olsen
J. Olsen took 81 wickets.

entries.heading: Peter Yates
paras: Wickets at the Rectory Park had become very much of the "feather bed" variety.  Fast bowlers could get neither pace nor lift, and it had therefore become necessary to "buy" wickets as cheaply as possible, and these two bowlers proved highly successful in these tactics.
Peter Yates actually headed the bowling averages with 39 wickets and performed an excellent "hat trick" against Burton's first three batsmen.

entries.heading: Vince Fitzgerald
paras: Vince Fitzgerald, only available during the latter part of the season, took 25 wickets for only 5.8 runs each.

entries.heading: Alan Bedggood
paras: Alan Bedggood (slow left arm) bore the brunt of the attack with the 2nd Xl and he collected a hundred wickets, including 9 for 42 against Kynoch’s 2nd.

entries.heading: Pat Bowerbank and V.G. Gabriel
paras: A touring team from South Australia visited the country, at their own expense, during the summer, and one of their early fixtures was at Rectory Park.  Led by Reg Noblet, brother of the former Australian Test cricketer, they were defeated by Sutton largely through a good partnership by Pat Bowerbank and V.G. Gabriel.  A dinner at the Boldmere Hotel followed and many members gathered for what proved to be a convivial evening.

entries.heading: R.J. Wood
paras: The death of R.J. (Bob) Wood was a sad loss to the club.  Though he was never a playing member, he became an enthusiastic vice president upon his retirement from business, an enthusiasm which he put to full use both in his own interests and that of the club.  It proved beneficial to him for it provided him with a constructive hobby which in turn was devoted to the improvement of the amenities.  The major undertakings can be summarized, briefly, as follows.

The catering department was overhauled and the facilities improved.  Under the "House Committee" which he originated and of which he acted as Hon secretary in the early stages, general repairs and decorations to the buildings were carried out by his own and other voluntary labour.  But perhaps the greatest "monument" to his memory was the bar, for it was mainly through his industry and supervision that it was erected in 1952, at negligible cost, and subsequently he played a great part in its efficient running. The club will forever be grateful for the services he rendered.

entries.heading: Arthur Terry
paras: The Freedom of the Royal Town was conferred upon the President, Alderman Arthur E Terry. This supreme honour was richly deserved for he had for very many years given his unstinted loyalty to the work of the borough and to the community, in many spheres.

entries.heading: W.B. Price & J. Bannister
paras: Before 1940 the Sutton Coldfield Thursday C.C., comprised mostly of local business men, shopkeepers, and a few professional footballers, rented the lower ground and had their own dressing accommodation, but through shortage of players, were unable to resume after the Second World War.  The club was finally disbanded and the funds which had remained "frozen" at the bank were released by the few remaining members, of whom W.B. Price and J. Bannister were the principals.  These gentlemen made a most generous gesture to the Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club by deciding to use the money for the benefit of the club, and accordingly presented six Burma Teak seats and an Electric Clock for the pavilion.  The long and happy association of the two clubs was thus commemorated and "plates" were later attached to the seats.

entries.heading: P.J. Lowe & J. McCarthy
paras: In the 2nd team P.J. Lowe and John. McCarthy both averaged 35 with Pete Lowe having 56 victims from behind the stumps.

entries.heading: Norman Sharp
paras: For the Hawks -3rd Xl, N. Sharp, in a limited number of appearances, averaged nearly 60.  An indication of how much the batting strength had improved in so short a time, in what were virtually third teams of the club, can be assessed by the fact that centuries were scored by three players

R. Cooley, George Beech, and W. Turner, and in a season, too, when wickets were not very advantage to batsmen.  It indicated the strength of the club as a whole and proved justification in the policy adopted a few years earlier

entries.heading: W. Turner & S.G. Pearce
paras: The highest partnership in the season by the Grasshoppers was 153 for the second wicket by W. Turner (101 not out) and a young player S.G. Pearce (45 not out) against Coseley.

entries.heading: D. Norton
paras: D. Norton had taken over the office of Hon secretary upon the retirement of Paul Terry in 1952, and had, during his five years in office, acted in a most efficient and diplomatic manner, and the smooth working of the club was a tribute to his organisation.  His departure was a severe loss, and particularly as rather short notice, unavoidably, had to be given.  The members recognised his valuable services by presenting him with a handsome bookcase.  His cricket ability, too, was a loss to the club, for he was a sound batsman and made many runs, mostly with the 2nd Xl.  He scored two centuries and in 1953 completed a thousand runs, and during his ten years with the club participated in many long partnerships.  He was elected a vice president, and in the following season continued his activities with Kenley C. C, in Surrey, nor was it long before he again found himself organizing things in that club.

entries.heading: P.J. Tansley
paras: P.J. Tansley had moved to Liverpool.  He, too, had proved himself a valued administrator and a good cricketer.  For the past three years he had made a great success of his job of Team Secretary.  The completion of seven teams each week is no easy task, and it calls for great care and often last-minute activity, and the fact that no captains at any time had cause for complaint is a tribute to his ability.  He also ran a number of social and income raising activities during his eleven years with the club.

As a cricketer he was an accurate medium pace bowler, but was distinctly unfortunate in that he never secured a permanent place with either of the senior teams, for, (though it is open to speculation) there always appeared to be somebody just a shade better.  Perhaps it was that his bowling style failed sufficiently to impress the selection committee, but nevertheless in his only full season with the 1st team he secured 64 wickets, a meritorious performance in itself on wickets not normally suitable to bowlers of his pace.  He was elected a vice president.

entries.heading: G.B. Thompson
paras: The sudden loss of Percy Groves, Hon Secretary and Arthur Lilly, Hon Treasurer caused a breach in the organisation, but, as frequently happens "the right man in the right place was soon found", and Gordon B. Thompson stepped in at short notice.  G.B. Thompson had joined the club during the Great War years and the fact that little has previously been written about him in these pages is purely that he had not hit the headlines as an outstanding player with the bat or ball.  It frequently happens that the best cricketers do the least for a club, and the best administrators are found amongst those who have less ability.  Gordon Thompson was a case in point for his loyalty and popularity made him one of the most respected of members.  Always ready and willing to assist in any way, he had already rendered many services in a practical manner, and was always an ardent supporter of the club's social activities.  He played his cricket because he loved it, and became a popular skipper of the Hawks.  With his wife, who organised the catering for a number of years, they comprised an excellent "team”.

entries.heading: Hugh Leigh
paras: Bob Wilkinson had been in office for the past five years and had now handed over the reins to J.H. (Hugh) Leigh, who with his enthusiastic and realistic approach, set about the task of improving the Sunday fixtures and also those of the Hawks and Owls.

Hugh, as a wealthy business man in the new industry of plastic molding did not like playing in the Sutton lower sides with such a title as the “A” side or the 3rd Xl title resulting in introducing the Sutton Coldfield Hawks and the newly 4th Xl under the name of the Owls. These two name were for Saturday matches and on Sunday the “A” side became the Grasshoppers.

entries.heading: Pat Bowerbak & A.K. Couchman
paras: Pat Bowerbank was incapacitated for a considerable period the aggressive role in the batting order was taken over by A.K. Couchman, who had recently transferred his affections from Aston Manor C.C., and at the end of the season he topped the batting averages.

entries.heading: Geoff Pritchett
paras: Geoff Pritchett was the most prolific run getter with 1072 runs in 41 innings.

entries.heading: Officers
paras: At the Annual General Meeting the appointment of G.B. Thompson as Hon secretary was unanimously confirmed, with R.H. Smith elected as Hon treasurer, J. Clayton became the Team secretary and P.D. Hutton Social secretary.
L. Pellow
season. Les Pellow secured a hundred wickets for the fourth time.

entries.heading: Neil Houghton and A. Giggins
paras: Neil Houghton and A. Giggins were two young players to make their mark towards the end of the season.  They both showed outstanding promise.
2nd G Robinson Xl
.The outstanding batsman in the 2nd team was G Robinson, who in 28 innings scored 1074 runs with an average of 49, without making a century.

entries.heading: A. Giggins & N. Jones
paras: Tony Giggins and N. Jones both scored fine centuries against Wednesbury 2nd and Coventry & N.W. 2nd respectively.

entries.heading: E. Biggs, Alan Bedggood & R.M. Wilkinson
paras: The bowling honours in the 2nd Xl were shared by T.E. Biggs (64 wickets) Alan Bedggood (87) and R.M. Wilkinson (72).

entries.heading: George Beech and J. Lewis
paras: The lack of success by the Hawks, who only won four of their twenty matches, was in no way attributable to the captain, G.B. Thompson.  The disparity in results between the Hawks and Owls, was due the Owls strength with 14 wins in 19 games, was largely due to the much stronger fixture list of the Hawks, who often had the weaker of teams of the two elevens as well. Also, George Beech and J. Lewis playing most of their games with the Owls and had averages of over 30.

entries.heading: E.G. Mann and Peter Wells
paras: E.G. Mann and Peter Wells both took a lot of wickets at economical costs, as also did

entries.heading: P.J. Tansley
paras: P. Tansley on his occasional visits from Liverpool to play with his old club.

entries.heading: R.S. Hill
paras: Stan Hill, after a lifetime of club cricket, played his last game against Walmley on his sixtieth birthday, before retiring his earlier playing days were mostly occupied with Chester Road C.C., for whom he was a reliable opening batsman.  With the loss of their ground to Boldmere St Michaels F.C. this old and once famous cricket club faded from the picture at the outbreak of the Second World War, and Sutton were indeed fortunate in gaining the services of so able an administrator and good club man as Stan Hill, even though his best playing days were of the past.  His heart was always in the game, he gave every encouragement to the advancement of juniors, and a more loyal member it would have been hard to find.  From 1940 to 1958 his work and sound advice were of extreme value to the club in the process of rebuilding after the war, and he became a capable captain of the "A" team.

entries.heading: R E Pearce
paras: R.E. Pearce, a non-playing member, made himself responsible for taking round the collection box throughout the season.  His devotion to this self-imposed duty resulted in about £94 being added to the income of the club, a figure far in excess of any previous year.  In electing him a vice president the committee conveyed their thanks to him for his efforts.

entries.heading: N. Sharp and G.B. Thompson
paras: An approach was made to the Borough Council with a view towards discussing various aspects of the club's security, renewal of the lease due to expire in 1967, and certain improvements to the ground and its approaches.  In due course a meeting was arranged and N. Sharp and G.B. Thompson were deputed from the club to meet the Mayor, Councilor Mrs. F. Grounds, representatives of the Parks & Estates Committee, and council officials.  The following points were put forward for consideration: -
A.	Security of Tenure and extension of lease.
B.	Roadway improvement to the pavilion.
C.	Extension of top side boundary fencing.

entries.heading: D.	Leveling of top side of ground at some future date
paras: Though nothing could be decided at this juncture, the meeting gave a sympathetic hearing and promised to review and discuss the whole position.

entries.heading: Obituary E.B. Crockford
paras: The death of E.B. Crockford “known as Tom” in February 1958 was received with sincere regret.  His prowess and ability in the world of sport has been recorded earlier in these pages, but with his passing it is considered some repetition may not be out of place.  He was a member of the club for over fifty years - as a player and as a vice president - and one of the best all round cricketers ever to play for the club.  In fact, all sports came naturally to him.  His relaxed approach, suppleness of wrists, and perfect timing, made the execution of his strokes at both cricket and hockey a delight to see.

He was "capped" for Warwickshire at cricket, and many times for England at hockey, and was on numerous occasions’ amateur billiards and snooker champion of the Midlands (one of the few amateurs to make a hundred break at snooker).  He also possessed more than average ability at other games, including Hockey in which he represented Great Britain and Ireland in the Antwerp Games of 1920 wing a gold medal.  Though he loved his cricket he was not particularly interested in his own personal achievements, otherwise his name would have appeared more prominently in the statistical records.  His legal knowledge made him the obvious choice as the club's solicitor, and he played a large part in obtaining the twenty-one-year lease in 1946.

entries.heading: ERIC BERTRAM CROCKFORD
paras: Eric was born on 13th October 1888 and lived in Vesey Road, Wilde Green, Sutton Coldfield and was educated at Eastbourne College, Eastbourne.  He died on 17th January 1958 in Four Oakes, Sutton Coldfield.  Eric was known as Tom and articled to his father business A. L. Crockford, solicitors of 71 Temple Row, Birmingham. He Joined in September 1914, as a Private, in 14th Battalion Royal Warwickshire Regiment; Gazetted 2nd Lieutenant into the 6th Battalion of the Royal Warwickshire Regiment in August 1915, subsequently promoted to Lieutenant & served in France in 1916 and 1918.

entries.heading: Sidney Barnes
paras: England's famous wicketkeeper, Godfrey Evans, was the principal guest at the Annual Dinner held at the Fox, Walmley.  Despite arctic conditions there was an excellent attendance, Sidney Barnes, generally accepted as the greatest bowler of all times, and still remarkable fit and active at 85 years of age, was also an honored guest.

entries.heading: Mrs. N. Sharp
paras: During the previous season the ladies made a profit of £80 on the teas. In appreciation of this fine effort the club entertained them to cocktails at the Royal Hotel before the commencement of the new season.  During the evening Mrs. N. Sharp was presented with a silver fruit bowl in recognition of the twenty-five years she had assisted with the catering.

entries.heading: J B Russell,	 B. Clark, and R. Marsh Evans
paras: By this time, it had become customary for the Hon secretary, when issuing the notices convening the annual general meeting, to give his annual report in the form of a circular to all members.  Included in this report tribute was paid to J B Russell, B. Clark, and R. Marsh Evans, all of whom had been members for over fifty years.

entries.heading: R.A. Janney
paras: During the close season a new bar frontage had been constructed and it was generally accepted as an improvement to the appearance of the pavilion interior.  Running hot water bad also been installed.

R.T. Janney retired from the office of Hon auditor.  He had acted in this capacity for a number of years and thanks were expressed for his long and valuable services to the club, not only as Hon auditor but in other respects as well.  He was succeeded by H.R. Cadman, the Hon treasurer, R.H. Smith, reported that a loss of £90 had been sustained during the previous year.  The annual election of officers showed little change.

entries.heading: P. Bowerbank and L.R. Collier
paras: P. Bowerbank was elected captain for the eighth successive year, and L.R. Collier became chairman of the bar committee in succession to Len Bindon.

entries.heading: Len Bindon Retires & A New Flag
paras: The retirement of Len on his doctor’s advice, gives the opportunity to put on record the excellent work he did for the club.  He first became a member in 1945, having played his earlier cricket elsewhere.  He was not a cricketer of outstanding ability, but he loved the game, and rendered, in his unassuming manner, many services to the club.  Perhaps his greatest contribution was his ten years (1948 - 1957) as 1st Xl umpire, in a voluntary capacity.  He "stood" on both Saturdays and Sundays and throughout that time missed very few matches, and those who appreciate how exacting this job can be will realise his worth.

For a period, Len had been responsible for the smooth running of the catering, and was also for a time chairman of the bar committee, and would frequently help behind the bar after a long day in the field.  As a member of the general committee, he gave loyal support to all matters appertaining to the welfare of the club, and particularly in support of money raising ventures.  Upon his retirement he and Mrs. Bindon presented a new flag to the club, and the members, in their turn, showed their appreciation with a gift to them both.

entries.heading: A Press Cutting
paras: A new green and white flag flew over Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club's ground in Rectory Park on Sunday during the tea interval at the 1st XI's match with Wednesbury. It marked the retirement of 61years-old Mr. Len Bindon of 18, Maple Road, Maney, who or 12 years has been umpiring matches at home and away for Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club.

He announced his retirement at the club's annual meeting this year but delayed his "good-bye" until Sunday. when in recognition of his service. captain Pat: Bowerbank presented Len and his wife with an automatic tea - making machine which had been given by members. And in return Len gave the club' a new flag which was received by club chairman Norman Sharp, who said: "We do hope that you will have very many more happy years with us."

entries.heading: STERLING SERVICE
paras: Before he became umpire in 1946, Len played for the second XL Since then he has hardly missed a match.

In presenting the tea-machine Pat Bowerbank said: "Len has done very sterling service for the 1st XI for 12 years. For a club to have an umpire home and away year in and year out for that time is a very great boon indeed Len has been active in administrative duties. as a member of the general committee and the bar committee. Such has been his popularity that people came with money in their hand and asked if they could contribute to this present."

“With this tea machine it will up at seven o'clock every morning." said Mrs. Bindon. "It was rather a rust when Len was umpiring every Saturday during the season especially if we had to go away. Now we will be able to take things easy, at least for a bit.”

entries.heading: B.H.D. Clewer
paras: B.H.D. Clewer's was the only player to pass a 1,000 runs with 1,031 runs and an average of 36 was a meritorious performance.  He was also the only 1st team player to score a century.  It was a most disappointing season for cricket - ruined by the weather.  Over all the teams nearly thirty fixtures were either cancelled or abandoned early, and many more suffered through the unpleasant conditions.  There was scarcely a firm wicket throughout the season and consequently the aggregate runs by players were lower than usual.  Under the circumstances

entries.heading: Geoff Pritchett
paras: Geoff Pritchett also did well with nearly 900 runs, on damp and very soft pitches

entries.heading: . L. Pellow & T.E. Briggs
paras: The brunt of the bowling was again borne by the spin attack of Les Pellow and T.E. Biggs.  The former again took more than a hundred wickets, including 9 for 67 against Olton, whilst the latter mainly through variations in pace aided by spin proved very successful.

entries.heading: G.Y. Wilkes
paras: The 2nd Xl broke about even on the season with eight wins, eight losses, and seven drawn games.  The batting averages were headed by the evergreen Gordon Wilkes, and it may now be an appropriate moment to record his contribution over the years towards the club.  Little mention of him has previously been made, due largely to the fact that his cricket had been of the reliable, rather than spectacular, variety.  First joining the club in the late "twenties" as a young man, his potential ability was not fully recognised and before long he sought his cricket in other places.  In 1949 he re-joined Sutton, and though he never gained a permanent place in the 1st Xl he was always a most reliable and consistent batsman with the 2nd team, as is confirmed by his end of season average which was never less than 22 and never more than 32.  He invariably showed up best in a crisis, and his fighting spirit often extricated the side from seemingly irretrievable positions.  For several years he acted as Hon secretary of the House Committee, and in this capacity rendered valuable services in performing some of the many necessary jobs there are in club life.

entries.heading: G. Robinson
paras: G. Robinson scored a century in the opening Sunday game of the season against Pickwick.

entries.heading: Alan Bedggood & R.M. Wilkinson
paras: Alan Bedggood with 81 wickets, closely followed by R. M. Wilkinson.

entries.heading: W.J. Turner, Frank Lamb & D. Baker
paras: W.J. Turner, who scored a century against Pickwick 2nd at Wake Green Road and was the most successful batsman during the season for the Hawks.  In scoring his century, he and Frank Lamb had a partnership of 105 for the first wicket, and this was followed by an unfinished stand of 99 with D. Barker for the second wicket.

entries.heading: Three Hat tricks
paras: In early September one weekend provided three "hat tricks" for the club;
E.G. Mann for the 1st Xl against Wednesbury;
J. Frisby for the 2nd Xl against Wednesbury 2nd,
P. Wells for the Hawks against Pickwick Nomads.

entries.heading: R.T. Janney
paras: A "match levy" had been introduced at the beginning of the season, and, on subsequent review, had proved a wise decision, for not only did it bring in additional income, the policy of "pay as you play" gave greater justice to those members who had less games.  The renewal of the Football Pool in a different form also provided additional revenue.

entries.heading: John Pritchett
paras: In October of this year John D Pritchett was fatally injured in a motor accident. He was the son of Arthur D. Pritchett, a vice president, and brother of G.A. Pritchett, and a former member of the club.  As a boy he showed signs of becoming a fine cricketer, but with a natural aptitude for golf he took that game up as a career, and it was not long before he became one of the leading young professionals in the country.  His tragic and untimely death was a sad loss to his many friends and admirers.

entries.heading: L.R. Collier
paras: The Bar & Pavilion alterations produced a new high level in the bar profits was attained under the chairmanship of L.R. Collier - £230. It was decided to devote some of this money to increased storage space, and other desirable amenities.  The visitors’ dressing room until this time was incorporated in the main body of the pavilion.  A year or two earlier the partition was made to fold back in order to give more space in the bar after the game.  It was now decided to remove the partition altogether and to erect a new structure at the rear.  The work was undertaken by contractors during the winter months in order to be ready for the opening of the 1959 season.

entries.heading: G.B. Thompson
paras: The planning and detailed work of these improvements mostly fell upon the shoulders of the Hon secretary, G.B. Thompson, who also put forward a long-term plan for the re-development of she general structure on a more elaborate and permanent basis.  Briefly, his scheme consisted of three phases, each to be undertaken as and when money became available: -
Phase 1.  Consisted of the erection of new dressing rooms on the site now occupied by the home team's dressing room, at the top side of the main pavilion.
Phase 2.  Incorporated the toilet, showers, and washing facilities adjoining and at the rear of the dressing rooms.
Phase 3.   Was the re-organisation and link-up of the tea pavilion with the main 	body.
By a narrow margin the committee did not accept the scheme.

entries.heading: P.F.S. Bowerbank
paras: P.F.S. Bowerbank retired from the captaincy of the 1st Xl, and though he continued as a player it would now seem an opportune moment to summarize his activities since joining the club in 1949.  Sutton cricket had barely recovered from the war years when he became captain in 1951, and under his leadership during the following eight years the club regained its former status.

His strong personality and his own personal ability laid the foundations of this revival.  His great knowledge of the game and of the tactics to be employed under varying conditions, combined with shrewd field placing’s, and his own fearless skill close to the bat, were the deciding factors in numerous victories, and it was rare to see him drop a catch in any position.  Invariably he closed an innings to give both sides an incentive to go for a result.  He was a forceful batsman as his record of 1445 runs in 39 innings proved, and during his career he made a number of centuries.  He was also a useful bowler until an injury prevented further activity in this direction.  In 1952 he took over the office of Hon Ground Secretary, and in this capacity his knowledge and manual work proved of immense value to the, club in the improvements to the turf itself and to the pavilion enclosure and gardens.  The club was fortunate in that he continued his keen interest in this work after retiring from the captaincy.

entries.heading: Brian Clewer
paras: To succeed a man like Pat Bowerbank was not an easy task for B.H.D. Clewer, who was unanimously elected as his successor, and subsequent events proved the members had made a wise choice.  He was popular with both his own team and with the opponents, nor did he fail in his duties as skipper.  Captaincy of a cricket eleven, and particularly of a large club, is not a simple task.  The job can only be learned from experience, combined with the ability to adapt oneself to the needs of the moment, both on and off the field.  There are, of course, other qualities required, but in all respects Brian Clewer did extremely well in his first season in his leadership of the club.

entries.heading: Brian Clewer & Pat Bowerbank
paras: The 1st Xl won nineteen and lost twelve of the 47 matches (one of two days) played on Saturdays and Sundays.  P. Bowerbank headed the batting averages with 36 in sixteen innings, but the outstanding batsman of the season was Brian Clewer who did not miss even one match and scored 1,472 runs in 48 innings - average 33.  This aggregate was in 1st Xl matches only and constituted a new club record.  In addition, he made 126 runs during the Cricket Week, bringing his season's total for the club to 1,598, including three centuries and two scores in the nineties.

entries.heading: Brian Clewer & Peter Yates
paras: Perhaps the most noteworthy innings was against Knowle & Dorridge when with six wickets down for 104 he was joined by Peter Yates, and together they added 88 runs in thirty-four minutes before the declaration.  Clewer's share of the partnership was 65 and his 109 runs were scored in 124 minutes.  With his slow spin bowling he also accounted for 41 wickets and made 25 catches, an all-round excellence which contributed largely to the success of the team.

entries.heading: Neil Houghton
paras: Neil Houghton, elder son of the popular sportsman Eric Houghton (Aston Villa and England footballer, Manager, and Warwickshire and Lincolnshire cricketer) had a fine season too, though only in his twentieth year.  His consistent and correct batsman-ship earned him 1,097 runs with an average of over 30, and he also secured 61 wickets including a "hat trick".

entries.heading: Geoff Pritchett and Alan Couchman
paras: By narrow margins both Geoff Pritchett and Alan Couchman failed in the quest for a thousand runs though, by including matches other than 1st Xl, they both reached the target.  The former made a fine century against Warwickshire Pilgrims and, with Neil Houghton, created a new first wicket partnership record for Sutton of 192.

entries.heading: L. Pellow
paras: Les Pellow, for once, did not attain his hundred wickets, but his aggregate of 87 was a good performance in a season when batsmen held the upper hand.

entries.heading: P.J. Lowe
paras: Peter Lowe, with 57 victims behind the stumps, represented Warwickshire 2nd in most of their matches and was later presented, together with other members of the team, with a silver salver in commemoration, of Warwickshire's first Championship in the Minor Counties competition.

entries.heading: Brian Clewer and J. Eardley
paras: The Cricket Week in August again provided some interesting games for those members able to participate. Undoubtedly, the outstanding feature of the week was the magnificent third partnership against the Old Blundellians.  The visitors scored 230 and Sutton lost their first two wickets with only 15 runs on the board when Brian Clewer and J. Eardley became associated.  They were still not parted when the opponents score was passed, and the partnership of 217 ranks as the highest for any wicket, to date, for the club.
Norman Horner,

Playing for Warwickshire in A.V. Wolton's benefit match at Sutton, Norman Horner gave a wonderful exhibition of stroke play in scoring 145 out of the opening partnership of 219 in eighty-three minutes.

entries.heading: P. Mantle
paras: P. Mantle, a fast medium bowler, took 17 wickets for the 1st Xl, and was honoured in being selected for the English School's Xl (Under 15), and performed creditably against the Public School's (Under 15) Xl.

entries.heading: T.E. Biggs, Peter Wells, and R.M. Wilkinson
paras: The 2nd Xl, again under J. Frisby's captaincy, won twelve of the twenty-four Saturday fixtures.  Nine members of the side averaged over 20, a healthy sign that there were a number of players capable of performing well with the bat if called upon by the 1st team.  The bowling was shared by T.E. Biggs, Peter Wells, and R.M. Wilkinson, who between them took 92 wickets, not including Sundays.

entries.heading: Peter Cadman and John Ratledge
paras: The Sunday 2nd Xl, under P.M. Wilkinson's captaincy, won eight of the nineteen matches, with Peter Cadman (39) and John Ratledge (35) at the head of the batting. Against Moseley 2nd,

entries.heading: A. Giggins
paras: In the 2nd Xl A. Giggins took four wickets in successive balls.

entries.heading: Hugh Leigh
paras: The interest in the Sutton Coldfield Festival Shield "knock out" competition, inaugurated in 1951, had been waning, largely due to the lack of central control.  In 1957, J H Leigh undertook to put it on a firm footing with the sanction of the committee, and as a result there was a marked revival of interest by the local clubs. All matches were played at the Rectory Park in the mid-season period, in the final this year Sutton defeated Streetly and the Shield was presented by Tom Graveney, of Gloucestershire and England.

entries.heading: Mayor, Councilor A. Gunby
paras: The clubs playing in the competition contributed an amount of money with which a silver candelabrum was purchased and presented to the Mayor, Councilor A. Gunby, towards the Mayoral collection of civic plate.

entries.heading: R. Mee and P. Impett
paras: Two schoolboy cricketers showed promising form during the season and all played for the 1st X1 in several games.  R. Mee and P. Impett were both concerned in century partnerships against Aldridge and Wednesbury C. C’s. respectively and in each case when the side was in trouble.

entries.heading: Sam Bridgens, T.E. Biggs & D. Alford
paras: The profits on the bar was £331, during the season soared to new heights under the chairmanship of T.E. Biggs.  Although it was a good "drinking" summer, this figure was not achieved without some hard work and organization.  In this respect, Sam Bridgens, a vice president in retirement, was a tower of strength, and his consistent and valuable work was both appreciated and recognised by the members.  He was ably assisted by T.E. Biggs and David Alford.

entries.heading: R. Hill
paras: R.S. Hill (Stan) passed away in January.  As mentioned earlier in these pages he satisfied an ambition by playing cricket until he was sixty years old, but since that date in 1957 his health had deteriorated.  At times he was so ill that his doctor (jokingly, referred to himself as “umpires") twice "signified his dismissal", but on both occasions he proved their decisions to be wrong.

He recovered sufficiently to be a regular attender at the M.C.C.C. Umpires meetings, and "stood" in a few games during the 1959 season.  Details of his career have already been written, and to these may be added that with his passing the club had lost a true friend and a sportsman whose dedication and devotion to the game was an outstanding example to all.

entries.heading: Brian Clewer, J. Frisby, C. Groves, R.H. Smith, G. Beech & Tony Reason
paras: For the first and only time, to date, the Annual General Meeting was held in the pavilion.  This had become possible by the recently increased amount of room following the absorption of the visitor’s dressing room, and the installation of heating facilities a few years before.  The meeting was well attended and a better financial position was reported by the Hon treasurer who stated that there was an excess of income over expenditure of, £216 on the accounts.

The meeting decided that the end of the financial year should in future be 30th September instead of 31st January.  Brian Clewer was re-elected 1st X1 captain, J. Frisby 2nd X1, C. Groves - Hawks, R.H. Smith - Owls, and G. Beech - Grasshoppers. Tony Reason took over the duties of Team secretary.

A few weeks prior to the commencement of the season some alarm was caused by secretary reporting on a shortage of playing members, but with the influx of seventeen new applications the position had righted itself by the end of April.

entries.heading: Mrs. M. Thompson and Mrs. E. Smith
paras: After years of loyal service Mrs. M. Thompson and Mrs. E. Smith found themselves unable to devote as much time as previously to the catering.  Members expressed their gratitude and warm thanks to these ladies, who were later presented with suitable mementos in appreciation of their services.

Brian Clewer and T. Biggs, with their respective wives, and Mrs. J. Locker, undertook the onerous catering duties, and by a different method of organisation, the necessity of appealing to unwilling volunteers, which had or some years proved unsatisfactory, was avoided, though it was not anticipated that there would be the handsome profits accruing as in the past.

entries.heading: Norman Sharp
paras: Some years earlier R.J. Wood had presented the club with an Honours Board, of Life Members.  Two further boards were presented by Norman Sharp, for Presidents and Captains.

entries.heading: Norman Marsh & G.B. Thompson
paras: The lower ground pavilion, for a long while, had, of necessity, had to take a back seat in the improvements programme.  By current standards the amenities were unsatisfactory.
Half the membership used the ground, and to suffer those conditions was not considered fair either to the members or to their opponents.

Accordingly, the committee decided that improvements here were the first priority and arrangements were out in hand for completion before the season commenced.  The water supply was extended to the lower ground, toilet and washing facilities added at the rear, alterations were made to the dressing rooms, and a verandah added along the frontage.  The total cost exceeded £800, towards which the Warwickshire C.C.C. Supporters Association generously donated £400.  The "Norman Marsh Memorial" clock was re-erected in the gable of the main pavilion. Much of the planning, detail work and supervision were as usual, in the capable hands of the Hon secretary, G.B. Thompson, to whom the members owe a deep debt of gratitude.

entries.heading: Jack Frisby
paras: In early May 1960 the sudden death of Jack Frisby shocked and grieved his many friends. He had skippered the 2nd Xl since 1953 and had missed very few games during that time, and had even played for the team on the Saturday before his death.

Jack had proved himself an efficient and popular captain, and though, as most captains’ are, naturally keen upon the performances of his own side, he was always anxious to advance the claims of young players.  Only a few days before he died, he remarked to the writer that the team had reached the stage for which he had strived for many years - namely - that the team was now largely composed of younger members capable of performing creditably in higher circles if called upon.

Jack Frisby was a good club man, always supporting the club's social and other activities, whilst his ready wit and jovial personality made him a popular figure with the members of his own club and those of the opponents. As a cricketer he was a useful fast medium bowler, though latterly he had largely subjected himself to the interests of the younger members, and a batsman capable of keeping an end up if the necessity arose.

entries.heading: Alan Couchman
paras: Hopes of a repetition of a summer like the previous year were dispelled when   towards the end of June the weather became unsettled and remained so until the end and caused considerable interference to a number of matches.  However, the Festival Shield "knock out" again proved a source of attraction and provided some keen and attractive games.  Highcroft Hall defeated Sutton in the final, and presentation of the Shield was made by John Warr, the Middlesex captain.  A feature of the competition was Alan Couchman's two successive centuries, a remarkable achievement in space of twenty overs.

entries.heading: Frank Styles
paras: In spite of unsettled conditions, the cricket week, which had now become an established feature of the club, provided some exciting games. Frank Styles (now over 80) was a welcome visitor during the week and did a little umpiring as well.

entries.heading: Clewer, Couchman  & Bowerbank
paras: A fine finish against Ashfield on Whit Monday is worthy of some detail.  Ashfield declared with 222 for 7 on the board leaving Sutton ample time in which to get the runs.  A disastrous start.  However, with the first three wickets going down for 7 runs and the fourth at 47, left the home side well behind the clock.  At this point Clewer and Couchman became associated and 176 runs were still needed in ninety minutes.  After "digging in" for a time the pair batted so well that in a partnership of 139 they finally caught up with the clock.  Both lost their wickets at a critical time, when 37 were still required in eighteen minutes.  Yates and Lowe left quickly, but Bowerbank held firm. With four balls to go thirteen runs were wanted.  These, Bowerbank hit for 2,6,4,4, and Sutton won an excellent match by two wickets.

entries.heading: Geoff Pritchett
paras: Leicester Ivanhoe, against Sutton's 195 for 2, declared, (Geoff Pritchett 99), made the winning run off the fifth ball of the final over with the last pair at the wicket.

entries.heading: N. Houghton and B. Clewer
paras: The two outstanding players during the season were N. Houghton and B. Clewer.  The former made 1,131 runs with an average of nearly 30, and also took 63 wickets, whilst the latter obtained 991 runs and secured 71 wickets.

entries.heading: John McCarthy and Geoff Pritchett
paras: John McCarthy and Geoff Pritchett were also in consistent form, as was R.A. Mee, who in twenty-four innings made 574 runs (ave. 27).  He headed the Saturday side's batting with an average of 34, a fine performance and bright outlook for a boy only seventeen years of age.

entries.heading: Peter Cadman & Roger Coombs
paras: Upon the death of Jack Frisby, P.H.B. Cadman was elected to the vacant position of captain, on both Saturdays and Sundays.  The Saturday team won ten of the twenty-two matches and the Sunday side fifteen of the seventeen.  The combined total of twenty-five victories constituted a record for one team, although at this time the official records did not combine the two days.

Nevertheless, the fifteen wins on Sundays had never before been equaled by any one team on any day. Peter Cadman scored 877 runs (average 27) with a century against Wolverhampton 2nd. Roger Coombs obtained 657 runs and had 47 victims behind the stumps.

entries.heading: T.E. Biggs and Alan Bedggood
paras: Perhaps the greatest contribution to the success of the team, however, was made by the two slow bowlers, T.E. Biggs and Alan Bedggood.  The former took 83 wickets (ave. 8.7) and for the club reached a hundred wickets in the last match.  The latter took 91 wickets (ave. 11.3) for the 2nd team and a total of 114 for the club.

entries.heading: G.Y. Wilkes, D. Barker, P. Webster, D. Barker & C. Groves
paras: Though the Hawks, led by C. Groves, only won four matches they gave a much-improved account of themselves against strong opposition (for a 3rd X1).  Four of the drawn games ended with the team in a winning position for nine of the opponents were back in the pavilion.
The outstanding batsmen were G.Y. Wilkes, D. Barker, and P. Webster, all averaging nearly 30.  D. Barker scored a century and C. Groves obtained 37 wickets.

entries.heading: D. Whitehead
paras: For the Owls, the most noteworthy achievement was D. Whitehead's ten 'wickets against Walmley for 28 runs.  This was the first time on record that a Sutton player had performed this feat on the Rectory Park ground in one innings.

entries.heading: Geoff Hadfield
paras: Geoff Hadfield for the Owls, against Lapworth, had the remarkable bowling figures of 8 wickets for 2 runs, and only one scoring stroke was made off the fifty-two balls delivered.

entries.heading: Grasshoppers
paras: The Grasshoppers won 9 of the 18 matches. T. Lock and A. Rice did well with the bat, whilst R.H. Smith, G. Beech, and K. Pickering, and also E. Mann, exceeded twenty wickets.

entries.heading: P.D. Hutton
paras: After a membership of over twenty years, P.D. Hutton's business commitments took him south, and he was elected a vice president.  Though seldom hitting the headlines as a player he was a most useful batsman and made many good scores, and it is also on record that he captured four Knowle & Dorridge wickets in four balls.  He did good work for the club in many ways, particularly as Social Secretary.

entries.heading: Pat Bowerbank & Eric Beavan
paras: The pavilion with its thatched roof and timbered walls, and the enclosure itself had always been an object of admiration, but never more so than, in 1960.  Pat Bowerbank had made himself responsible for the enclosure lawns and flower beds (as also for the playing area improvements contained in the last paragraph) and in the autumn he planted several hundred rose bushes of named varieties in and outside the enclosure.  A few years previously, Eric Beavan, a vice president, had supplied the gravel for the paths.

Of the Rectory Park itself it will be remembered that it was purchased in 1939 by the Corporation from the Ecclesiastical Commissioners.  Prior to that date it was a private park with the cricket grounds the only part devoted to recreational facilities.  Only a few of the local inhabitants ever visited the park and the rural surroundings gave much pleasure to the cricketers and to the spectators.  Since the park has become public property, the Corporation have made full use of it as a recreational centre, and numerous football grounds have been made.  There has also been a greatly increased, amount of vandalism.

entries.heading: Tribute to Patrick E. S. Bowerbank
paras: Although Pat Bowerbank has only been playing cricket in the Midlands for three seasons, he quickly made his mark as one of the leading personalities in club cricket. A powerful and consistent run-getter for Sutton Coldfield, he is also one of the fastest scorers in the game.
He has made centuries against Harborne, Olton, Bournville (in 70 minutes) and for Warwickshire Clubs versus Staffordshire Clubs, and made seventeen centuries in club cricket.
His figures for 1951 were: -38 innings, 13 not out, 1,319 runs, highest score 135 not out, centuries 3, average 52.7.

He was a good fast-medium bowler with a very short run-up, a shining example to those who waste so much energy and time. In 1939 took 100 wickets, and once all ten wickets in an innings. As captain of Sutton Coldfield, he was fast becoming known as a keen and shrewd skipper, who gets the best from his side, who is not afraid to make an early declaration, and who goes for a result, win or lose.

Before coming to the Midlands, Pat Bowerbank, played minor Counties Cricket for Devon (his native county) and for Suffolk in 1947. He has also played club cricket for the Devon Dumplings, Exmouth, Sidmouth, Colchester and East Essex, and for the Bournemouth Sports Club. During three years in the Middle East, he played cricket with Norman Yardley, Jack Marshall and Vic Cannings.
Whilst cricket is his first-love, Pat Bowerbank has played representative Rugger and Squash, and is a keen shot and fly fisherman.
Pat was employed at IMI Kynock in Birmingham and left the Midlands to take up a senior post with the National Rifle Association at Bisley in Surrey.

entries.heading: T.E. Biggs, Peter Cadman, and J. Salmon
paras: Most of the officers of the preceding year were re-elected at the 1961 Annual General Meeting.  The only exceptions were that T.E. Biggs assumed the 2nd Xl captaincy on both Saturdays and Sundays, replacing the late Jack Frisby and Peter Cadman the Hawks and J. Salmon became the newly elected captain of the Owls.

An amendment to the rules was passed to the effect that the Committee should consist of the Hon Secretary, Hon Treasurer, the Captain of the First Eleven, and six members, the Chairman of Committee to be elected from their number. This replaced the old rule of the 1946 code whereby all officers, captains of all teams, and secretaries of the various activities, as well as six other members, comprised the committee.  With the growth of the club since that time it can be assumed how top heavy the committee had become with, sometimes, nearly twenty members present, and in consequence it was difficult to get through the business satisfactorily in the requisite time.

entries.heading: G B Thompson
paras: G.B. Thompson announced his retirement from active participation in the game, though he continued in the responsible and onerous duty of Hon secretary.  He had joined the club in 1945 (he played his earlier cricket in the London area) and had always rendered loyal and consistent service to the club, and his practical value in many ways cannot be over-estimated.  He was elected a vice president.

entries.heading: The Jack Frisby Memorial Seat
paras: To perpetuate the memory of Jack Frisby a seat was presented to the club by some of the members as a permanent memorial to a popular member and captain. The membership continued on the up-grade, with 3 Life Members, 94 playing, 78 Vice Presidents, and 147 non playing members, a total of 322.

entries.heading: Brian Clewer
paras: Under the captaincy of Brian Clewer, the 1st X1 again proved themselves one of the strongest of Midland clubs with ten Saturday and eleven Sunday victories.  13 Matches were lost and 8 drawn, with a TIE with Burton-on-Trent, a match in which Sutton declared at 182 for 8 and Burton, on the stroke of time, were dismissed at the same total.
The "spell" that had existed against Coventry & N.W. was broken at last.  They were defeated by Sutton for the first time since 1938.
Sutton was defeated by Harborne by one run in a thrilling finish.  Chasing a score of 210, they lost the last two wickets off the third and fifth balls of the final over.

At an early stage and throughout the game against Pickwick it appeared odds on a victory for Sutton. Pickwick wickets tumbled regularly, 95 for 9, but the last pair held fast and finally enabled a declaration to be made with 148 on the board. Sutton coasted along comfortably to 124 for 4 and with ample time at their disposal.  It appeared all over bar the shouting, but a dramatic collapse left Pickwick the winners by 2 runs on the stroke of time.

entries.heading: Neil Houghton, Geoff Pritchett, & John McCarthy
paras: Against Market Drayton at the Rectory Park the home team declared at 222 for 1. Neil Houghton (121 not out) scored 94 for the first wicket with Geoff Pritchett, and 127 for the second wicket with John McCarthy.

entries.heading: W.N. Houghton
paras: Neil Houghton was the outstanding player of the 1961 season.  He scored 1332 runs with an average of 37.  With matches for Warwickshire 2nd, the Midlands C.C.C., and others, he made nearly two thousand runs during the season, and was honoured in being selected as one of the Conference "Cricketers of the Year".  He also took 47 wickets.

entries.heading: Bedggood, Wells & Fitzgerald
paras: A Bedggood secured 102 wickets and was well backed up by the pace bowlers, Peter Wells and Vince Fitzgerald who claimed 56 and 45 wickets, respectively for the 1st Xl.

entries.heading: T.E. Biggs and L. Pellow
paras: The 2nd Xl, under T.E. Biggs, won eleven Saturday and thirteen Sunday fixtures, compared with ten and fifteen, respectively, the previous year. The losses were sixteen, but with only four drawn games the cricket was highly entertaining.  In the batting there was nobody who stood out above the rest, the successful results were achieved mainly by the slow bowlers, T.E. Biggs and L. Pellow. The former took 109 wickets for 10.1, and the latter 115 wickets for 10.7.

entries.heading: Roger Coombs Wicket-keeping Record
paras: A wicket-keeping record was established by Roger Coombs who claimed 76 victims behind the stumps during the season.  This remarkable achievement was accomplished mainly with the 2nd Xl - 73.  The other 3 were for the 1st Team.  For the past fifty years the club had possessed wicket-keepers of the highest class in club cricket, and this period
was no exception.  Roger Coombs would have gained a place in almost any club's 1st team, but with Sutton he was unfortunate in that he had to play "second fiddle" to P.J. Lowe.

entries.heading: Jack Wood
paras: Jack Wood passed away during the year.  He had been associated with the club for about sixty years, first as the scorer for the 1st Xl, and later as a vice president.  He was a keen and regular spectator at most home games, and also did a little umpiring.  In this respect he once gave eleven balls in an over and would probably have increased this total if the batting side captain had not decided to close the innings.  (He had dozed off).

entries.heading: Norman Sharp & Club Officers
paras: Alderman A E Terry was re-elected President, and the "working" officials, too, were all re-elected. Brian Clewer was again 1st Xl captain, whilst Pat Bowerbank, emanating from semi-retirement, succeeded T E Biggs, who had left the district, as captain of the 2nd team.  The Hawks, Owls, and Grasshoppers were to be captained by C. Groves, J. Ratledge, and G. Beech, respectively.  Only Norman Sharp of the general committee did not offer himself for re-election, and his place was taken by L.R. Collier, who was subsequently appointed committee chairman.  N. Sharp had served on the committee since 1930.

entries.heading: Norman Sharp
paras: Throughout the period Norman had attended all but about half a dozen meetings and every General Meeting (except one when he was away from the district) since becoming a full member in 1919.
At the Annual General Meeting of the Midlands Club Cricket Conference Norman Sharp was elected President of the Conference, an honour not only to himself but also to the club.

entries.heading: R. H. Smith
paras: The Hon treasurer, R H Smith, in his report stated that there was a profit of only £10 on the year, and gave a warning to the members present that with ever increasing expenditure efforts would have to be made in order to make ends meet.

entries.heading: Mrs Clewer, Mrs Biggs, Mrs Locker & Ken Walker
paras: With two matches on the ground every Saturday and most Sundays, the catering department had been fully extended in providing teas for both players and spectators, and it was not surprising that Brian Clewer and his wife, who bore the brunt of the organising found the responsibilities too great, even though they had been ably assisted by T. Biggs, his wife, and Mrs. Locker. Upon their retirement a non-playing member, Ken Walker, stepped into the breach, a gesture which was much appreciated.  The weather throughout the season was not conducive to watching cricket and with the consequent big drop in spectator attendance it was not a good result from the financial angle, but nevertheless with his equanimity and untiring efforts his services were much appreciated.

entries.heading: W.N. Houghton
paras: Neil Houghton was selected as a Conference "Cricketer of the Year 1962", and was the outstanding player in the club, though the general team work was excellent.  In scoring 1359 runs Houghton topped the batting averages with 37.7, making two centuries and ten half centuries.  He also secured 51 wickets, mostly in the first half of the season, after which, following the arrival of D. Drake, he had fewer opportunities.

entries.heading: D. Drake
paras: D. Drake, an off-spin bowler, was attached to the Fusiliers at the newly built St George Barracks and in his first season with the club obtained 116 wickets.  Commencing with the Owls he soon graduated to the Second team where he took 65 wickets, and then to the First where his 45 victims cost only 9.2 runs each.

entries.heading: Geoff Pritchett, Alan Couchman, Bob Mee & John McCarthy
paras: Geoff Pritchett was his usual consistent self with the bat, as also was Alan Couchman, whilst R. Mee of the younger generation batted very well at times in scoring 677 runs.
A bad start was made against Little Aston Stragglers but the side was rescued by Alan Couchman (121) and John McCarthy (74 not out) in a fine partnership of 176.

entries.heading: Bedggood & Wells
paras: Alan Bedggood was the most successful bowler with 94 wickets, and was well supported by Peter Wells whose pace howling earned him 63 wickets, a creditable performance on the easy paced wickets

entries.heading: Bowerbank and Les Pe1low
paras: There were two main contributory factors in the outstandingly successful season of the 2nd Xl - Pat Bowerbank's captaincy and his batting and Les Pe1low’s bowling, of 38 completed matches (10 others were rained off) 29 were won, 5 lost, and 4 drawn. To obtain results in all but four of the games was in itself, a tribute to Bowerbank's captaincy, and in a season when the weather caused so much interference.  The winning of 29 matches constituted a record for any of the club's teams, and even this may have been bettered had the weather been kinder.
Pat Bowerbank scored 921 runs with an average of 38.3, and made one century, against Leicester Ivanhoe.

entries.heading: Roger Coombs, N. Goldsby T. Aston & P. Baker
paras: Also in the 2nd Xl was Roger Coombs who scored 619 runs and obtained 62 victims behind the stumps,
One of the more youthful generation, N. Goldsby, obtained 556 runs (Ave. 29) and was a magnificent fielder.  T. Aston made 508 runs including a century against Ashfield 2nd.
T. Aston and P. Baker were also associated in a first wicket undefeated partnership in the 2nd teams win over Ashfield 2nd by ten wickets, their combined ages being only thirty-eight.

entries.heading: Charles Groves
paras: The Hawks were unable to repeat their success of the previous year, winning only five of the nineteen matches.  With a side less agile in the field than many of their opponents it was not surprising that the fielding let them down on numerous occasions.  Charles Groves secured most wickets (48) but with more support in the field may have considerably improved upon these figures.

entries.heading: R. Cook and D. Whitehead
paras: The Owls, however, did exceedingly well in winning twelve of the fourteen completed games.  Two games were lost and none drawn, with no fewer than eight matches rained off.  R. Cook in seven innings averaged 44, and D. Whitehead obtained 31 wickets for an average of 8.80.

entries.heading: R.J. Pickwell, E. Mann, A. Butler & G. Beech
paras: The Grasshoppers had an average season with 9 wins, 8 losses, and satisfactory results were no doubt achieved through the consistent bowling of R.J. Pickwell, E. Mann, A. Butler, and G. Beech.  Abbots Bromley was defeated by one wicket after scoring 78 and having eight Sutton batsmen back in the pavilion for 38.

entries.heading: Alderman Sidney G. Brown
paras: During the season the death of Alderman Sidney G. Brown, a vice president, was a sad loss to the club.  A keen all-round sportsman, he spent much of his leisure time at the Rectory Park, and as a practicing solicitor in the town, and also Chairman of the Parks & Estates Committee on the Town Council, he was always helpful in advising1 the club upon matters within his province.

entries.heading: Ralph E. Pearce
paras: Ralph Pearce, another vice president, also passed away. As an ardent follower of the game, he had rendered good service to the club.  A few years prior to his death his self-imposed task of taking round the collection box had resulted in the handsome figure of £90 being added to the club's income, an amount which had not been approached either before or since, and only proved what could be achieved by a little earnest endeavor.

entries.heading: A.D. Whittaker and John Ratledge
paras: The Annual Dance held in the Town Hall just before Christmas was a great success, again-due to the efforts of the social secretary A.D. Whittaker, with the assistance, amongst others, of John Ratledge.  A profit of £109 was made.

entries.heading: R.M. Wilkinson
paras: By reason of ill health, R.M. Wilkinson retired from the scene as a player.  It was in 1927 that he first joined the club, and at that time he showed every promise of becoming an outstanding player.  This early promise never fully materialized but nevertheless, throughout the thirty-five years he was always a very reliable cricketer mostly with the 2nd team as a medium, pace seam bowler, for whom he had many good performances, as also on occasions with the 1st Xl.

He was a good middle order batsman, and in spite of his lack of stature, capable of hitting the ball hard.  He also rendered constant administrative services to the club in various capacities, including those of Hon minute Secretary, Hon Team Secretary, Hon "Treasurer, Captain of 2nd Xl, and as a committee member for a number of years.  He was always one who could be relied upon to support all social and fund-raising activities, and upon retirement gave his services in the important' role of umpire.

entries.heading: L R Collier
paras: As usual the year commenced with the Annual General Meeting held at the Royal Hotel, with L R Collier in the chair, deputising for the President, Alderman A. E Terry.  The Hon secretary’s report had been circulated to the members prior to the meeting and covered the main activities of the previous year.

entries.heading: The accounts showed a surplus of £65, a satisfactory position
paras: The membership continued to increase and had now reached over 150, of which about a hundred were players.  The custom until some ten years prior to this date had been to elect vice presidents from anyone willing to subscribe to the club, and upon any members nomination.  Accordingly, there was an ever-increasing list.

At that time, it was decided that in future the office of vice president should be regarded as an honour both to the individual and to the club, and nominations were to be made according to the person's services to the town or to the club, and to be elected by the committee.

All other subscribers, other than players, were to be regarded as non-playing members.  It will be appreciated that at the time there were some vice presidents who were scarcely deserving of the honour, and though there are still a number of those remaining, that have now been subscribing for many years and one would consider they have earned this recognition.

Discussions on a New Pavilion, but no minutes were recorded – it was an open forum – A brain Storm on what was requires for the future.  During the previous season L.R. Collier had issued an appeal to members for donations towards the cost (£184) of a new building.  An excellent response produced all but £26, and as a result the new structure appeared before the commencement of the season on a site not far removed from the position of the old building including the Groundsman’s Tool Shed. The shed in which the club's equipment was stored had been in a state of collapse for several years.  It was an old army hut which had been purchased by the Corporation after the Second World War, and for which the club paid an annual rental of £5

entries.heading: Neil Houghton
paras: The previous year's administrative officers were all re-elected.  Brian Clewer was unable to continue as captain and W. Neil Houghton was appointed skipper of the 1st Xl.  Though none doubted his capability, there were some who doubted the wisdom of saddling such responsibility upon so young a man who had some stiff examinations ahead and it was also considered that his own great ability as a player may suffered.   However, as subsequent events proved, those fears were unfounded, and he carried his responsibilities extremely well.

entries.heading: Martin Bloomer & Neil Houghton
paras: Of the 41 games played by the 1st Xl, 19 were won, 10 lost and 12 were drawn.  The outstanding batsman of the season was Martin Bloomer.  Previously, a most successful batsman with Streetly C.C. this young player made his debut with the 2nd team, and soon showed his ability by scoring 281 runs in a short space of time.  Promotion to the 1st Xl followed and where he soon replaced Geoff Pritchett who had occupied the number one batting position with such great distinction for so many years, and by the end of the season he had completed his thousand runs for that team, with an aggregate of 1,300 for the club.  In thirty innings for the 1st Xl, he averaged 35 and made one century.  With Neil Houghton as his opening partner, they were a formidable combination and three times shared opening partnerships of over 100 and against Aston Manor and Olton exceeded 150.  Neil Houghton, too, had another fine season with 1181 runs (average 33).

entries.heading: Chris Barber
paras: Another young player to do well was Chris Barber.  Though unable to play as regularly as he would have wished he came second in the batting averages (34) and topped the bowling.  He was unlucky not to record a century, for against Ashfield he made 99 not out, at which time the captain declared.  The full story is that when on 98 he hit a 2 which would have given him the century but the skipper had sounded the bell before he realised the umpire had signaled "one short".  As a bowler he secured 39 wickets, including a spell of 6 for 7 to finish off the Nuneaton innings after five other bowlers had been used before, he was given the ball.

entries.heading: Fitzgerald, Wells, Barber, Houghton, Bedggood, and Drake
paras: Generally the 1st team bowling honours were shared by the "seamers" Fitzgerald, Wells, and Barber, with a combined total of 137 wickets, and the "spinners" Houghton, Bedggood, and Drake, with 148 wickets.

entries.heading: Bedggood
paras: Alan Bedggood obtained a "hat trick" against Stafford, and with four wickets in the over.

entries.heading: Pat Bowerbank
paras: Pat Bowerbank's 2nd Xl again had a most successful season. A side containing a happy blend of youth won 26 of the 40 matches.  Eight were lost, six drawn, and eight were rained off.

entries.heading: T. Aston, J. Watson, G.A. Pritchett, and M. Bloomer
paras: The batting averages were headed by eighteen-year-old T. Aston, who in 16 innings scored 457 runs (ave. 41) including a century at Newport.  Later in the season he joined Moseley in the Birmingham league. J. Watson, G.A. Pritchett, and M. Bloomer, followed closely behind, all with averages of over 30.

entries.heading: Les Pellow &  Andrew Beach
paras: The slow bowling again proved the mainstay of the attack.  Les Pellow was only sixteen wickets short of his previous season's amazing record, and his 149 wickets (4 with the 1st Xl) cost only a little over ten runs each.  Andrew Beach, a youthful off spinner, claimed 94 wickets (5 for the 1st X1), for thirteen runs each.

entries.heading: Roger Coombs
paras: Their success was enhanced by the fine wicket-keeping of Roger Coombs, who stumped 40 of his 57 victims.

entries.heading: R H Smith and A. Rice
paras: The combined results of the Hawks, Owls, and Grasshoppers, showed 27 wins and 24 losses. R H Smith was the most successful batsman, averaging 34 with the Grasshoppers.  He, and A. Rice showed their liking for the Hampton in Arden ground by repeating their stand of 190 two years before except that this time they were parted after 141 runs had been added for the third wicket.
Six bowlers shared 250 wickets, though again R.H. Smith was well to the fore with 51 wickets for fewer than 9 runs each.

entries.heading: George Beech
paras: Against Pickwick Nomads the Hawks scored 195 for 5 (George Beech 100), before the closure was applied.  They then dismissed their opponents for 7, one of the runs was an extra.  In fairness to Pickwick it perhaps should be mentioned that, on paper, they had a reasonably good batting side and had done well previously during the season, and this debacle was just one of those oddities that occasionally happen in the game.  Upon their return to the Wake Green Road club house later that evening, and before the result was announced, "NIGS" Halliwell was celebrating his achievement of being top scorer by standing drinks to the all members present.  He made 2 runs.

entries.heading: Peter Cranmer
paras: The Festival Shield competition of 1963 again proved a popular feature during the mid-season evenings. The final was contested between the 1962 winners, Walmley, and the Old Veseyans’, with Walmley in a strong position, rain caused an abandonment, and in the replay the following week the Old Veseyans were victorious, an injustice (perhaps) to Walmley.  Peter Cranmer, the former Warwickshire captain and England Rugby footballer, presented the trophy.

entries.heading: J.B. Russell
paras: For the first time, at least during the past sixty years, no sight screens were in operation on the top ground throughout the season.  The tubular frames, originally supplied by J.B. Russell some thirty-five years earlier, had finally reached the stage when no more repairs were possible.  The canvas sheets, many times repaired, had also become useless.  In view of the heavy cost of replacement the decision to renew was shelved until such time as there was general agreement upon the type of screen best suited for the purpose.  In fact, there were some who considered sight screens a doubtful luxury.

In support of this school of thought the runs obtained without them did not show any noticeable drop by comparison with other years, and in spite of the poor visibility caused by the surrounding greenery.  It is considered that batsmen are at a disadvantage during their first few overs but after surviving that initial stage their subsequent sight of the ball is not greatly impaired.   Nevertheless, a cricket ground without sight screens appears to be "undressed".

entries.heading: C. Howl
paras: C. Howl died during the summer.  Joining the club in 1930 (his earlier cricket was played at Wolverhampton) he retired from active participation in 1947.  During those years he was completely dedicated to his cricket, a little selfishly perhaps, but nevertheless it would be hard to find anyone keener on the game, and he scarcely missed a match.  But since his retirement he had not visited Rectory Park but had maintained his membership as a vice president and as a trustee since 1950.  As a player he was far from being a natural cricketer, his success as a batsman, and in fact in all departments of the game, was achieved by practice, perseverance, and the will to succeed.  He was unattractive to watch but in spite of his laboured batting techniques he made many runs and was an invaluable member of the side during the club's lean period prior to and following the war.

entries.heading: F.S. Orford
paras: F.S. Orford, a vice president, also passed away during the year.  He was the son of Doctor Orford who had played for the club about seventy years earlier, and he was a regular member of the 2nd Xl in the early part of this century before taking up a business appointment in India.  Upon retirement he returned to Sutton and, with his brother John, was a regular spectator at most matches at the Rectory Park.
