He was sadly missed by his many friends, and in his memory the family donated the cost of a new motor mower.

entries.heading: Peter J. Lowe
paras: The Midlands C.C.C. elected Peter J. Lowe. as one of the "Cricketers of the Year".  This well-deserved honour acknowledged the fact that he was one of the best wicketkeepers in Midlands’s cricket, and yet again accentuated how fortunate the club has been over the years to possess wicketkeepers of such high standard.

entries.heading: Charles Groves
paras: During the past few years, the "Penny a Week" Football Pool had made a steady income for the club of about £120 per annum.  The organizer, Charles Groves, put in a lot of work in an endeavour to make this a success, but, unfortunately, the club members, in general, failed in their support.  With just a little more interest on their part the profits could at least have been doubled.

entries.heading: Sam Bridgens
paras: For the past five years it had been unusual not to see Sam Bridgens behind the Bar counter.  As mentioned previously, he had offered his services for this duty following upon his retirement from business, and for the last four years he had undertaken the complete management as well.

It was a sad blow when at the end of the season he announced that he could not undertake the duties any longer, but nevertheless the members were very appreciative of the fine service he had given so consistently - a service, incidentally, which had almost invariably prevented him enjoying the closing stages of the cricket.

entries.heading: Ken Walker
paras: Ken Walker also found it necessary to give up the onerous catering duties.  In the past two years he had worked extremely hard in providing teas for eight elevens most weekends, with spectators in addition.  With the ever-uncertain weather conditions it was never easy to forecast the quantities of provisions that would be required.  It was unfortunate that during his period of office two poor summers were experienced, and it was through no fault of his that the financial returns were low.  Here again the members expressed their gratitude for his efforts on their behalf.

entries.heading: A. D.  Whittaker
paras: The final event of the year was, as usual, the December dance in the Town Hall, again under the care of the Social Secretary, A. D. Whittaker, who handed over to the club a profit of £133.

entries.heading: J. St Felix Dare
paras: J. St Felix Dare, the President of the West Indies Cricket Association visited this country during the season for the dual purpose of attending the meeting of the Imperial Cricket Conference in London, and in support of the West Indies side touring the country.  His name is mentioned here because of his connection with Sutton.

He was a nephew of Horace Lott, a stalwart of the Sutton Coldfield C.C. in the early part of this century, and through him; came to Bishop Vesey's School to complete his education.  Upon leaving school and before returning to his home in Guyana he played for, the club for a season.  He was a good, though not outstanding, all-round cricketer, but subsequently he played for and, it is believed, captained Jamaica.  He re-visited Sutton during his brief stay in Birmingham on the occasion of the Test Match.

entries.heading: Alderman A.E. Terry, J.P
paras: Alderman A.E. Terry, J.P. was re-elected President at the Annual General Meeting, as were the following officials for all the principal offices.

entries.heading: Tony Reason, & C: H. Maddocks
paras: Tony Reason relinquished the position of Hon Team Secretary after four years in this exacting job.

Though perhaps not showing the same mark of efficiency as some of his predecessors, he had, nevertheless, carried out his duties well.  Prior to the meeting members had been circulated appealing for a volunteer, but the only response was from a non-playing member, I. Crichton.  After being elected, business commitments in the north necessitated his resignation before the season commenced.  Subsequently, C: H. Maddocks accepted the office.

entries.heading: Captains
paras: W.N. Houghton, P.E.S. Bowerbank, and J.W. Ratledge, were all re-elected, but G.H. Hadfield and G.W. Beech replaced C. Groves and T.C. Lock in the Owls and Grasshoppers respectively.

entries.heading: R.H. Smith
paras: A loss of £110 was reported by the Hon Treasurer, R.H. Smith. The full subscription plus, a match fee of 2/6 for playing members had remained at two and a half guineas for a number of years, and in view of the heavy costs of running the club and the amount of cricket many members obtained the figure was considered inadequate.  Accordingly, the subscription was raised to £4-0-0, with the same match fee for members over 25 years of age, and scaled downwards for those under that age.  Non-players were raised to £1 10 0.

entries.heading: D.P. Locker, G.B. Thompson, and C. Groves
paras: Extending over several years negotiations had been in progress with the Borough Council regarding an extension of the existing lease, due to expire in 1967.  D.P. Locker, a playing member, had been acting as legal adviser on the club's behalf, and together with the Hon secretary G.B. Thompson, and C. Groves, the views of the club had been put forward to the Parks and Estates Committee.  Prior to the present date the Council had agreed to grant a further twenty, one year lease provided the club accented certain conditions.

One of the conditions was that the fence, trees, and hedge on the north side be uprooted and two hockey pitches made each extending in a north to south direction from the edge of the cricket square.  This plan was not acceptable to the club and after further negotiations, in which the President took part, the Council finally reversed their previous decision and accepted the club's proposal that another hockey pitch be made running in an east-west direction between the north fence and the gardens of the Rectory Road houses, this area to be under the control of the club.  At the Annual Dinner the final acceptance was announced, and the thanks of those present was expressed to the sub-committee, for their perseverance towards this satisfactory conclusion.
L.R. Collier, H.A. Couchman, J.W. Ratledge, D.P. Locker, B. Clewer, J. McCarthy,

After two years as Chairman of the Committee L.R. Collier found himself unable to continue in office.  He had been an able and enthusiastic chairman and had conducted the affairs of the club in a businesslike and conscientious manner. H.A. Couchman, who had been elected to the committee, succeeded him as chairman.  J.W. Ratledge and D.P. Locker were elected to the Committee, replacing B. Clewer, who had moved to live in Coventry and J. McCarthy, who had taken a dental appointment in Borneo.

entries.heading: N. Sharp
paras: Norman Sharp was elected as a Trustee of the club to fill the vacancy caused by the death of Clifford Howl in 1963.

entries.heading: Ken Walker  Gordon Thompson
paras: Considerable difficulty was experienced in finding a successor to Ken Walker following his retirement from the catering duties.  A member offered his services but then declined when it was found that a circular letter to all the ladies produced only a poor response.  Gordon Thompson, Hon sec, was left "carrying the baby".  By personal contact all ladies connected with the club were invited to a meeting at his house.  The meeting was well attended and as a result a Ladies Tea Committee was formed, and sufficient support guaranteed, but only just in time for the commencement of the season.

entries.heading: Sam Bridgens
paras: The retirement, too, of Sam Bridgens had also left the bar without a leaded. However, under Peter Cadman, a satisfactory committee was organised and players and non-players volunteered to steward when necessary.  Incidentally, Stan, though not in charge of the ordering, probably gave more service behind the bar than any other member throughout the season.

entries.heading: Pat Bowerbanks
paras: In the early part of the year Pat Bowerbank, in his capacity of Hon Ground Secretary, carried out considerable ground repairs and to the perimeter fencing.  However, financial assistance was sought from the Borough Council but it was not granted.

Mention has been made previously of the flower garden and rose beds under his care.  The roses in particular had been greatly admired and as a keen member of the Royal National Rose Society he tended them with expert knowledge and produced some magnificent blooms.  During his spare time, he compiled a complete encyclopedia with full details of every variety.  He also planted many trees and quick thorn round the ground for the ultimate benefit of future generations.

entries.heading: J. McCarthy, A.A.N. Bedggood, D. Drake and J. Watson
paras: By the start of the season the playing strength had become somewhat depleted.  Four 1st Xl players had left the district for various reasons., good cricketers, had been members for only a short while.
As it happened, Bedggood, Drake, and D. Barker (Hawks Xl) all linked up with the Shrewsbury club.

entries.heading: Neil Houghton
paras: However, the departure of four 1st Xl players did not prove as serious as was at first anticipated for there were some good players in the 2nd Xl capable of filling the gaps created by their departure, and the 1st Xl in winning 19 of the 43 matches had a successful season under the captaincy of Neil Houghton.  Eleven were lost and twelve drawn, with a most exciting "tie" against Leamington at Rectory Park.  Sutton declared at 185 for 8 and Leamington lost their last wicket to the fifth ball of the last over.

The outcome of the experiment of the two-day week-end fixture at Wolverhampton was not altogether successful as the game fizzled out in a tame draw.  It is doubtful whether any advantage is to be gained from a two-day fixture in club cricket.  A failure in one innings can so easily lead to an early finish of the match, and moreover, the end of the first day's play can prove uninteresting both to players and spectators.  It is considered that two one day fixtures are more preferable from all angles.

Although Neil Houghton did not head the batting averages, he was undoubtedly the outstanding player of the season.  For the 1st Xl alone, he made 1,062 runs and took 99 wickets as well as holding the most catches (other than wicketkeepers).  He would almost certainly have performed the "double" had he not missed playing in six matches during the season.  But in all club games he played during the season he aggregated 1300 runs and obtained 109 wickets thereby completing a fine and rare "double” for a club cricketer.  His best bowling performances were 8 for 16 at Stafford, and 6 for 14 against Harborne.

entries.heading: C. Groves and P. Wells
paras: At Market Drayton a last wicket partnership by C. Groves and P. Wells saved the match for Sutton.  After the first nine wickets had fallen for 91, they increased the score by 61 in the next fifty-seven minutes.  Market Drayton also collapsed in the early stages losing six for 38, but recovered to finish with 90 for 6.

entries.heading: Neil Houghton & Brian Clewer
paras: On August Monday, on Ashfield's ground, Sutton commenced well, the second wicket not falling until the score had reached 198.  Neil Houghton caught at the wicket when on 99, and B. Clewer (76) participated in a partnership of 151.  With the scoreboard at one time reading 198 for 1, a remarkable transformation took place. P.T. Richardson took the next nine wickets for 13 runs (full analysis 9 for 51) and Sutton were dismissed for 224.  Ashfield made, 201; M.S. White also just missing a century, by three runs.

entries.heading: A.K. Couchman
paras: A.K. Couchman made a hurricane 94, including 28 off one over (three sixes, two fours and a two) against Old Edwardians.

entries.heading: Martin Bloomer & Neil Houghton
paras: The batting averages were headed by Martin Bloomer who scored 1204 runs with an average of 31.7.  This young and very promising cricketer had made further headway during the season, his attacking style proving of great value to the side.  He made a century against Coventry & N.W. and with Houghton participated in many good opening partnerships, and he represented Warwickshire 2nd in a Minor Counties fixture.

entries.heading: Brian Clewer
paras: Brian Clewer's best season was undoubtedly in 1959.  In that year he narrowly missed being elected a Conference "Cricketer of the Year", but in 1964 he was accorded the honour even though he did not quite reach the standard he attained five years previously.  He scored over a thousand runs in the season but, for the 1st Xl only he was a few runs short.  He was not frequently called upon to bowl, but when he was his teasing slow spinners were often the means of splitting threatening partnerships.

entries.heading: Charles Groves
paras: After Neil Houghton, the most successful bowler was Charles Groves.  For a number of years his talent had remained in obscurity, mostly in the lower teams.  Perhaps it was that his well-controlled leg breaks and googly bowling was not treated with the respect they deserved, and also because the support in the field was of a lower standard.  However, the gap caused by the departure of A. Bedggood for a slow spinner was offered to him and well he seized his opportunity by taking 65 wickets.

entries.heading: Vince Fitzgerald, Peter Wells, Peter Yates and Chris Barber
paras: Good support was given by the pace bowlers Vince Fitzgerald 55 wickets Peter Wells 34 wickets, Peter Yates (31), and Chris Barber (28)

entries.heading: Peter Jones
paras: Peter Jones, returning home after several years in Australia, headed the batting averages and also figured we11 in the bowling.  In his first match after his return, he made 99 not out and stumps were drawn before he had the opportunity of adding the extra run.

entries.heading: P. Baker
paras: Phil Baker made 117 not out against Ashfield.

entries.heading: Les Pellow and Andrew Beech
paras: In bowling, Les Pellow was again away out in front with 117 wickets (ave. 13.0). Andrew Beech took 36 wickets but was out of action for a considerable period through the loss of a finger in a motor accident.

entries.heading: Les Wilkes
paras: The Hawks won only four out of twenty fixtures.  Depleted strength and a shortage of members had an adverse effect on the team, and the only man who could claim any distinction was Les Wilkes who topped the batting and took most wickets.

entries.heading: Geoff Hadfield & G. Maxwell
paras: Geoff Hadfield, the Owls captain, was also handicapped through being unable to field a complete side regularly.  17 matches were played, 7 of which were won and 7 lost, and only G. Maxwell, with 46 wickets for 11 runs each, could produce any noteworthy figures.

entries.heading: G. Maxwell
paras: The Grasshoppers won 6 of the 21 matches G. Maxwell obtained 37 wickets for 9 runs each.

entries.heading: R.H. Smith
paras: Playing in a match on the lower ground in mid-season, Reg Smith was taken suddenly ill and rushed to hospital where he remained in a serious condition for six weeks.  He made a good recovery and to the delight of everybody was again in circulation before the end of the season.  The illness probably put an end to his active participation in the game and it may therefore be timely to add a few words on his career.

Most of Reg Smith's earlier cricket was associated with club cricket in the Metropolitan area and he was well advanced towards middle age when he moved to the Midlands and joined Sutton.  He had no high aspirations and was perfectly content to enjoy the game he loved amongst third team players, and he soon established himself as a decided acquisition to those teams.  With just two paces to the wicket his slow left arm bowling had many experienced batsmen in trouble, whilst as a batsman he was particularly severe on the pitched-up ball, a stroke which earned him many runs, with a top score of 90.  In turn he captained both the Owls and Grasshoppers, in which capacity he became a popular personality with members and opponents alike.  In 1957 he was appointed Hon treasurer, a job he performed exceedingly well.
G.B. Thompson, D. Alford, L.O. Tippins, D.P. Locker, W.N. Houghton and J.W. Ratledge.

Upon the completion of the signatures required by the terms of the new Lease, the General Committee, in September, began to think about the erection of a new pavilion.  The existing building was now 74 years old, and for a timbered structure was still in a remarkably good condition. The thatched roof pavilion was built in 1890 and within 4 months it was opened 1st May 1890 but was showing its age.

From time-to-time additions and improvements had of course been made, but the main structure was still the same as that erected in the days of the Rev. Bedford.  In its isolated position and with its vulnerability to fire and vandalism it is perhaps remarkable it had existed so long.

However, it was considered that its life was limited and that the time was ripe to go ahead with plans for a more modern building.  Accordingly, a sub-committee was appointed to review the prospects.  The sub-committee consisted of the Hon Secretary, G.B. Thompson, D. Alford (Quantity Surveyor), L.O. Tippins (Architect), D.P. Locker (Solicitor), W.N. Houghton (Captain), and J.W. Ratledge.

entries.heading: Les Pellow
paras: L.N. Pellow, after fourteen years with the club as a playing member, resigned his playing membership at the end of the 1954 season, by reason of a transfer of his business commitments to take up an appointment at IMI in Kiderminster. Mention has already been made of his earlier association with Kynoch's C.C. although considered by most to be approaching retirement age and past his prime from serious cricket, his ambition was to continue playing club cricket. So, Les joined his work’s colleague, Pat Bowerbank and joined the Sutton Coldfield Club where Pat had taken on the 1st Team captaincy and had Les as his vice-captain.

Les’ cricketing prowess first came to light at the age of 15, when playing for Aston Commercial School he took five wickets in six balls and was immediately offered a trial with Warwickshire County Cricket Club. He soon became well-known in the Midlands, hitting the headlines with some wonderful displays for Kynoch C.C. Performances as an all-rounder were admired throughout the county, and in the 1937 season he scored 892 runs (three centuries) in 22 innings, for an average of 40.5. Small wonder then that the name of Pellow became familiar with Warwickshire 2nds, but as a member of the Territorial Army he found himself whisked abroad at the beginning of hostilities in 1939.

Captain L. N. Pellow, R.A., served in India, Ceylon and Burma—still found time for a little cricket and played in several Army representative games, although he did spend some time as a prisoner of the Japanese. Following his “demob” he rejoined Kynoch's and was their skipper for two seasons. However, having been born and bred in Sutton Coldfield, Leslie was keen to join Sutton C.C. and in 1951 he arrived at Rectory Park to become a prolific match winning bowler.

For ten years he was a regular member of the 1st team, but for his last four seasons he retired to play in the 2nd Team.  His cleverly flighted left arm spin bowling brought him 1441 wickets for Sutton alone (there is no record of his successes before he joined Sutton) at a cost of under 14 runs each, and included the club record of 165 wickets in the 1962 season. As a man standing well over 6 ft tall and with his left arm round leg-breaks and Chinamen, plus today he also bowled a ball out of the back of the hand.

entries.heading: Back of the Hand		Arm Ball			Chinerman
paras: He took over One hundred wickets in 7 season with the 1st team and two in the 2nd team a season. Les’ best bowling performance was 9 for 67 against Olton and 9 for 71 against Wednesbury in 1958 and 1959 respectively, he also took 5 or more wickets in an innings on over 50 occasions. However, in the 1962 and 1963 season when playing for the 2nd Team he took 160 wickets and 148 wickets plus 5 and 4 wickets respectively when called into the 1st team.

Les, in more youthful days was a fine batsman, but with Sutton his opportunities in this direction were limited on account of batting lower in the order, because of the Club’s batting strength well over 3,000 runs have flowed from his bat and one innings to recall was in a representative game for the Midlands Club Cricket Conference against the Universities' Athletic Union, when selected as a bowler, he batted number eight and hit a superb 57. However, Les went on to play a number of games for the MCCC and was Lesha elected “Cricketer of the Year” by the Midland Club Cricket Conference in 1956’ Les had played for Warwickshire 2st before the war and the Warwickshire Acorns CC made Les a vice-president on 11 April 1957. After leaving Sutton Les joined Bewdley CC and at the end of his first season with them in 1965 finished top of their 2nd Team bowling with 84 wickets for 777 runs at an average of 9,25. In the batting he finished 3rd with 415 runs with a highest score of 54 runs and a season’s average of 24.41.
Leslie Pellow also played soccer and enjoys snooker and golf. A fine sportsman and a humorist both on and off the field lie has made a host of friends.

Well known as a “humorist” on and off the field, it was alleged that Les was the only player to have given his wife a pair of size 10 cricket boots as a Christmas present and failed to understand her lack of appreciation.

entries.heading: Peter Lowe
paras: Peter J. Lowe, who, incidentally, was employed by the same Company as Pellow, also resigned following a move to the Bristol area.  A product of Bishop Vesey's School, he played for the 2nd Xl for one season before becoming the regular 1st Xl wicketkeeper for the next nine.  During this time, he was generally accepted as one of the best wicketkeepers in Midlands club cricket, and had he wished, he could have made First Class cricket his career.

As it was, Peter represented the Conference and Warwickshire 2nd on numerous occasions, and in 1964 was honoured with a 1st Xl game for Warwickshire. In this year too, he created a 1st Xl wicket-keeping record for Sutton with 70 victims.

entries.heading: Andrew Beech
paras: There were few changes amongst the ranks of the administrators at the A.G.M. Andrew Beech took over the duties of Team Secretary following a year when the position was not satisfactory and when the team captains had to undertake most of the work.

entries.heading: Hugh Leigh
paras: Hugh Leigh relinquished the post of Fixture Secretary in favour of Paul McCarthy. During his nine years in office Hugh Leigh had carried out his duties in an exemplary manner and, in particular, had considerably, improved the fixtures standard for the teams on the lower ground.

entries.heading: A.D. Whittaker & C. Barber
paras: A.D. Whittaker after six years yeoman service as Assistant Sec and Hon Social Sec, also retired.  Foremost, he had made the Annual Dance a great success and had been largely responsible for the much-needed assistance to the club funds.  He was succeeded by Chris Barber.

entries.heading: H.R. Cadman, N. Wilkinson & R.H. Smith
paras: H. Cadman retired as Hon Auditor upon leaving the district, and appreciation of his services were acknowledged at the meeting. N. Wilkinson, a playing member, succeeded him in office, but on leaving the area the duties were later accorded to R.H. Smith after he had retired from the office of treasurer.

entries.heading: T. Daly & P Bowerbanks
paras: T. Daly was elected to the committee in place of P.E.S. Bowerbank who retired as a committee member, though carrying on as Hon Ground Sec.

entries.heading: R.H. Smith
paras: A loss of £22 on the season was reported by the Hon Treasurer by R.H. Smith.  This compared favourably with the previous year’s loss of £113, and the improved position was mainly due to the increased subscriptions.

entries.heading: Captains
paras: W.N. Houghton was re-elected 1st Xl captain, P.H.B. Cadman succeeded Pat Bowerbank as skipper of the 2nd Xl, whilst J.W. Ratledge, G, Bryant, and G.W. Beech, were elected captains of the Hawks, Owls, and Grasshoppers, respectively.

entries.heading: D. Whittaker & J Ratledge
paras: The Annual Dance was held in December 1965, and produced a record profit of £189.  As mentioned above this was largely due to the efforts of Douglas Whittaker with the assistance of J. Ratlege who ran the "Tombola".
H.A. Couchman.
H.A. Couchman was re-elected Chairman of the Committee.

entries.heading: Martin Bloomer
paras: Martin Bloomer headed the batting averages for the third successive season since joining the club, and also completed a 'hat trick" of achieving the target of a thousand runs in a season.  He made one century.

entries.heading: M. Payne & A. Beech
paras: The bowling honours were divided, as no fewer than eight bowlers secured 25 or more wickets.  The averages were headed by M. Payne with 29 wickets at a cost of 9.2. Andrew Beech each took 36 wickets for 12.7 each, although only appearing in the side for half the season.  He took 5 wickets against Craven Gents in 3 overs for 3 runs, including a "hat trick" and became the first player on record, to obtain four wickets in four balls in a 1st Xl match.

entries.heading: Neil Houghton
paras: Neil Houghton maintained his consistency with both bat and ball.  He made 794 runs (ave. 28) and took 50 wickets (19.6).

entries.heading: Chris Barber had a 6 for 18 spell against Wightwick
paras: An exciting match at Leicester against the Ivanhoe finished with the scores identically the same. 179 for 8.

Another good match was on the August Monday when Sutton, declared at 218 for 7, only to be beaten by Ashfield by 9 wickets (Mason 124 not out and White 80 not out making 204 in an unfinished partnership for the 2nd wicket).

entries.heading: R. Bradshaw, M. Payne, A. Beach & J. Johnson
paras: The Second Team had an average season with wins and losses the same - 17 -and 8 drawn games.  R. Bradshaw headed the batting averages (27.8), whilst in bowling M. Payne, though not playing many times for this team took 17 wickets for the small cost of 5.9 each.  Against Coventry & N.W., a devastating performance of 7 for 10 put the visitors out for 30.  He also took 7 for 19 against Bromsgrove. Andrew Beach, with 50 wickets for this side before promotion to the senior eleven, secured 86 wickets in the season.  J. Johnson was also very successful with 62 wickets at (13.9).

On a rainy day against Little Stoke, Sutton lost seven wickets for 56, and finally declared at 113 for 7.  The visitors totaled 112, failing by one run.  The match at Coseley was won by one wicket thanks to the last Sutton pair adding 15 in a tense finish,

entries.heading: J.W. Ratledge, G. Hadfield, & Peter Bell
paras: During the latter part of the 1965 season, John Ratledge had stood down from the captaincy of the Hawks and Geff Hadfield took over.

On the August Bank Holiday, Peter Bell called in to Rectory Park and meet up with Norman Sharp, whom he had met recently. That was when Peter was umpiring a 2-day Worcestershire County 2nd Xl game at Kidderminster. Having been introduced to Neil Houghton and then to Geoff Hadfield during the tea interval. Peter was asked if he would umpire the second half of the Hawkes game as Geoff had no appointed umpire. Peter agreed and found the game on the Lower Ground interesting. This was Peters commencement of over 60 years with the Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club.

entries.heading: W.J. Turner, A. Stralford and T. Mallender
paras: Owing to the shortage of players the Owls only won 2 games as the batting strength was weak, only W.J. Turner emerging with satisfactory figures, but the bowling was quite up to standard, with A. Stralford and T. Mallender both obtaining "hat tricks".
The Owls also had a “tie” with Wolverhampton Danes proved an exciting match, with scores of 146 each.

entries.heading: P. Jones, G. Beech, & K. Pickering
paras: The Grasshoppers had an equal number of wins and losses. P. Jones and G. Beech both averaged over 20.  Most of the wickets were shared by K. Pickering and G. Beech.

entries.heading: A.R. Phelps
paras: A.R. Phelps, a B.V.G.S. schoolboy made 117 not out against Walsall for the Grasshoppers.

entries.heading: Mayor, Councilor S.C. Rawlings of 1965
paras: The Festival Shield competition provided the usual keen interest and competitive spirit.  Four Oaks were the winners over Little Aston in the Final, and their success proved to be a popular victory.  In the presence of the Mayor, Councilor S.C. Rawlings, the shield was presented by A.C. Smith, the Warwickshire and England wicketkeeper.

entries.heading: J.B. Russell and C.E. Francis
paras: Two old stalwarts and Vice Presidents passed away in the autumn.  Much has been written on previous pages about J.B. Russell and C.E. Francis, that repetition here is unnecessary, but suffice it to say that their loss was a sad blow to the club and to those who remembered their prowess in the world of sport.

entries.heading: Presidency. Ald. A.E. Terry
paras: Having reached, the advanced age of 90 years, Alderman A.E. Terry J.P. a Freeman of the Town and a "not out" member of the club since 1914, decided he must retire from the Presidency, an office he had held since 1950.  In the long history of the club, he was the first president to relinquish the office of his own volition.  His reasons for doing so were understandable in view of the fact that he had always taken a keen and active interest in the affairs of the many organisations with which he was connected, and though still a remarkable man for his age he considered he was not able to carry out the duties he felt the office entailed.

Tributes to his activities on behalf of the club and of the Town have already been recorded, but there is one thing that has not previously been mentioned.  In 1939 when negotiations were taking place concerning the future of Rectory Park, it was Alderman Terry who was the prime mover in saving it from the builders.  It was largely through his influence that the Rectory Park was purchased by the Corporation from the Ecclesiastical Commissioners as an open space for the development of sporting activities.  But for his foresight, the club would probably have found themselves without a ground, almost certainly not at Rectory Park, even if it had been possible to continue as a club.

It was with sincere regret that his resignation was accepted, and at the Meeting thanks were expressed for his fine services over the years.  He was elected a Life Vice President, the first in the club’s history.

entries.heading: Norman Sharp
paras: Alderman Terry was succeeded by Norman Sharp who had been actively engaged in the affairs of the club for a long period of time.  His first connection was in 1905 when his father moved to Sutton and became a member.  When a little older he acted as 2nd Xl scorer, played his first game for the club in 1915, and became a full member in 1919.  During his playing career he scored 25,000 runs in club cricket, about 19,000 for Sutton, and as a member of the committee for 32 years he had undertaken many of the duties associated with the running of the club.

entries.heading: G.B. Thompson
paras: Gordon B Thompson retired from office after a period of ten years as Hon general secretary. Taking over the duties "temporarily" in 1956, upon the departure of D. Norton, he proved himself to be a most excellent secretary during his term of office. The membership had grown vary considerably and in consequence the work entailed had also increased to a proportionate extent.

When the affairs of a club go smoothly it is frequently not fully appreciated that this state of affairs is often due to the efficiency of the Hon secretary, supported by his committee. Contrariwise, he is often blamed when things go wrong.  That things did go well during his ten years is in itself a tribute to his valued services.

In addition to the work of running the club the added responsibilities of social events, the planning of new developments of two grounds, etc., and including the work in connection with a new lease, it will be realised the amount of work undertaken by Gordon Thompson.  Not only in these connections did he prove invaluable but also in the many unseen and often unnoticed practical jobs he performed, such as general repairs, decorating, and by no means least, the necessity, on occasions, to visit the ground in the middle of the night when called out by the police concerning burglaries.
All these duties and many more fall upon the shoulders of an Hon. secretary and they were all carried out by Gordon Thompson in a most efficient and undemonstrative manner.
At the Annual Dinner he was the recipient of a silver Salver in appreciation of his services.

entries.heading: R.H. Smith
paras: The Hon treasurer, R.H. Smith, also retired after nine years as the keeper of the club's purse.  This, too, carries onerous responsibilities, for though much of the bookwork can be done at leisure and in comfort, the actual control of cash, particularly during the season, involves considerable care and devotion.  Money is frequently thrust into the treasurer’s hand at inconvenient momenta (the writer once received a subscript-Ion when walking out to the wicket to bat) and he also has to keep open a keen eye for monies taken during his absence.  These things present problems. and Reg Smith not only performed the duties in an exemplary and cheerful manner but also controlled the financial affairs of the club in a way befitting his office.
He too, was presented with a silver salver at the dinner.

entries.heading: Gordon Thompson and Reg Smith
paras: Both Gordon Thompson and Reg Smith were elected vice presidents at the AGM.

entries.heading: Mrs. Thompson and Mrs. Smith
paras: One cannot pass over the retirements of G.B. Thompson and R.H. Smith without reference to their respective wives, who, for many years not only supported their husbands in their duties, but also performed such excellent services themselves in connection mostly with the catering and social events of the club.  Reference has been made on previous pages to these ladies.

entries.heading: C.L. Groves, and G.A. Pritchett
paras: With the changes in the administration, one could not help the -feeling that another era had come to an end, but, as in most cases, there are others willing to step into the shoes and take over the duties vacated, and in this respect the newly appointed officers were C.L. Groves, and G.A. Pritchett, as Hon secretaries and treasurer, respectively, Plans had been prepared at an estimated cost of £15,000/£20,000 for a new pavilion, but due to the National economic crisis, little headway could be made during the year.

entries.heading: R.T. Wilson
paras: The club was fortunate in having such a keen sportsman as Roddy Wilson to assume the secretarial duties.  As a boy he was anxious to follow in the footsteps of his father (who played for the now extinct Chester Road C.C.), and become a good cricketer, but at an early age he was stricken with polio and deprived of his ambitions.

Such was his courage and enthusiasm for the game however, that he did not allow this handicap to interfere with his love of it and under this physical disability he applied himself to umpiring and it was not long before his sound knowledge of the Laws and of his ability to apply them were recognised.  Before offering his services to Sutton, he umpired with Streetly C.C. and at that time too he was devoting some of his activities to gliding, a courageous sport for one handicapped as he was.  It should also be mentioned that it was through his initiative that the B.B.C. put on a radio programme in the interests of Midlands’ club cricket.

entries.heading: C.T. Groves
paras: Charles Groves was elected Assistant Hon secretary, a post that had been vacant for a year.  Since joining the club some ten years earlier he had always proved himself to be an ardent worker as well as a useful spin bowler.

He had been a committee member for a considerable time and ran the “Football Pool” which provided a handsome contribution to the club funds, and which, with better support from members, would have been much greater.  Reference to his bowling has previously been made, and one feels that more will be written in future.

entries.heading: G.A. Pritchett
paras: The newly elected Hon treasurer Geoff A Pritchett had been a member since 1948. At the AGM he raised concern on the loss sustained on the 1965 season of £67, and this in spite of a handsome bar profit of £310.  The reasons given by the Hon treasurer were rising costs and the lack of support by many members in money raising activities.

Geoff had already rendered valuable services to the club, particularly as a batsman.  To date he had scored about 13,000 runs for the club, mainly as the opening batsman for the 1st Xl, for whom, over the years, he had always been one of the stalwarts.  For a number of years too he had acted as the clubs press liaison officer, an important duty which is apt to be taken too much for granted.  Upon the completion of his playing career there is no doubt that more will be written of him in these pages.

entries.heading: Captains etc
paras: With the commencement of this new era - a year of numerous changes in the administration, and not, it may be added, caused through any dissatisfaction of the management - other members elected to office were G. Hadfield and W.J. Turner as captains of the Hawks and Owls, in place of J.W. Ratledge and G. Bryant respectively. Joe. Ifrati replaced P.H.B. Cadman on the committee.

entries.heading: D. Salberg
paras: Derek Salberg, a man of many activities in the theatre world, as well as a member of the Warwickshire and Warwickshire Supporters Association committees, was the principal speaker at the Annual Dinner, which as usual, was a well-attended gathering at the Parson and Clerk.   He was supported by the Mayor Councilor S.C. Rawlings and several officials of the Town.  Mounted cricket balls were presented to A. Beach, A. Mallender, and A. Stratford, all of whom performed "hat tricks" during the 1965 season.

entries.heading: George Beech
paras: Before the commencement of the season George Beech, in his capacity of House Manager, undertook a number of minor repairs to the club's property.  He was assisted by several keen members.  Over the years George had saved the club a considerable sum of money by his efforts in this direction, a voluntary duty for which the club was duly grateful.

entries.heading: Martin Bloomer
paras: The team broke fairly even over the year with wins, losses, and drawn games. Batsmen, on the whole, did not have a very good time largely because the wickets were seldom suitable for run getting.  Martin Bloomer with an average of nearly 29 was the most consistent and frequently held the brittle batting strength together.  He fell a few runs short of a thousand runs, made one century, and participated in several century partnerships.

entries.heading: Neil Houghton & Chris Barber
paras: Neil Houghton and Chris Barber proved most useful all-rounders, both having a batting average of over 20 and sharing 81 wickets between them.

entries.heading: Andrew Beach, Vince Fizgerald, Peter Yates & Paul Greetham
paras: Andrew Beach was less successful than in 1965 but took 62 wickets.  Vince Fizgerald and Peter Yates also took 38 and 35 wickets respectively. However, one of the best bowling figures was by Paul Greetham who took 8 for 28 runs against the visiting Old Blundellians.to give the Sutton side a 38-run victory.

entries.heading: Roger Coombs
paras: Perhaps the closest match of the season was on the opening day when, against Lichfield’s declaration of 185 for 8, Sutton, thanks to a boundary hit by Roger Coombs off the fifth ball of the final over, won by two wickets.

entries.heading: Michael Dixon
paras: Michael Dixon, in eleven innings averaged 24, and also played some good innings for the First team.

entries.heading: Steve Pile, Ian Nuttall, Charles Groves & Peter Wells
paras: Steve Pile averaged 21 and took 23 wickets, a fine all-round achievement for a boy who was only available on a limited number of occasions.

Another most encouraging aspect was the success of Ian Nuttall, a pace bowler, who took, 31 wickets for under 8 runs each, including performances of 6 for 12 and 6 for 14, and he also obtained 22 wickets for the First team.

entries.heading: Charles Groves had 48 wickets and Peter Wells 30
paras: In a particularly exciting finish, the match at Rugeley ended in a draw.  The home side scored 187 for 6 declared and Sutton ended with the same score with the last pair together.  In another close game at Coseley, Suttons score of 223 for 4 (Peter Cadman 101 n.o.) and Roger Coombs (90) in a partnership of 152 for the 3rd wicket, was passed by the home team with the last man at the wicket.
2nd Xl.

This side, too, had a less successful season with 13 wins in 32 matches, though only 9 were lost. The 14 fixtures in which there was rain interference may, if completed, possibly have put a different complexion on these figures.  P. Ray, though only batting ten times (5 not outs) finished with an excellent average of 55.4, and Peter Cadman was the most consistent with 458 runs (ave. 25.4). Granville Jones, who joined the club midway through the season, was a tower of strength in the nine innings he played. a scored 376 runs with an average of 75 including a century against his old club Bromsgrove.  Two boys still at school showed fine promise.

entries.heading: George Beech, Roy Catt, David Alford, A. Mallender and K. Pickering
paras: A disappointing season was experienced by the Hawks and Owls largely due to depleted sides, but the Grasshoppers, under George Beech, did very well to win 10 of their 14 completed games.  In a spell of nine matches in July and August no fewer than six games were cancelled and one abandoned because of the weather.  Roy Catt and David Alford made most runs and wickets were shared by A. Mallender and K. Pickering.

It is worth noting that A. Malander took 6 for 18 runs in 5 overs to win the game by 3 wickets against J. A. Smith at Tettenhall. He went on to take 5 wickets for 21 runs against an Inland Revenue side and took another 5 for 20 against Four Oaks. Both games were won by the Sutton side by 27 runs and 42 runs respectively.

K. Pickering also took 5 for 16 in the game against Abbotts Bromley who were bowled out for 41 runs, giving the Sutton side a 90-run victory. However, at Nuneaton Pickering took 6 for 31 runs giving Sutton a 22-run victory.

entries.heading: Andrew Beech
paras: Andrew Beech, who took 5 for 31 to win the game away at Hampton in Arden.

entries.heading: M.J.K, Smith
paras: In an exciting final the Old Veseyans defeated Water Orton.  M.J.K, Smith, the England and Warwickshire captain, presented the Shield, and also in attendance were the Mayor and Mayoress, Councilor and Mrs. H. Herringshaw.

entries.heading: Hugh Leigh
paras: Following an illness in the spring Hugh Leigh decided to retire from active participation in games with the club.  He first became a member upon leaving Bromsgrove School during the war years and throughout his career he was one of the most ardent and enthusiastic followers of the game though seldom rising to any heights as a player.  He was a splendid organiser, and, amongst other things, he was mainly responsible for the success of the Festival Shield competition, which, until all matches were played at Rectory Park, appeared to be dying a natural death.  After the war it was Hugh who revived the Little Aston C.C. and later became its first Life Member.  He also ran his own side the “Little Aston Stragglers”.  The game of cricket is indeed fortunate to have men like Hugh, men who dedicate themselves to it and yet obtain so little limelight on the playing fields themselves.  Hugh Leigh was one of these characters and there are numerous stories concerning him.  One of these concerned his dismissal after being clean bowled.  Returning to the pavilion Hugh apologised to the captain remarking that the ball came back "off the seam”.  The skipper's remark was brief - "We have used the same ball for eight matches and it has not got a b..... seam to start with".
For his services to the club Hugh was elected a Vice President.

entries.heading: Joe Ifrati
paras: Under the guidance of Joe Ifrati, the football pool was revived.  The scheme was as before, half-crown tickets to cover the whole season, thirty weeks, but as is so often the case, the selling of tickets was confined mostly to a few enthusiastic workers, and as a result the profits were not nearly as high as they might well have been.

entries.heading: Mr. H. Tudor
paras: Whilst the construction of the proposed new building “The Pavilion” was not much nearer to commencement, there was throughout the year quite an amount of activity by virtue of meetings and discussions towards this end.  Approaches had been made towards a joint venture with the Sutton Coldfield R.F.C. and the Sutton Coldfield H.C., though by the end of the year nothing concrete had emerged, though all parties were in agreement with the possible advantages of the scheme.

Money was one of the principal obstacles.  The proposed pavilion was estimated to cost £15,000 - £20,000, and none of the clubs concerned were able to lay their hands on anything approaching those figures without the aid of Grants from outside sources.  The financial state of the country was such that Ministry Grants had been suspended and there was a long list of hopeful applicants.  The Warwickshire Playing Fields Association was approached through Mr. H. Tudor and he was able to give valuable advice on the subject, but it was felt that before any outside aid could be requested the club should have a substantial financial backing of its own, and towards this end various money raising activities were initiated. Amongst these was the "Ladies Coffee Mornings", at various houses, the Summer Dance at Penns Hall, and a successful Jumble Sale, etc.  At all of these the ladies connected with the club rendered yeoman service.

entries.heading: Arthur Spencer
paras: Following a season when many matches were cancelled owing to the waterlogged state of the ground and drainage problems, the Hockey Club, under their President Arthur Spencer, (who was the President of Walmley Cricket Club) decided to acquire the pitch at Salford Stadium for First and Second Eleven hockey.  There were many who regretted this move after more than half a century's occupation of Rectory Park, even though the club maintained its headquarters there.  For the past few years, the 3rd and 4th teams had used the Sutton Corporation pitch at the North-West end of the Rectory Park, but it had not proved satisfactory for good hockey, and these teams now moved to the ground vacated by the other sides.

Under the terms of the new cricket club lease the land between the north boundary fence and the Rectory Road houses had been granted for the making of a new hockey ground and work by the Council had commenced in the previous winter by the felling of two old trees.  The opposition to this move had been raised by the local residents and the scheme was abandoned, and in any case the hockey club had decided that the area was scarcely large enough for their requirements.  Subsequently, the cricket club decided to relinquish the lease of this area in exchange for a little more land behind the existing pavilion.

entries.heading: R.T. Wilson
paras: Under the auspices of the Town Council an Advisory Sports Council was initiated in the autumn.  The main idea behind this innovation was to link up the many activities in the Town for the general advancement of recreation within the borough.  R.T. Wilson was elected to the committee to represent cricket in the locality.

entries.heading: Jack Garland
paras: For many years prior to the past two decades umpiring in club cricket had been quite a problem, at least as far as finding competent men was concerned.  In this respect Sutton had perhaps been more fortunate than others, but after the formation of the Midlands C.C.C. Umpires Section in about 1950 both the number of volunteers to the cause and the standards of the umpires began to improve.

Jack Garland officiated for the 1st Xl for over twenty years in the earlier part of the century, and was considered to be a good umpire, but with advancing years and deterioration in health, sight, and hearing, he eventually became somewhat of an embarrassment.  The team paid him ten shillings a week and as this was his only means of subsistence the club had not the heart to dispense with his services.  At this time the club's captain and wicketkeeper was J.B. Russell, a sportsman of the highest caliber, and Garland knew that Russell, when behind the stumps, would make no appeal unless he felt certain the batsman was out, and out he went if Russell appealed and stayed if he did not.  In other cases, he somehow managed to "get by", but nobody will pretend to agree this was a satisfactory state of affairs, but, surprising, as it may seem, things did work out fairly well, though it did come as a relief when he finally retired.

entries.heading: H.E. Robinson
paras: H.E. Robinson succeeded Jack Garland as first team umpire.  As previously mentioned, a train accident in which he lost an arm prevented his active participation in the game, but he did prove himself to be an exceedingly good umpire.  In 1940 he moved south and it was not long before he made a name for himself in Minor County cricket and Club Cricket Conference circles, and was highly respected in the area.

entries.heading: W.J. Belton
paras: The 2nd Xl at this time and for a period after the war was well served as an umpire by W.J. Belton.

It may be of interest that nearly all umpires, at least amongst the larger clubs, were paid for their services until 1939, but since then the great majority have given their services in an honorary capacity.

entries.heading: Len Bindon
paras: After the 2nd World War, Len Bindon assumed the role of 1st team umpire and until he was forced to retire for health reasons after ten years’ service he served the club well.

entries.heading: Roddy Wilson & Bert Thompson
paras: The club was fortunate to have Roddy Wilson and H.E. (Bert) Thompson available to step into the breach.  For a period they 'stood' for the 1st and 2nd respectively, but later shared the duties for the 1st team.  Roddy Wilson ceased to be available on Saturdays for business reasons, and Bert Thompson was not available on Sundays by virtue of his long association with Little Aston C.C. of which he became president.  Both men were umpires of a high standard and in their devotion to the game undertook other duties for the betterment of cricket. Roddy, as mentioned before, became Hon secretary of the club, and Bert Thompson had become Chairman of the M.C.C.C Umpires Section.

entries.heading: W.B. Price, E. Mann, P. Stevens, and R.M. Wilkinson
paras: Over the last decade the 2nd team had also been fortunate in being able to call upon very competent umpires in W.B. Price, E. Mann, P. Stevens, and R.M. Wilkinson, nor were the teams playing on the lower ground suffering from incompetent officials, though in many cases the duties were shared by quite a number of men.

entries.heading: Peter Bell
paras: The essential qualification for an umpire is the knowledge of the laws and of their application, and confidence in one's decisions.  With these anyone can become a good umpire, and though it is by no means necessary to have been a player it is natural that an old player takes to the duties more naturally.  Mostly, it is a pleasant task and a retiring player can often feel he is more “in the game” Peter Bell was well qualified; as he had qualified as an umpire with the ACU, MCCC & MCUA and had experience with the Birmingham League, and both the Warwickshire & Worcestershire County 2nd Xl Cricket matches, as well as a winner in the National Jarvis Umpire Cup

entries.heading: George Swift
paras: Shortly before the close of the year the death of George Swift came as a severe shock to his many friends in the club he had served so well.  A former captain of the club, Chairman of the Committee, a useful batsman, and a wicketkeeper of outstanding merit, were amongst his many qualities, and his loss was a sad blow to the club.

entries.heading: Stacey Jackson
paras: Stacey Jackson, a vice president and former outstanding batsman for West Bromwich Dartmouth.  S. Jessop, for very many years associated with Knowle and Dorridge C.C., and Lionel Foster, a vice president and the first Midland player to gain international honours for England at hockey, also passed away during the year.

entries.heading: Ladies Dinner
paras: The Hardwick Arms was the scene of the first Ladies Dinner ever to be held by the ladies connected with the club, and a highly successful evening it was with an excellent attendance.

entries.heading: Pat Bowerbank
paras: This chapter of the club's history cannot be closed without reference to Pat Bowerbank whose playing days were drawing to a close.  During the past season he had played very little cricket and this mostly for the Warwickshire Pilgrims, of which club he was captain.

Since joining Sutton in 1951 he had been an outstanding personality, a fine player whose deeds have been mentioned many times on these pages, and a tireless worker on the maintenance and improvement of the ground for the past fifteen years.  Amongst other things he made himself responsible for the general appearance and tidiness of the ground, with the rose beds and pavilion enclosure his own personal hobbies, and for these self-imposed duties the club was extremely grateful, and more so for his continued activity in this direction.

As captain of the club for eight years he enthused new life into the team, and afterwards performed a similar duty for the 2nd team.   An advocate of getting results, he took risks and expected others to do the same, and it was largely through his influence that Midlands club cricket took a turn for the better.  He was a fine forcing batsman, made seven centuries for the club, a thousand runs on several occasions, and was a magnificent close to the wicket fielder.  His deeds before coming to the Midlands are not fully known, but with numerous appearances for both Devon and Suffolk County cricket clubs his earlier performances 'can readily be assumed, and in younger days he was also a fine bowler.

Since the previous paragraphs were written further information has come to hand.  For S.C.C.C. 1st Xl he made 10,542 runs with an average of 34, and 1,644 for the 2nd (ave. 26), a total of 12,186 runs for the club.
In addition to the seven centuries already mentioned he made 75 half centuries. As a fielder, other than a wicketkeeper, he created a club record in 1956 by holding 34 catches.
In 1951 Pat was elected a, "Cricketer of the Year" by the Midlands Club Cricket Conference.

In all matches, including those before joining Sutton, he made 23 centuries, and in 1939, when with Exmouth C.C. he performed the "double" of a thousand runs and a hundred wickets in club cricket (no Sunday play).

As an "After Dinner" speaker he excelled, and from 1953 to date, he never failed to amuse his audiences at the Annual Dinner, although in 2017 several of Pat’s stories would be considered to have a racial content.

entries.heading: H.A. Couchman, C.T. Groves & R.T. Wilson
paras: At Extra-ordinary General Meeting in 1967, H.A. Couchman was created in a new office of Chairman of the club, in place of Chairman of Committee, who previously had no official standing apart from committee matters. Charles Groves was elected as General Secretary in place of R.T. Wilson, who for business reasons, was unable to continue.
Geoff Pritchett, the Hon treasurer, reported a loss of £120 on the previous season.

entries.heading: Gordon Thompson
paras: The annual dinner did not produce any profit, it was well Supported, and, as usual, was well organised by Gordon Thompson.  The principal guest speaker was M.J.K. Smith the Warwickshire and current England captain, and former rugby football International.

entries.heading: Alderman Arthur E. Terry
paras: The death of the late president at the advanced age of 91 was a sad loss to the Club.  Until the end he maintained a keen interest in the affairs of both the town and the club, and only a few days before he passed away, he attended a Town Hall function in his honour, and the honours bestowed on both he and his wife throughout their lives bear testimony to the esteem in which they were held.  A keen sportsman, his particular interests were in cricket and golf, and he was no mean performer at either, and furthermore his influence and personality proved of immense value to the club.

entries.heading: A.K. Couchman
paras: A notable loss to the playing strength was the retirement of Alan Couchman who had been a 1st team player since 1957.  Before joining Sutton, he had been one of the leading batsmen with Aston Manor C.C.  Since the retirement of Pat Bowerbank, he had occupied the important middle order position which, in club cricket, either calls for aggression or defence, and success can so often alter the fortune of the game.  In this capacity he proved very successful.  Perhaps his most outstanding achievements were in the Festival Shield competition, when in two successive matches, limited to twenty overs, he scored centuries in both.

entries.heading: H.A. Couchman
paras: It came as a great shock to his many friends when the newly elected Chairman, Harry Couchman, passed away suddenly in June.  He had become a member at the same time as his son Alan, and, with his quiet unassuming disposition he had endeared himself to all.  For the past four years he had been committee chairman and during his term of office had shown sound judgment in the management affairs of the club.  His playing career ended at the outbreak of World War 2, when the Erdington club, to which he belonged, became defunct upon the loss of their ground for military purposes.

entries.heading: First Neil Houghton and Martin Bloomer Xl
paras: With the 1st Xl only securing nine victories out of 39 matches played they could not regard the season as good.  Fifteen were lost and fourteen drawn, but there was a most exciting “tie” with the Old Edwardians when the last batsman was run out in the final over with the scores level at 140.

Only Neil Houghton and Martin Bloomer reached the standard of batsman-ship required, and but for these two the overall results would have been decidedly worse.  Nor did the bowling compare favourably for with six men sharing about 200 wickets none could better an average of 18 runs per wicket.  The only century was a fine 129 by Martin Bloomer against Harborne.

entries.heading: Peter Cadman & Richard Bradshaw
paras: This 2nd team did not fare much better.  They won ten out of 37.  Batting honours went to the captain Peter Cadman who scored 731 runs with an average 28, although Richard Bradshaw, with a creditable average of 32 runs, topped the batting list, but playing in only half the number of matches for this team.

entries.heading: Peter Wells, Steven Pile and Charles Groves
paras: The bowling was mostly shared by Peter Wells, Steven Pile and Charles Groves.  The old stalwart Wells (not one wonders how, year after year, he manages to maintain his pace) bowling for long spells, and took 47 wickets for an average of under 15 runs each.

With a “hat trick” against Bromsgrove, Charles Groves as usual, was amongst the wickets, whilst young Steven Pile, with his cleaver flighted deliveries, took most wickets (48) and with greater experience should have a bright future ahead.  His outstanding performance was 5 for 7 runs against Bromsgrove 2nd.  More solidity in the batting would have given the spinner a greater opportunity with the ultimate beneficial effect on the final seasons’ results.

entries.heading: W. Turner & Frank Lamb
paras: W. Turner had been the elected captain of the Owls, but relinquished the position after a few games, and it was then capably taken over by Frank Lamb. Also, the Hawks scorebook was lost so no comments for the Club’s history.
However, the Owls only achieved three victories it was generally accepted that it had been an enjoyable season for those taking part.

A record first wicket partnership for the Owls (3rd XL) cricket of I86 (unfinished) against Four Oaks was made by P. Ellis (128 not out.) and W. Turner (53 not out).  At this point the innings was declared but Four Oaks obtained the runs with five wickets to spare.

entries.heading: J. Watkins & N. Dawson
paras: Against Sutton Cong’s and Meth’s, J. Watkins carried his bat through the Innings for 99 not out, but ran out of partners, the last man being run out in attempting his hundredth run.
An encouraging aspect of the season was the batting form shown by Neil Dawson for this team. Though only 15 years of age, he scored 235 runs with an average of 29.

entries.heading: George Beech, David Alford
paras: Under the leadership of George Beech, the Grasshoppers (the 3rd team Sunday side) cricket was always entertaining, but even so the side did not meet with much success.  The captain comment was “lack of good players reflected in the results”.  David Alford was the mainstay of the batting with an average of 32 and participated in a third wicket stand of 103 with Mackenzie.

entries.heading: G. Beech & P.J. Blundell
paras: George Beech obtained most wickets and P.J. Blundell had the best average for the Grasshoppers.

entries.heading: Major. Councillor F.E. Whitfield
paras: The keen competition and excitement surrounding this competition was again much in evidence.  Sutton Hockey Club defeated Highcroft hospital in the final, and the Festival Shield was presented by the Major. Councillor F.E. Whitfield, a vice president and former playing member of the club.

entries.heading: New Pavilion & Amalgamation with Hockey Club
paras: Little progress had been made towards the new pavilion scheme.  For nearly two years discussions and negotiations had been going on between the club and the Rugby Football Club with the Hockey Club as an interested outsider.  It was not the wish of the cricket club to 1eave the hockey members out of the reckoning but as thing progressed it became evident that the R.F.C. who expected to have use of the pith at the rear of the pavilion.  had little intention of allowing them much say in the conduct of the affairs of the Association, and as a result the attitude of the cricket club gradually hardened.

There were also wide differences of opinion in the figures involved, and when the R.F.C. would not deviate from a minimum figure of £25.000 matters finally came to a head.   Even if it bad been possible to raise this sum it was not considered in economic proposition in view of the tenure or the lease, and moreover the running costs would also have been proportionately higher.

However, the deciding factor was that the R.F.C. was not agreeable to the hockey club using the dressing rooms, but that they should use those in the pavilion in Hollyfield Road, and furthermore that they should have only minor representation on the Management Committee.
These facts left the cricket club in no doubts whatever that the interests of the R.F.C. and the Cricket Club were not in harmony, and as a consequence any further negotiations were pointless.

If the writer may express a personal opinion, it was a mistake in the first place for the Cricket Club to make any approach to the R.F.C. for not only do their season’s overlap, to the probable inconvenience of both, but also the activities of cricket and rugby clubs lie in rather different spheres.  As amalgamation between the cricket and hockey clubs was more in the natural order of things, and particularly so in view of the happy relationship that had existed between the two clubs for nearly sixty years, and it would have been a major tragedy if the close association had been broken.

The next stage was an approach to the hockey club who gladly accepted the suggestion put forward, and by the end of the year the preliminaries had been completed, and a Management Committee of five members from each formed the basis of the Association.

entries.heading: Peter Yates and John Ratledge
paras: A New Pavilion & Amalgamation with Hockey Club was now a reality throughout the year of 1967 and new sources of income were generated. The Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club Supporters Association, led by Peter Yates and John Ratledge, had formed the “120 Club” whereby members contributed at five shillings a week for a year with prizes of £5 each week, two of £50, and a Mini car to be won at the Annual Dance.

The ladies association with the club made a splendid effort by raising nearly £100 from “coffee mornings” and “cheese and wine parties”, etc., but their “Piece de Resistance” was the Autumn Fare in Fellowship Hall when over £350 was raised on a Saturday afternoon.  Lady Agnes Bennett performed the opening Ceremony.
A jumble sale in October added the best part of £100 to the funds. A barbeque and dance held on the ground in July produced a further sum, as did the football pool during the winter months.
By the end of the year about £1,500 stood to the credit of the Fund.  Nor had the hockey club been idle and their “Mini Car Club” was also doing satisfactory.
As a results of these and further efforts, and with the addition of possible Grant Aid it was anticipated that a commencement on the building might be made in the autumn of 1968.

entries.heading: P.E.S. Bowerbank
paras: At a November Extra-Ordinary Meeting, held primarily to confirm the formation of an association with the hockey club.  Pat Bowerbank was elected an Honorary Life Member in recognition of his valuable service over the past eighteen years.

entries.heading: Alderman A.E. Terry
paras: Obituaries for Alderman A.E. Terry and H.A. Couchman had already been mentioned. But Francis Grant, a previous manager of Lloyds Bank, Sutton and a vice president of the club for nearly forty years, passed away.  In pre-war days he and his family rarely missed a match.
G.W. Brown died during the summer.

entries.heading: S. Bridgens
paras: The death of Sam Bridgens, following an accident, a few days before the AGM, a silent tribute was paid to his memory before the meeting commenced, Sam’s passing cast a gloom over the early days of the year.

For about ten years following his retirement Sam had devoted much of his leisure time to running the bar and all the work that goes with it.  His self-imposed task and devotion proved of great service to the club and his portly figure was sadly missed by both members and visitors alike.

entries.heading: David P Locker
paras: At the Annual General Meeting held in the pavilion a few changes were made when the officers were elected. David P Locker succeeded H.A. Couchman as Chairman of the Club, P.B.H. Cadman became 1st Xl captain, with P.J. Yates and P. Wells respectively taking over the 2nd Xl on Saturdays and Sundays. F.W.J. Lamb was elected skipper of the Owls, whilst R. Sperryn, by a subsequent committee appointment, became captain of the Hawks.  Other officers remained as before.

The Hon treasurer reported a loss of £132 on the previous seasons’ accounts.  Presentations were made to P.E.S. Bowerbank and H.B. Thompson (Bert), the former in recognition of his election as a Hon Life Member received an Oxford Dictionary and an Oxford Atlas, whilst the latter was the recipient on his retirement of a silver tankard for his services as umpire for a number of years.

entries.heading: Mrs. L. Balmer
paras: The function of the Annual Dance proved to be as great a success as was the previous year’s failure.  The excellent attendance was accounted for partly by the good support of the members and partly by the incentive of the draw for the winner of the “120 club” mini car.  Mrs. L. Balmer was the winner, and the dance made a record profit of £234.

entries.heading: Ted Crowe
paras: Another successful Annual Dinner was held at the Parson and Clerk with Alan C Smith, the newly elected captain of Warwickshire and former England wicketkeeper, as the principal guest.  Ted Crowe, captain of the Old Blundellians, who motored both ways from Tiverton in the day proposed the club toast.  F.B. Clark, together with E.H. Walters, made a welcome re-appearance after many years absence from club activities.

entries.heading: Peter Bell & George Parsons
paras: Following the retirements of Bert Thompson and Roddy Wilson the duties were taken over by Peter Bell and George Parsons. The former had experienced umpiring in the Birmingham League and was a member of both the Conference and the Leagues umpires’ sections and had recently qualified under the Association of Cricket Umpires examination, the highest degree an umpire can attain other than on the field, whilst George had successfully passed the examination of the Midlands Club Cricket Conference.

entries.heading: F. Lowson
paras: The opening Yorkshire and England batsman of a decade ago, Frank Lowson, joined the club, but as he was only available on Saturdays, June had arrived before he was able to take his stance in the middle.  At 42 years of age, he obviously still possessed much of his former technique, but he did not succeed in making many runs and on occasions when he did occupy the crease for any length of time runs came too slowly for half day cricket, and though everybody was keen for his success it was a disappointment when he – to put it bluntly – failed to make the grade required in club cricket.

entries.heading: Dr. Tony Robinson
paras: From time to time every club has characters and in 1968 both Sutton and Olton each had a contestant, Sutton with Dr. Tony Robinson a Rhodesian gynecologist on a 3-year contract at Good Hope Hospital, a quiet man who chose his words carefully, as he had a slight stammer.  Olton had Mike Ellis, a Local Councillor in Solihull, a politician, very quick to give you his opinion before he gave the topic any serious thought. “Open Mouth before engaging brain”

So, we had two incidents in one game Mike, generally field at slip for Olton when they were fielding as he had a pair of very capable hands, Over had just been called and Tony who was batting would be facing the bowler, Mike in the meantime was moving from the slip position at one end to take up a similar position at the other when Tony exploded.  Calling to the umpire attention, about a very large of now flavorless chewing gum being deposited on the playing surface around where a good ball would be pitch.  Tony could not get his words out, furious about the lack of hygiene and it was clear that Tony was not going to move it and the umpire had to visually inspect the large very wet looking discarded material.

Once Tony had composed himself and we establish that Mike was the culprit, he was ordered by the Olton captain to dispose of the unwanted material over the boundary fence “at third man” and to field there.  However, it was clear that the Olton Captain was not happy with Mike’s behavior for at the end of the over, Mike came trotting up from “third man” to take his place in the slips only to be told by the captain Mike you are field at “third man” so hurry up.  Captain kept Mike running the length of the ground for two or three overs before he relented and allowed Mike back in the slips.

entries.heading: Mrs. Markham and Mrs. Stonehouse
paras: In the other incident Mike Ellis nearly caused out two “Tea Ladies” to turn round and go home, Mrs. Markham and Mrs. Stonehouse always walk into the Rectory Park via the small entrance alongside Rectory Cottage and make a straight line to the tea room, which was situated close to the flag pole regardless to the game being played.  We always just stopped playing and allowed the elderly ladies to make their way across the ground.  However, on this occasion Mike who was batting and facing the bowling from the pavilion end just shouted at the ladies to get off the ground.  Mike was very quickly told to shut up as we all want tea to be available and he was going the right way to see that we did not get any.
Neil Houghton, Chris Barber & Michael Dixon,

The First team again did not prove themselves to be a strong side.  Only two Saturday matches were won with a few more on Sundays.  The batting strength relied upon Neil Houghton and Chris Barber with good support from Michael Dixon, a promising younger member, but the bowling was inadequate against the stronger Midland clubs.
Neil Houghton had a splendid game against Walsall, in which he performed that extremely rare double of a century and a 'hat trick' in the same match.
Against Bromsgrove, Houghton and Barber participated in an opening partnership of over 160.

entries.heading: Geoff Pritchett and Roy Catt
paras: The Second team also had an uninspiring season.  The bowling was quite up to standard and they were frequently able to dismiss their opponents for moderate totals, but apart from Geoff Pritchett and Roy Catt there was no reliability in the batting.

entries.heading: Michael Dixon
paras: The Hawks sides met with moderate success. The membership position had improved since the previous year and they were more able to fulfill their fixtures without having to resort to last minute cancellations.
Michael Dixon, following cancellation of a 1st team match, distinguished himself with a fine century for the Hawks with 183 not out.

entries.heading: Mayor, Councilor R.H. Phillips
paras: The Festival Shield was deservedly won by Water Orton who defeated Little Aston in the final, His Worship the Mayor, Councilor R.H. Phillips making the presentation.  In addition to this knock out competition teams were entered for the Birmingham League and Walmley trophies. Sutton lost to West Bromwich Dartmouth in the first round of the former, and in the Walmley competition Lichfield, were the eventual winners, defeated Sutton in the semi-final.
Note: - For 1969 the club would enter for the newly instituted” Cricketers Cup”, a national competition instigated by Derrick Robins on a knock out basis and zoned throughout the country.
R.H. Nuttall,
The pavilion clock had again been giving trouble and as a result a new clock was donated by R.H. Nuttall, a non-playing committee member, and gratefully accepted.

entries.heading: Mrs. Janet Groves and Mrs. Hadfield
paras: As voluntary helpers were not favourably disposed towards the responsibility of providing teas for both the top and lower grounds an experiment was tried whereby the work was reduced by restricting the tea interval to ten minutes for light refreshments with more substantial food to be available for players at the conclusion of the match. Mrs. Janet Groves and Mrs. Hadfield undertook the major roles with the assistance of paid helpers Mrs. Stonehouse and Mrs. Markham. Whilst many players favoured the experiment the break from normal traditions did not, on the whole, meet with popular approval.

entries.heading: John Maynard
paras: John Maynard successfully administered the bar arrangements for the season.

entries.heading: Norman Sharp
paras: In April 1968 the official amalgamation of the cricket and hockey clubs was confirmed, and at the joint General Meeting the Association officers were elected as follows under the president Norman Sharp: -
President - Norman Sharp,
Hon Sec, Charles T. Groves –

entries.heading: Hon Tres, H. Ford
paras: Five members from each section in addition to the ex-officio officers formed the Management Committee.in the new pavilion so a building sub-committee was set up in the spring who would report to the main body.  The sub- committee consisted of the president Norman Sharp, Hon sec, E. Walters, J. Woodall, and R. Simpson.  Their proposals were submitted to the Management committee, who, subject to a few minor alterations, accepted the proposition for a pavilion costing a little over £11,000 to be erected by Lessar Bros Ltd and consisting of six dressing rooms, club room, and the normal amenities.
This left the necessary planning permission and the confirmation of applications for grants before the work could be commenced.

Earlier in the year the Town Council had agreed to an extension of the lease of the ground for an additional term of seven years, making twenty-eight, a concession which would tend to increase the possibilities of generous grants.

In November the Midlands C.C.C., administering the funds at their disposal by the courtesy of the Warwickshire C.C.C., Supporters Association, made a grant of their maximum amount of £500, a sum gratefully accepted by the club.

The Hon secretary, Charles Groves, had been in contact with the Ministry of Education and Science on several occasions and as a result it was hoped that an amount of around £5,000 might be available from this source.

With the success of the “120 Club” now running in its second year, the amounts already put aside, the hockey club contributions, estimated donations by members, grants, etc., it was anticipated that about £9,000 would almost immediately be available.  The balance would have to be obtained by loans or other means, but on the whole, it was considered the financial aspect was not unhealthy.

entries.heading: R.T. Janney
paras: Hon Sec of the club from 1927 to 1929.  A 2nd Xl fast medium pace bowler with occasional successes for the 1st team, and in later years the Hon auditor of the club’s accounts passed away.

entries.heading: Mrs. A.J. Terry
paras: Wife of Jim Terry.  A former skipper of the 2nd team, and daughter in law of the late president.  Between the wars she was a regular helper with teas and undertook the organising responsibility for a number of years.

entries.heading: H.F. McCarthy
paras: The father of Paul and John, and a respected vice president who rarely missed watching a match, home or away passed away.

entries.heading: A. L. Leigh
paras: Father of Hugh, and a non-playing member whose support was always appreciated.

entries.heading: H.E. (Bert) Thompson
paras: Although Bert Thompson had officially retired as umpire with Sutton at the end of the 1967 season, his departure from the district cannot be passed over without reference to his outstanding services to the game in the Midlands.  A native of Kent, he played for the county 2nd Xl before coming to Birmingham in 1920.  In 1948 he became associated with Little Aston C.C. as umpire, a position he held until his retirement, and for the past eight years he was the president.  He never needed to be persuaded to “stand”.  If he saw a game lacking an official, he invariably offered his services, such was his love for the game.  It was in this way that he was first introduced to Sutton C.C.C., in 1954 with a match for the Hawks.

He was soon with the Second team, and later with the First on Saturdays (Little Aston were mainly a Sunday club) for whom he officiated for a number of years.  During the period 1948 to 1968 the total number of his "Witch Doctor" appointments amounted to 1,147, and these included fixtures in the Minor Counties and Second Xl County competitions with Warwickshire and Worcestershire, Conference matches, Public Schools, Mayflies, Warwickshire Pilgrims, etc. according to a Sutton Coldfield News article “The man in the Middle” they estimated that Bert was in the Middle for some 6,000 hours”.
