Roger was also a competent batsman and would have made any other club’s 1st team as either a batsman or wicket keeper and during his period with the 2nd team he scoring 657 runs in 1960 and had 47 dismissals behind the stump’s plus 3 victims with the 1st team.  Roger in 1961 broke the club record with 76 victims (34 caught and 42 stumped) mainly with the second team.  Now in the 1st team Roger was the preferred 1st team keeper to Tony Robinson in 1969 and to James McDowall ex Cambridge University and Warwickshire in 1971 who were quality wicket keepers. Roger had no real challenger for the gloves until Gavin Weston arrived. However, in 1969 a young fast bowler, Ian Nuttall arrived at the club, who did not cause Roger any problems, but by 1973 Ian second spell down the slope was Rogers undoing, as Ian’s direction was off line and the ball was a projectile towards the groundsman’s shed leaving Roger watching the ball go bye and was replaced by Gavin. You could not have had so differing a character to Roger who was an immaculately turned our wicket keeper whereas Gavin’s kit was said to be able to walk out of the dressing room on its own.  Roger accepted playing for Sutton as a privilege whichever team he was selected to play in whereas Gavin would tell you how good he was.  However, when in the 1st team Roger batting at either No. 6 or 7 so his opportunities to make big scores was limited although his runs came quickly.  Gavin now with the gloves and also on many occasions opened the batting outscoring Michael Dixon, when at home to Mosley Ashfield had an opening partnership of 102 runs with Michael Dixon and again against Stratford they shared an opening partnership of 129 runs, Gavin contributing 73 to Michael’s 53.  No doubt about Gavin ability with the bat.  He scored a century against Redditch at Rectory Park for the 2nd team with 126 runs not out.  However, on the arrival in 1974 of a very young 16-year-old wicket-keeper in the name of Chris Maynard, Gavin was dropped into the twos.   Chris, who played for the School or the County Colts on Saturdays, took over the 1st team’s glove duties on Sundays in 1975 to play alongside his father, John Maynard.  This left a very unhappy Gavin, who always referred to Chris as “Wonder Boy”, but Gavin was also a hypochondriac, he had ever known fatal illness but always made a speedy recovery, “You name it and Gavin had suffered from it”.  Chris was also a fast-scoring middle order batsman who had several scores in the 60’s and 70’s for the first team before signing professional terms with Warwickshire in 1978.  He later moved on to play for Lancashire in 1982.  He appeared in 117 first-class marches, scoring 2,541 runs with an average of 20.65 and a highest score of 132 not out and held 186 catches and 28 stumpings before retiring from county cricket in 1986.  Gavin left the Club following the Maynard’s, and Petch’s to live in South Africa, with Roger retaining the 1st team gloves until the arrival of Andy Biddle in 1984, but that’s another story.  Roger continued playing with the 2nd team for a few more seasons before taking on umpiring duties and in 1986 he was elected a Life Member for services to the Club and was a playing member of the Warwickshire Pilgrims.  Roger became Ground Secretary in 1975 and it was always reassuring to members who visiting Rectory Park in the early morning when the due was on the ground to see Roger on the roller giving the next weekend wickets his attention before he went to his paid job.

entries.heading: Naeem (Bobby) Arif
paras: In a 2nd Xl Warwickshire Sunday League game in the 2001season, Naeem, but always referred to as Bobby scored 165 not out in a partnership of 156 runs in 18 overs against Griff & Cotton, declaring on 365 for 8 wickets.  Bobby scored a total of 510 runs in that season at an average of 51.0, including another hundred against Kenilworth.  In the following season Bobby captained the Saturday 2nd Xl and in reply to Sutton’s modest score of 136, Pelsall were all out for 112 with Bobby bowling unchanged taking 7 wickets for 18 runs in 23 overs.
In 2010 Bobby was elected Chairman of the Club, a post he also held in the following year.

entries.heading: Bilal Aziz
paras: Bilal in the 2001 season for the 2nd Xl in a Warwickshire Sunday League 40 over a side game at Rectory Park against Kings Heath scored 212 runs before the captain declared on 340 runs for the loss of 6 wickets

entries.heading: H. Baker
paras: Hayden Baker was mainly a 2nd team bowler in 1979, although he did play a few games for the 1st team.  He finished top of the two’s bowling averages in his first season with an average of 14.3, taking 54 wickets.  Hayden at home to Bromsgrove in an opening unchanged spell of hostile bowling for a 2nd Xl game of 12.3 overs he took 8 wickets for 23 runs at 2.90 rpw.  In what appeared to be his last season with the Club in 1980 he took 33 wickets at a cost of 16.4.

entries.heading: Tom Banton
paras: Tom joined the Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club in the Junior section in 2009 aged 10 years of age and made a great impression by scoring 203 runs in a match for Warwickshire Under 13’s against Herefordshire, a performance that earned him the Neil Abberley Trophy as Warwickshire Young Player of the Season.  Tom moved on to play at Barnt Green before moving schools to Taunton and was soon involved with the Somerset County Cricket Club.  He was selected and played in the County side against Middlesex on the 16th July 17 as a wicket keeper batsman at Uxbridge in a NatWest 20T Blast game where he scored 4 runs before being dismissed by the New Zealand pair, caught Brendon McCullam, bowled Tim Southee.  Keeping wicket Tim stumped Dawid J. Malan. Somerset went on to beat Middlesex by 21 runs in NatWest 20T Blast on 16th July 17.

entries.heading: Tom Banton & Ian Bell
paras: A Match report by the ECB Independent reporter stated as follows: - “Michael Leask’s off spin then accounted for the equally prized scalp of Dawid Malan, the left-hander dragging his back foot out of the crease when he attempted to flick to leg and being smartly stumped by 18-year-old debutant Tom Banton for 7. The delivery was signalled a wide but the dismissal left Middlesex 25 for 2”.

On the 18th September 2018 Tom made his Somerset County Cricket debut, opening the innings with Martin Terescothick in reply to Surrey score of 485 against the bowling of M. Morkel, South Africa’s quick bowler.  Tom went on to score 30 runs and was 8th out to Tom Curran.  In the second innings Tom scored 4 runs in a game that was drawn due to bad weather.  Marcus Terescothick will also remember the game, getting a duck in both innings and faced a total of 7 ball from Morkel, who had his wicket in both innings.  Tom had also captained the England’s Under 19 side.

entries.heading: Chris Barber
paras: Joining the Club in 1963 having learned his cricket in Canterbury, Chris Barber was a very under estimated cricketer with either the bat or ball, having a great deal of talent but happy to bat in any position the captain suggested, and he would be the opening bowler one weekend and a change bowler on another, only coming on to bowl when the captain had to do something.  Looking through his record shows that he played in some 17 century partnerships, 10 as an opening batsman, he only scored one century at home to Stafford in 1963.  However, he was run out twice on 99 when Chris scored the 2 runs for his hundred whereupon the captained declared unaware the square leg umpire was signalling one short because his batting colleague had not grounded his bat at the striker’s end

Chris’ cricketing opportunities were limited in 1963 to 65 for one reason or another, however in 1966 he was a regular 1st team player until the end of 1983 season although no records were found for 1967, 1977 and 1978 seasons.  However, in the 15 years he scored 8,992 runs with an average of 31 runs per innings.  In 1980 he scored 1,169 runs and 943 in the following season.

Chris managed to play two seasons 1975 & 76 in the two’s and scored 659 runs at an average of 25.    His bowling in his early days at Sutton of 1963 to 67 was a major part of the 1st Team’s opening quick ball attack in which Christ took 147 wickets at a cost of 16.3 runs per wicket.  In fact, he had the best bowling figures in 1963 and 1966 as some of his bowling spells were outstanding, in 1963 he took 6 for 7 runs against Nuneaton and in 1966 on two occasions against Wightwick and Bromsgrove cricket clubs he took 5 wickets for 10 runs in 9 and 12 overs respectively and in 1973 he took 5 for 10 runs against Nuneaton in 4 overs.

Chris was an unassuming person and a chatter to the umpires when batting and while at the none strikers end, he constantly kept the umpire informed what he was going to do if that bowler pitches the ball slight over a length, he is going to put the ball back over the bowler’s head and the groundsman’s shed for 6.  Which he generally proceeded to do so.  However, when speaking at the Club’s annual dinner in 1975 he astounded everyone present by the manner in which he opened his speech prior to proposing a toast to our guests, which included David Barnes as captain of Wolverhampton in the previous season had made an appalling miscalculation in his declaration, who would reply on behalf of the guests. However, towards the end of Chris’ address he gradually made all the guests including David very welcome.

entries.heading: Mark Bell
paras: Mark, the son of Peter Bell, the Club’s 1st team umpire 1966 to 1990, started playing serious cricket in 1974 and played in the 1st Xl when he was 12 years of age against Aldridge that year.  He was also part of Peter Yates’, successful Alpine Under-16 Cup Winners team of 1977.  Mark played most of his cricket oscillating between the 2nd team and the lower ground sides initially as a bowler-batsman and finally finishing his playing days as a batsman-bowler

In 1979 Mark playing for the Sunday 2nd took 5 wickets at Pickwick for 13 runs and in the following season for the Grasshoppers against Pedmore he took 6 wickets for 72 runs in 16 overs.  Back in the Saturday two’s in 1983 and at home to Hampton-in-Arden Mark took 6 for 22.  Again, playing for the 1st team in 1980 against Aldridge Mark took 5 wickets for 14 runs in 10 overs.  Mark’s batting was slow to develop mainly due to the number of overs he was bowling in a game, resulting in Mark being batted low in the order.

Mark scored his first centaury for the Club 31 years later in what was his penultimate season in 2005 in a 3rd Xl game against “The Valley” on 7th August with 100 not out.  In this game, he also kept wicket taking two catches, but took the gloves off to have a bowl and took two wickets.  He also scored another century when sharing an opening partnership of 322 runs with Bilal Aziz, who scored 188 for the Hawks against Studley in 2006 on the lower ground.  Mark was not out on 100 when the captain declared on 330 for the loss of 1 wicket.  Mark went on to score a total of 843 runs in 22 innings that season at an average of 42, including five consecutive 50’s before retiring at the end of the season.

entries.heading: Peter R.G. Bell - Life Member
paras: Peter joined the Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club on 28th August 1965 as an umpire who had umpired previously in the Birmingham League that season but was not happy with the attitude of some of the captains involved with the second eleven sides.  He had played his cricket with Burbury Cricket Club later renamed Lea Marston on Sundays as athletics was his main interest involving most Saturdays.  While playing with Lea Marston Peter had completed the courses and passed the umpires exams of the Midland Counties Umpires Association, the Midland Club Cricket Conference Umpires course and the Association of Cricket Umpires, the latter when he was working in London.  In fact, he became an ACU examiner and was in the MCUA successful Jarvis Cup national quiz team, winning the trophy in 1965.  However, he had become disillusioned with the Birmingham League match appointment system, although he was being appointed for mid-
Peter Bell Umpiring in the 1979 ICC Trophy Game between USA & Sri Lanka. Walter Bevell bowling for the USA.

entries.heading: As published in the Ultimate Encyclopedia of Cricket
paras: week 2- and 3-day games involving both Warwickshire and Worcestershire County 2nd team matches

These games, plus Conference appointed matches showed Peter a standard of cricket that he was never going to be able to play but wet his appetite when watching young players of great skill and potential a desire for Pater to watch the game from close up behind the stumps, as an umpire, but within Club Cricket.  With a young family and living in Sutton Coldfield he arranged with Norman Sharp, (whom he had met when umpiring a conference game against Worcestershire Club & Ground at New Road,) to meet up with the 1st team captain Neil Houghton at Rectory Park on the Bank Holiday Saturday during the tea interval in 1965 as he did not have a Birmingham League appointment.

So, his long association with Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club had begun, umpiring on Saturdays in 1966, although playing on Sundays for Lea Marston, he wore the white coat for the Hawkes under the captaincy of Geoff Hadfield, an extremely pleasant captain who was delighted to have an umpire for the season.  He had a totally different perspective regarding umpires compared to those he had experienced in the Birmingham League, which he later realised was his age as he was under 30 compared to most of the League umpires who were in the main twice his age and umpired for the remuneration.

Peter only ever played in a handful of games for the Grasshoppers on an occasional Sunday but he remembers to his cost when Peter Wells in the bar late on a Saturday evening asked Peter if he would turn out the next day for the Grasshoppers at Marston Green.  The pitch was rather bumpy but having played the odd game in the Parks, Peter knew how to duck and dive and it was soon put to the test when Nick Roy was struck on the head and retired for medical attention.  He was now in facing a quick bowler who took great delight in missing his bat and striking his person on those unprotected areas.  After a few more deliveries he too required treatment for a rather sore finger, as the ball jumped off a length and again avoiding his bat.  He still has the misshapen finger today which reminds him that he did score 27 runs, one of his highest scores.  Back with his umpire’s coat on he felt reasonable safe although he did get hit in the back when standing at square leg, Malender throwing the ball in from mid-wicket managed to hit Peter.  Nevertheless, he enjoyed his season on the lower ground and felt he did a good job, so much so Peter Cadman the second team captain asked him if he would like to umpire the 2nd team next season as their umpire Percy Stevens was retiring at the end of the season.  Percy had a reputation of succumbing to pressure, especially when Sutton needed a little help.

Now with the second team in 1967 he had the opportunity of watching 1st team players who had to play in the twos because of the abundance of very good players available from time to time and if a player was not available for both Saturday and Sunday’s he was automatically dropped into the second team.  However, one particular game was at Coseley, when the Coseley captain won the toss and elected to bat and presented Peter Wells, the Sutton captain that day with a new bright shiny red ball and Richard Newton, a 1st team young left arm quick sharp bowler, was invited to open the bowling.  The first 5 ball delivered created no response from the batsman, so the last ball in the over was extra quick and somewhat short of a length, which woke the batsman up with a fine hook, dispatching the ball over the square leg six feet high wooden boundary fence for six.  That was the last seen of the ball, although time was spent looking in the resident’s front garden, there was no sign of the ball although there was a telltale streak mark across a freshly painted garage door and a pot of green paint alongside.  No resident was opening the door, so a box of old ball was presented by the Coseley captain with apologies that had all been well used and with a surface closely resembling chamois leather.  A disappointed Peter Wells bowled the second over from the other end.

Bert Thompson, Chairman of the Midland Counties Umpire Association, had umpired Sutton’s 1st team on Saturdays and Little Aston Stragglers on Sundays for many years.  He was also President of the Stragglers and was retiring at the end of the 1967 season to go back to live in his native Lincolnshire.  Having stood with Peter in various matches he recommended to Sutton that Peter should umpire the 1st team in 1968, under the new 1st team captain, Peter Cadman.  Peter was now where he wanted to be watching players who had retired from 1st class cricket like Frank Mitchell, Phil Bromley and Norman McVicker, and young players who were making names for themselves, Alan Gordon, Andy Moles, Barry Flick and Eddie Hemmings.

Apart from umpiring the Sutton 1st team on Saturdays for close on 30 seasons, 1968 to 1997, and a season with the Birmingham League prior to joining Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club, Peter was invited to umpire many County 2nd Xl matches covering both Warwickshire and Worcestershire games in which new players to the county like Kallicharran’s first appearance at Edgbaston in 1971, turned out in a 2nd team game and entertained me with the quality of his batting and the speed he was in position to dispatch the ball to the boundary.  The arrival of Bob Willis from Surrey in 1972 at Knowle & Dorridge ground in his first game for his new county in the 2nd team as a warm up game was disappointing because Bob having bowled a few overs at my end was taken off, rather than risk any injury on a slippery surface after a heavy shower.

Peter also recalls umpiring a Warwickshire 1st team game against Worcestershire in a 3 day none county championship game.  So, it was great delight to meet and watch batsmen like Mike Smith, Glenn Turner and Neil Abberley.  He went on to umpired in many MCC games, as well as touring with the Warwickshire Pilgrims, Greenflies, Mayflies, Staff Gents and Old Blundellians.  Peter also umpiring some 7 or 8 matches in the 1979, 1982 & 1986 ICC Trophy Competitions and that included both Sri Lanka and Bangladesh before they were accepted as full members of the ICC and he was extremely proud to be presented with a very attractive set of cuff-links by the Papua New Guinea manager.

During Peter’s time wearing the white coat he umpired probably close on 1,000 games of cricket, if you include junior games.  So, it’s not surprising that a number of incidents occurred.  Peter recalled one such event occurred when umpiring one of his first games in the Birmingham League at the Gorway ground, where Walsall were playing on a damp pitch, when his colleague asked for some more sawdust as the bowler was slipping.  No sawdust arrived and to my colleague’s annoyance he exclaimed very loudly “Sawdust”.  To which a wag in the paid crowd shouted back in a black-country dialect “Shake your ed its full of it.”

There are certain umpires you enjoy umpiring a game together, and Peter put his old friend and colleague, Phil Berry in that category.  They umpired a number of games together and they only had to look at each other for a nod or shake of the head and they would get the response they were seeking.  Phil and Peter were appointed to umpire the ICC in 1979 USA V Sri Lanka. The USA batsman, Stuger played a ball back toward the bowler DLS de Silver who dived forward and claimed the catch.  Peter’s view of the catch was obstructed by the bowler but by the sound of the ball bounced on the ground before the bowler caught it was a serious possibility.  Peter looked toward Phil and with a shake of his head Peter called “Not Out”.  The bowler insisted that he had caught the ball and instructed Peter to consult his colleague to which Peter replied saying “I have consulted my colleague”, the bowler’s response was that “you haven’t moved”.

One of the most pleasing and complementary comments made regarding Peter and Phil regarding the quality and honesty of their umpiring was made by the Knowle & Dorridge captain.  Before K&D were due to play against the Club’s 1st team at Rectory Park, he requested that both Phil and Peter umpire this league game as they did not trust their club’s umpire with this important MCCC League game.  Sutton batted first and limped to 161 runs all out in 58 overs. In Knowle & Dorridge reply they reached 162 for the loss of one wicket in 27 overs, with John Jameson opening the batting scoring 18 fours and 3 sixes in his 115 not out.  Our old friend and colleague James McDowall finished with 32 not out.

Peter also became aware of overdoing the courtesy afforded to a batsman when reaching a century when touring with the Staff Gents playing against the Yorkshire Gents at Normandy Park.  A batsman with his score on 99 with the last ball being bowled before the lunch break, hit the ball towards mid-off who was fielding a little deep and was not that agile a player, with a nickname of “The Oaf”, picked the ball up and tucked it under his arm pit to applaud the batsman’s century, only for the batsman to turn round and take a second run.  So, Peter was not happy with this and before the second run was completed, he called “time” and took the bails off, and walked towards the pavilion, to be applauded by both teams for his sporting intervention with the batsman still on a 100 not out at lunch.

Certain players names stick in your memory, none more so that Mike Ellis, who was a Solihull Councillor before retiring to live in the Isle of Man and was a very good free scoring batsman with the Olton & West Warwick Club.  In a game at Rectory Park when Mike was fielding at 1st Slip at the end of the over, he threw down on the pitch his discarded chewing gum close to where a ball was always like to pitch in front of Sutton’s Tony Robinson who exploded in annoyance and was speechless stuttering towards Peter what had occurred.  However, the Olton captain, and wicket keeper Stuart McLaren, enquired of Mike if that was his chewing gum and then told Mike to drop it over the boundary at 3rd man and to field in that position.  At the end of the over Mike ran to take his place at 1st slip only to be informed that his place was at 3rd man, so for the next few overs Mike had to make the trip from one end of the ground to the other until he realised that an apology to the batsman would release him for the penalty.

The following season back at Rectory Park, Mike was batting when two elderly ladies coming in from the Rectory Cottage entrance in a straight line for the tea room crossing the ground close to the stumps at the pavilion end much to the annoyance of Mike but to the Sutton fielders this was a regular path taken by the ladies.  Mike expressed his irritation with an unprintable explicit remark, only to be rebuked by several Sutton players with “If you want any tea today keep quiet as they are the tea ladies”

Peter was elected Chairman in 1983 and held the post for 3 seasons and was awarded Life Membership by the Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club in 1989 and in 2009 he was awarded the Midland Club Cricket Conference Cricketer of the Year for Administration.  Peter had been a trustee of the joint clubs and signatory to the Articles of Association from 1970 until 2016. He was also bar manager from 1970 to 1985 and at some date later became house manager.  He was requested in 2002 by Nigel Lion to be auditor dealing with the monthly Bar Trading Figures and Quarterly Stock Take data.

During my 30 seasons, Peter had watch with interest many good Sutton 1st team sides playing against quality players who had come out of county cricket or were taken into county cricket, players like John Jameson, David Cook, and spinners Kevin Flaherty and Derrick Flint and Suttons two spinners in Keith Gardom and Warwick Tidy and wicket keeper in Chris Maynard, plus so many batsmen who would always score runs against Sutton and Sutton batsmen who could do likewise.  So, Peter believes that you have a reasonable view on players of quality while wearing the white coat standing behind the stumps, but he would have loved to have been capable of playing at this high level, unfortunately it could not be so.  Although meeting up with old players like David Cook and to be greeted by “Hi Pugh how is your guide dog”, does bring back memories.

entries.heading: Simon Berry
paras: “Simon Berry joined the Club as a schoolboy in 1968, paying in Peter Wells’, August Holiday games, before turning out for Bishop Vesey Grammar School in 1970 for the annual fixture against 2nd team when he was 15 years of age. Simon also represented Warwickshire at Under 13, 15 & 19 and captained them on numerous occasions.  By the 1971 season Simon was in the 1st team as first choice off spinner.

However, it was in the 1972 season than Simon finished top as the first team leading wicket taker, with 43 victims at an average of 19.8 and again in 1973 he again headed the 1st team list of wicket taker with 35, at a cost of 18.4 runs per wicket. We lost Simon’s in the mid seventies’ while he was away at university.  On his return he teamed up with Mike Joseph (Incidentally later to become “Brother-in-Law”) as his vice-captain on both Saturdays & Sundays for the 2nd Xl in the 1982 season and in the following season he captained the Sunday 2nds.  During his last season Simon took 8 wickets against Moseley C.C. but it’s not clear for how many runs.

entries.heading: Andrew Biddle
paras: On the departure of Chis Maynard into the Warwickshire County Cricket Club and with an aging Gavin Weston, a young wicketkeeper in Andrew Biddle referred affectionately to as “Bids” joined the Club while still as Bishop Vesey Grammar School.  Bids did not only have a very reliable and quick pair of hands as well as being an extremely capable batsman, but he also possessed a great agility to run quickly, as many slow colleagues found themselves run out by Bids’ ability to see and take a quick single.  His early football career on the left wing for Sutton Town FC enhanced and coordinated his ability to think and move quickly.

Bids joined the Club in 1981 and figured in a record 8th wicket partnership of 80 runs with Richard Sperryn away against Leamington Lions for the Grasshoppers, and by 1984 Bids was not only 1st team choice of wicketkeeper but he was opening their batting.  No performance records were recorded between 1985 and 2005, except in 1993 when Bids played 17 games in the 1st Team scoring 225 runs at an average of 25 and claimed 18 victims behind the stumps (14 catches & 4 Stumpings).   Bids took great pride in keeping the byes column as low as possible, and in his 17 games he conceded a total of 18 byes.   He missed the first few games of the season, due to his playing commitments for Sutton Coldfield Town Football Club.

Nevertheless, Bids figured as the wicketkeeper batsman in Sutton’s 1st team winning “The Indoor 8 a Side League”, their own KO Cup and the “Wishaw 6-A-Side” in 1985 and again the “Wishaw 6-A-Side” competition in 1986.

In 1985 Bids organised the Club’s first cricket tour of East Anglia under the name of Sutton Coldfield Warriors a side made up mainly of junior members.  The games were played in August against Audley End, Bury St Edmonds, March, Camden Cricket Clubs with a final game back in Sutton against the Sutton 1st team.  The tour continued under Bids’ organization for 7 seasons until 1991 when Steve Russell took it over.
Bids has followed the fortunes of the 1st away in the Birmingham League games as an Officer in the “Pork Pie Army”

entries.heading: Martin Bloomer
paras: Martin Bloomer was educated at Bishop Vesey Grammar School, where he obtained his colours at cricket. He joined Streetly C.C. in 1960 and quickly made his mark as a batsman in as much that in 1962 he hit 1,125 runs, which still stands as a club record.
He joined the Sutton Coldfield club in 1963, initially playing in the 2nd team but in the 10 games he played he scored 281 runs at an average of over 31 per innings.

His immense talent was quickly recognised and he played in the 1st Team for the remainder of the seasons he scored another 1,019 runs with an average of 35.1.  During the next 7 season he played at Sutton, Martin amassed a total of 8,010 runs with an average of over 30 runs per innings including 8 centuries with his highest score of 159 was against Walsall.
Martin captained the 1st team in 1969 & 1970 and was elected by the MCCC as “Cricketer of the Year” in 1970 and played

entries.heading: Martin Bloomer
paras: a number of 2nd Xl games for the Warwickshire County Side.  To everyone surprise, early in the 1971 season Martin just walked away from cricket, never to play again.

entries.heading: D.J. Bridgeman
paras: Joe Bridgeman, an Old Reptonian, played for the Club rather infrequent and only for a very few numbers of season so did not figure in the club’s statics.  Nevertheless, Joe was a well-coached batsman with some style and a capable bowler, but played most of his cricket with the 2nd team and away game at Leamington in 1974 he took 7 for 56.  However, in 1977 Joe played for the MCCC league team against Swindon B.R. and scored 103 runs, he also played a number of games for the Warwickshire 2nd Xl.

entries.heading: Archie Bryden
paras: Second team players rarely get a mention but in 1975 Archie took 7 wickets against Stafford for 23 runs and its worth recording.

entries.heading: Tim Buckett
paras: Tim, an Australian, joined us as our registered overseas player in 1993, but due to an injury he was unable to play within his keen comfort zone so he returned in 1994 and it is worthy of noting that his contribution in the Club’s fortune during his time with us was outstanding.  He took 97 wickets for the Club at an average of 15.49 runs per wicket, with an 8 for 60 against Knowle & Dorridge; and 5 for 95 against Barnt Green, bowling unchanged in both games for 22 over and 23 over respectively.

entries.heading: Daniel B. Child
paras: Dan joined the Club from Boland, South Africa and is engaged as our overseas player in the 2012 season.  Dan was born 16 November 1988 in Cape Town, took 9 for 28 when he was 16 in a 2nd Xl match, represented South Africa U/19 side at the 2008 World Cup in Malaysia and made his debut for Bolamd in the same year.

Sutton 1st team now playing in the Warwickshire Cricket League Premier Division, having been relegated the previous season from the B&DPCL 3rd Division went close in the promotion back but finished runner up in the 2012 season with Dan being the leagues wicket taker with 54 wickets at an average of 9.17 runs.  His pace was too much for most opposition players.

Dan had a delightful personality and was very well liked by all he met, and we were delighted that he decided to return and play in the 2013 season, in fact he also returned for the 2014, 15 & 16 seasons.   In the 2013 season Dan took more than 50 league wickets in the season for the second consecutive season finishing on 56 at an average of under 11 runs per wicket, with quality performances at Bablake 6 for 24; 6 for 32 against Bedworth and 5 for 28 against Handsworth and helping to return Sutton back into the 3rd Division in the B&DPCL.  During the next two season Sutton moved up through Division 2 into Division 1 with the help of Dan’s hostile bowling, taking 34 and 58 wickets respectively at an average of 14.1 & 10.6 runs per wicket.  In the 2016 season Dan acquired a serious back problem and was unable to bowl. This was one of the contributing factors in Sutton loss of their 1st Division status at the end of the season.  Dan returned to South Africa and had some successful back surgery and acquired a teaching local teaching post back in Borland plus his wedding is forthcoming and the Club wish him well – a nicer South African you could not meet.

entries.heading: Tony Clamp
paras: Tony name does not crop up very often when looking through playing performances, although he has supported the Club for many years and was an active member of the “Pork Pie Army”.  However, he did catch the eye in a 3rd Team game away against Smethwick, who scored 285 runs for the loss of 8 wickets.  Sutton in their replied were all out for 193 runs with Tony scoring 76 runs

entries.heading: G. Clarke
paras: Graham Clarke joined the Club when he moved into Sutton in 1986 in furtherance of his career in banking and played for a couple of seasons before moving on.  He was a bowler with a lively pace, with accuracy rather than sheer pace.  He had a number of worthy performances in particular at Halesowen where he took 6 for 57 claiming the last wicket with what would have been the last ball of the game.   He also followed this up with 5 Walsall wickets for 98 bowling 23 overs in an unbroken spell before Walsall declared on 215 for 5.  Despite Dave’s performance Sutton were bowled out for 96 runs.

entries.heading: A. Colledge
paras: Adrian who had played for a number of clubs before he arrived in Sutton in 1991 was a useful bowler for the 2nd team for, he took 5 wickets for 36 runs against Evesham and further 5 wickets for 37 runs against Nuneaton.  Unfortunately, he disappeared as quickly as he arrived.

entries.heading: D. Collett
paras: Don had played for a number of clubs including Harborne, Pickwick Dartmouth as well as the Warwickshire County Club’s 2nd Xl, before he arrived at Sutton in 1988 and was immediately playing in the 1st team.

A quick bowler of a lively pace but found wickets hard to come by until the game against Evesham in 1990 when Don took 5 for 47 runs, but there is no record of Don playing for Sutton in the following season. During, about the three seasons he played for the Club he always had something to say, about the funny side of the game.

entries.heading: R.M. Cross
paras: Richard, bowled at a lively pace in a 3rd team game in the 1990 season against Streetly took 7 wickets for 16 runs.

entries.heading: Michael Dean
paras: Michael joined Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club in 1988 at the age of 16 having previously played junior cricket at Walsall Cricket Club.  He made his first team debut in 1989 under the captaincy of Geoff Hopkinson, in a team which contained some famous SCCC names that included Mike Hepburn, Graham Williamson, Andrew Luckhurst, Paul Junkin and Andy Biddle.

Mike was educated at King Edward’s School and left in 1990 to go to the University of Exeter. This coincided with the family moving away from the Midlands to live in the South West of the country.  He was away between 1990 and 1993, returning to Sutton Coldfield in 1994 and played continually in the 1st team until he retired in 2009.

During Michael’s cricketing career with the Sutton Coldfield Club, he captained the 1st team in both 1996 & 1997 seasons winning both the Warwickshire Sunday League’s John Whitehouse K.O. Trophy by beating Coventry & NW in the Final and winning the Sutton Coldfield Knock Out Cup in 1996.  He also played in the club’s 150th year celebrations and anniversary games played in 1997, including those against the MCC, and the Free Foresters.   Michael was a useful quick bowler who could bat with a reliable pair of hands in the slips.
Michael also played a single ‘List A’ one day game for the Warwickshire Cricket Board in 2002 against Herefordshire. And was elected a Vice-President on his retirement.

entries.heading: Michael Dixon
paras: Michael was born 12th December, 1948, and was educated at John Willmott Grammar School and joined the Sutton Club in 1965straight from School and by 1968 he was in the 1st team as a middle order batsman, however, by 1970 Michael was a regular open batsman scoring over a 1,000 runs a season for 10 seasons and now as captain in 1973 he scored a massive 1,639 runs.  His total runs was the second highest number of runs scored by a Sutton Coldfield Cricketer and amounted to 14,868 at an average of 34.1 before he retired in at the end of the 1981 season having scored 19 centuries with a highest score of 140 runs against Bromsgrove.

entries.heading: Michael Dixon
paras: In 1974 Michael was elected “Cricketer of the Year” by the MCCC.  In 1975, Michael scored 1,445 runs at an average of 41.29, including, 112 runs at home to Coventry & NW, 128 runs not out at home to Ashby Hastings and 133 runs not out away at Solihull.  In the 1979 season he scored 1,109 runs and passes 1,000 runs mark for 10th consecutive year,
He has scored over 1,000 runs for the last five seasons including seven centuries (three undefeated).

During his 5 years as captain Sutton won the Midland Club Cricket Championship in 1977 which was interesting to note that the 1st Team won 7 Saturday league games and lost the same number, because Michael always tried to win a game rather than settling for a tame draw which on occasions resulted in a loss. Michael was very much a front foot player taking a big step down the wicket, forcing the bowler to have to adjust his length.  He was particular very harsh on fast left arm round the wicket using his pads to the ball that came in and the one the bowler straightened resulted in an easy signal especially when we played against the Leamington, Stratford and Olton clubs.

entries.heading: Vincent A. FitzGerald
paras: Vince, as he was affectingly called, first came to providence as a fast bowler with the 2nd Team toward the end of the 1954 season at the age of 18, when in the record book recorder “no qualifiers” when the requirement was a minimum of 20 wickets in a season, although playing away against Solihull he took all 10 wickets in 10.2 overs for 18 runs, an average of 1.8. on a good Solihull pitch.  He was only the second player in over 100 years that all 10 wickets had fallen to the same player.   However, in the next two season 55 and 56 Vince lead the Saturday 2nd team averages with 20 and 26 wickets with an average of 11.6 and 5.8 and 26 respectively. His record showed that Vince took a wicket ever 4 overs, and he took 7 wickets for 17 runs against Harborne 2nd.

Vince had blossomed out as a strong young man and bowled up the hill from the groundsman shed end.  He took over 400 1st team wickets at a cost of 16.5 runs per wicket between 1957 and 1968, before leaving the club to play for Coleshill C.C. as a batsman in 1969.  Vince was quickly replaced by the arrival from Cambridge University of Tom Jameson although he did play a number of Warwickshire County CC 2nd Xl games.  It had always been a wish of Vince to be considered as a batsman but with so many quality batsmen available Vince was always batting at No. 10 with the sound of the roller being started up.

entries.heading: N. Gamble
paras: Neil as head teacher of King Edwards Handsworth Grammar School was very limited in his availability because of school commitments, playing only in 1986 season occasionally for the 1st team but in a 2nd Xl game against Stratford he took 6 wickets for 18 runs in 12 overs, when Stratford were bowled out for 34 runs.

entries.heading: B.K. Gardom
paras: The Sutton Club have no record of Keith, as he was known as, although he may have played in the summer schoolboys games organised by Peter Wells.  Keith was born in Birmingham on the 31 December 1952 and was educated at Bishop Vesey's Grammar School and toured the West Indies with the England Young Cricketers in August–September 1972.  He was awarded the Cricket Society prize for the most promising young cricketer of the year in 1972 as a polished right-handed batsman who bowled leg breaks and googlies.

Keith made his first-class debut for Warwickshire against Cambridge University in 1973, and went on to make sixteen further first-class appearances for the county, the last of which came against Essex in the 1974 County Championship.  In his seventeen first-class matches, he scored a total of 427 runs at an average of 18.56, with a high score of 79 not out.  This score, which was one of two first-class fifties he made, came against Surrey in 1974.

With the ball, he took 17 wickets at a bowling average of 41.17, with best figures of 6/139. These figures, which were his only five wicket haul, came against Essex in 1974.  His List “A” debut came in the 1973 John Player League against Somerset, with Keith making four further List “A” appearances, though without success.  Keith’s early retirement was a disappointment to the County who had great hopes for him in County Cricket but he wished to join the family business.

So, in 1973 Keith joined the club and scored 129 runs not out away at Nuneaton and 101 runs away at Solihull. In the following season he had a batting average of 50.55.  By 1977 Keith was a major player in Sutton winning the Midland Club Cricket Championship, taking 49 wickets at an average of 15.07 runs and scoring 784 runs at an average of 25.3.

On the retirement of Michael Dixon in 1978, Keith took over the captaincy and lead by example with centuries at Harborne with 109 & 105 runs not out at home to Stratford followed by 102 runs not out away at Litchfield, totaling 1,285 runs in the season.

In 1979 Keith has one of his best bowling performances taking 6 for 33 against Bromsgrove and in 1980, having relinquished the captaincy in what proved to be his last season with the Sutton Club at Barnt Green he took 5 for 34.  A short career but very productive with both bat and ball.

entries.heading: John Goring & Family
paras: John, respectively known as the Field Marshall, played virtually all his cricket at Sutton in the 2nd team and produced many outstanding bowling performances with his slow right arm off breaks.  In 1976 John finished top of the 2nd team bowling with 51 wickets at a cost of 18.1 per wicket and in the following season he again passed the 50 mark with 58 wickets at a cost of 11.2, including a 7 for 27 against Whitmore; 6 for 53 against Leamington & 6 for 44 against Barnt Green.

He passed the 50 mark in 1979 and again in the 1980 seasons with 50 wickets and 62 wickets at an average of 17.2 and 14.8 runs per wicket respectively.  John was not known for his batting but in 1985 season he scored 529 runs in 11 completed innings.

Both John’s sons Peter, and Steve played for the club as did his daughter, Claire.  Peter was a very good batsman scoring 122 against Abbots Bromley in 1977 and with his leg spin bowler took 35 wickets with an average of 16.3, in 1975 for the two’s, including 7 for 41 against Stafford, but an early marriage took him away from the game.

Steve, availability was limited but he did produce some remarkable bowling figures for the two’s against Four Oaks when he bowled 12 overs of which 8 were maidens taking 6 wickets for 14 runs.  He was a useful middle order batsman in the 2nd team and figured in a number of century partnerships, 114 runs for the 4th wicket for the Hawkes in 1978 in which he scored 44 runs.

John’s daughter Clare played for the Hawkes in the 1980’s (most likely in 1983) and was 12 Man in the England team with her spin bowling.  A truly remarkable Cricketing Family, incidentally they all played hockey at a high level.

entries.heading: G.H.W. Griffith
paras: Very little of George’s cricketing achievements were ever recorded, although he played for many seasons but mainly in the two’s.  The 1st Team first met up with George who was the wicket keeper when they played Moseley Ashfield away on the bank holiday Monday day game in 1980.  A Sutton win was clearly on the cards by tea time, with six of the home batsmen already dismissed when George came to the wicket with a bat that had more black tape than you can imagine holding his bit of wood together.  He proceeded to score freely around the ground with the Sutton bowlers unable to claim his wicket and finished with a creditable 51 not out, although Roger Coombs had a strong appeal for a stumping which was rejected by the umpire and so the game was drawn.

A couple of seasons later George was a married man living in Sutton and joined the Club after 16 years at Moseley Ashfield.  On his debut in 1982 playing in the second team in the opening game of the season he scored 115 runs not out away at Bewdley.

One of the best remembered games was in 1984 against Wolverhampton 2nd Xl, one of the strongest sides in Midlands Club Cricket at that time.  Batting first, the Sutton Coldfield 2nd Xl were in serious trouble with wickets tumbling, and finding Bob McGowen, going in to bat with 9 wickets down, who was not known as a batsman was allowed to receive a couple of ball, before the Sutton Captain, Dave Jackson had seen enough and to prevent Wolverhampton getting the full bonus points for bowling the side out declared on 83 for 9 wickets.
During the next two hours Wolverhampton against the bowling of Dave Jackson and Ian King were bowled out for 78 with Dave Jackson taking 4 for 49 and Ian King 6 for 17 and Sutton had won by 5 runs.

During the 1980’s George was a regular player in the Two’s, although he did keep wicket for the 1st Team on occasions.  From around 1992 - 03 George played regularly for the 3rd under a variety of captains opening the batting and keeping wicket.  One game of note was against Leamington when George scored 102 not out, remembered as Leamington were playing their club’s 1st Team opening bowler who had just recovered from injury.

Another memorable match was on the bottom ground when the 3rd XL was chasing down a score of 291 set by Halesowen, George scored 94 not out to win the game in 42.1 overs ably supported by Justin Roy and Mark Bell.

Describing George, it is true to say that he was “Larger than Life” a Charter Accountant who presence in the room was noticeable, but he was a good cricketer as well as a good hockey player and an excellent tourist with the Mayflies 1990 to 2003.

He knew how to entertain the opposition off and on the field against all the local sides in the Crickhowell and Abergavenny district.  One of Georg’s highlights of his Mayflies career was at Builth Wells in a day game in 1995 when he and Paul Bryan claimed the record 1st wicket partnership with 152 runs.  However, as tour captain for the week in 1998, George put himself on to bowl at Talgarth and achieved his only five wicket haul in his career with 5 for 32 runs off 6 overs - not bad for someone who was a confirmed wicket keeper.

entries.heading: George Griffith
paras: Extract from the 1986 Handbook & Fixture Card

entries.heading: Cartoon by Carol Griffith
paras: In 1983 George was elected the Club’s General Secretary a post he held until the end of the 1989 season.  During his term in Office, along with Peter Bell, the Chairman re-wrote the Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club rules and they also introduced the concept of advertising in the fixture card which is still a valuable source of income to the Club.  George also took the Chairman to meet the leader of the Birmingham City Council, Sir Neville Bosworth regarding the purchase of the Rectory Park cricket ground area, but not even a Conservative Council would sell their assets.
George was a regular player with the Worcester Gents from 1990 – 2005 as one of their wicket keepers.

In 1990 George was elected as Chairman of the General Purpose Committee of the joint clubs (SCCC & SCHC) responsible for managing the joint clubs but not the playing side of the business, before standing down in 1996.

It’s worth noting as a member of the hockey club, George formed the initial “Over-35” side and later in life as George aged, he formed the “Over-45” team, to be followed by the “Over-50” side.  The highlight of his hockey prowess was in 2010 taking the “Over-50’s” to play in the Veterans Plate Semi-final against Tunbridge Wells, only to lose 6 – 1.  However, the coach trip back to Sutton Coldfield consisted of some serious drinking and tall stories.
George continues to support both the cricket and hockey activities as a vice president of both Clubs.

entries.heading: C. Hart
paras: C. Hart scored 100 N.O. against Abbotts Bromley in 1990 for the Sunday 3rd team.

entries.heading: Andrew Hodder
paras: Andrew joined the Sutton Club as a School boy in 1981, under the guidance of Peter Well’s Summer Cricket Games in August after a short spell with Walmley. Andrew was a gifted leg spin bowler, somewhat to the surprise of the Bishop Vesey School sports master.  In 1982 hew in the 1st team and took 6 wickets for 49 runs against Streetly and also showed his batting ability with a 100 runs against Fordhouses.  In the 1983 season Andrew, now a serious 1st team batsman finished the season with a total of 724 runs at an impressive average of 31.5.  His bowling continually produced wickets and 4 for 3 runs at Bromsgrove, and later in the season he had a number of 6 wicket hauls, including Water Orton for 47 runs, Stratford for 60 and against Coventry & NW for 70 runs. Andrew’s availability was limited once he took a career in music at the Royal College of Music studying the “French Horn”, although he did play a number of games during the summer break and our last record shows that he did play for Sutton against the Canadian ICC World Cup team in a warm up game against the Sutton side.

entries.heading: F.J. Holeman
paras: Joe joined the Club in 1970 as a mature cricketer and played in the 2nd team on Saturday and Sundays until the end of the 1998 season and captained the side for 3 seasons 1976 to 1978.  He was a right arm bowler of medium pace who took 56 wickets in his first season with an average of 18.7 runs per wicket, and at Leamington that year he took 6 wickets for 13 runs.  Joe proceeded to take over 50 wickets per season finishing top or runner-up of the averages until he took on the captaincy allowing younger players to bowl in preference to himself.  His best seasons were in 1973 and 74, when he took 62 wickets each year at a cost of 17.3 runs per wicket and improved his average in 1974 to 15.4.  During Joe’s career with Sutton Joe took 455 wickets at an average of 18.3 runs in his 9 season as solely a 2nd team player, and never caught the eye of the 1st team captains when they were short of a stead but accurate bowler, but his age would have perhaps made Joe a liability in the field.

entries.heading: M. Hooper
paras: Mick Hooper joined the Club in or around 1983 and was quickly established as a 2nd team player although he turned out for the 1st team on many occasions when some of the stars of the day were unavailable.  Mick was mainly a batsman but could bowl and in the 2nd team in 1983 he led the batting averages with 55.5 having scored 495 runs.  In the following season he again was top run getter with 661 and an average of 25.5.  In 1985 Mick was again one of the leading players with 462 runs and average of 24.3.  He also featured in a number of century partnership.  In 1983 away at Coventry & NW, he and Georg Griffith for the 1st wicket scored 111 of which Mick’s share was 59 runs and George with 77 runs.  Later that season against the Old Blundellians, in a 2nd wicket partnership of 127 with James Ross he scored 70, with James not out on 74.   In 1988 Mick was selected by the MCCC to play against Chedworth Cricket Club and scored 100 not out.

In 1990 Mick played a first team game at Aldridge and was invited to bowl and took 5 wickets in 7 overs for 10 runs.  Although Mick player regularly throughout the 1980’s he does not appear in many records because of his willingness to play with either the 1st or 2nd depending on the availability of first team players.  Mick was a regular Mayfly tourist and was keeper of their statics transferring them electronically to CDs for all tourists to have a copy.  I can still remember the sound of Mick’s squeaky cricket boots when running between the wickets. Nostalgia!

entries.heading: W.N. Houghton - Life Member
paras: Neil Houghton, elder son of the popular sportsman Eric Houghton (Aston Villa and England footballer, Manager, and Warwickshire and Lincolnshire cricketer) was educated at Oakham School.  Neil first appeared in the writings of the late Norman Sharp, “as a young player making his mark, towards the end of the 1957 season, showing outstanding promise”.  How right Norman was for in the 1959 season, though only in his twentieth year, his consistent and correct batsman-ship earned him 1,097, 1st team runs with an average of 32.7.   Neil with Geoff Pritchett created a new first wicket partnership record for Sutton of 192.runs against Warwickshire Pilgrims, with Neil scoring 94 to Geoff’s 118 runs.  The opening 1st team partnership of 192 runs still stands today in 2017.

entries.heading: Neil Houghton
paras: Neil’s off spin bowling in the same season secured him 61 wickets including a "hat trick" at home against Aldridge removing the 2nd, 3rd and 4th wickets in his first over, and he finished the season with a bowling average of 17.3 and top of the Saturday Club games.
The 1958 season had been an illustrious season in the commencement of playing in Club Cricket, which continued into the 1976 season, when his domestic arrangements limited his availability.
During the 18 seasons Neil scored 8 centuries;
In 1960 against Nuneaton 122;
In 1961 against Market Drayton 121 not out, and in the same season 118 against 	Leamington;
In 1962 again against Market Drayton 101and against Leamington with 113 not out;
In 1963 against Stafford 100;
In 1968 against Pickwick 105; and against Walsall 110 runs plus a hat trick in the 	same game.

Neil was also involved in numerous centuries partnerships far too many to record.   In his first 6 seasons he scored over a 1,000 runs per season with 1,359 runs in 1962 beating his own record of 1,332 runs in the 1961 season.  However, in Club and representative cricket Neil scored over 1,700 runs and took well over 50 wickets.   Neil scored 13,200 runs during his playing career with the 1st team with an average of 31.7.  He was also a member of the 99 club when he was out away at Pickwick only the 7th member of the Club to have this distinction.  We now have in 2017 a record of 10 in the Club’s 171st years playing cricket.

Neil’s bowling was also very effective and during his playing days he took just over 600 wickets at a cost of just under 16 runs per wicket with his best performance was against Stafford when he bowled 16 overs, 10 maidens, 8 wickets for 16 runs.in 1964 when he took 96 wickets in the season. He also had the distinction of his 2nd “hat trick” this time against Walsall.

Neil played 400 games in the 1st team for the Sutton Club and captained the side 1963 to 1967 and was a playing member of the of the MCC, Warwickshire Pilgrims and the Imps as well as touring with the Mayflies and representing the Midland Club Cricket Conference on many occasions and in such a game against the Oxford Authentics scoring 106 runs not out.  In 1961 Neil was one of 4 “Cricketers of the Year” elected by the Midland Club Cricket Conference.

Neil also played in a number of games for Warwickshire County Cricket Club’s 2nd team games, but his talents were not just on the cricket pitch for he was an extremely good administrator, first as secretary to the Sutton Club for 5 years, 1973 to 1977; before being elected on to the Warwickshire County Cricket Club committee in 1982.  Neil’s first roll was as Chairman of the General Purpose & Finance Committee, 1988 to 1998; and became the club’s treasurer 1989 to 1998 as well as taking on the Chairmanship of the Cricket Committee 1989 – 1990 and was elected the Club’s Chairman in 2003, a post he held until he resigned after the rebuilding of the Edgbaston Ground had been complete in 2010.
Neil was also a good after dinner speaker entertaining not just the Sutton members but he spoke at many clubs across the Midlands and entertained them royally.

entries.heading: Joe Iafrati – The Italian Off Spinner
paras: Not many players, who spend, their entire playing career on the lower ground would get any mention or recognition of their ability.  However, I first came across Joe in 1968 when I played an odd game on a Sunday for the Grasshoppers. (Due to a sudden shortage of players available for the lower ground).  When introduced to the team I was informed that “We have our Italian test off spinner playing”.  I never did learn if Joe was an Italian or not, but he was certainly a pretty good off spinner, turning the ball from off to leg.  Looking through the 1968 records, Joe took 7 wickets for 13 runs in 5 overs for the Grasshoppers against the Inland Revenue.
In 1970 at Little Stoke playing for the Grasshoppers Joe took his career best figures of 8 for 15.
In 1972 Joe was top of the Hawks averages: - 26 wickets for 363 runs at an average of 14.

The following season playing for the Grasshoppers against Marchington Joe in a 10 over spell finished with 6 wickets for 10 runs and in 1975 he again finished top of the Grasshoppers averages with 31 wickets at an average of 13.9.

However, in 1976, in what appeared to be Joe’s last season, he again was top in the Hawks averages with 33 wickets at an average of 13.7.  Uncountable it can be said of Joe Ifrati that for the eight-year period that records are available he certainly contributed in a big way towards the Grasshopper – Hawkes success as a player capable of winning game with his outstanding spin bowling

entries.heading: D.M Jackson
paras: Dave joined the Club in or around 1983 and played as a quick bowler initially in the 2nd team and in 1984 distinguishing himself taking a “Hat Trick” but to save the embarrassed opposition their identity was never recorded. Dave also captained the two’s in 1984 and 1985 and did play an odd game for the 1st team but none of his performances were recorded.  After a brush with the local police resulted in him losing his licence he moving back to his home town of Doncaster, before taking on a senior role with British Steel in the United States.

entries.heading: Tom E.N. Jameson
paras: A very versatile cricketer with either the bat or the ball - or on occasions with both.  Educated at Taunton School he made his first-class debut for Cambridge University against Warwickshire at Fenner's in 1970. He made eight further first-class appearances for the university in that season, the last of which came against Oxford University in The University Match at Lord's.  He gained a cricketing Blue while at Cambridge. He also made a single first-class appearance in 1970 for Warwickshire against Cambridge University at Edgbaston.
His brother, John, played Test cricket for England and Warwickshire and was an aggressive opening batsman.

Tom as a top –middle order left-handed batsman who could always be relied upon to get the score moving or if necessary, just to occupy the crease and with the ball he would deny the batsmen the opportunity to score and on occasions picking up small clusters of wickets.  Tom joined Sutton in 1969 and finished the season as top dog with 57 wickets at an average of 10.7 runs per wicket forming a very strong bowling attack with Andy Beach also with 57 wickets and Warwick Tidy 50 wickets on Sundays only at the other end.

In 1970 Tom distinguished himself in a 166-run partnership for the 2nd wicket with Michael Dixon scoring 103 not out at Nuneaton.  During the two seasons Tom played for Sutton before moving to live in Knowle he scored 678 runs at an average of just over 25 runs per innings and took 94 wickets at 14.5 runs per wicket.

entries.heading: Jerman Family
paras: It interesting to note yet another Family, The Jermans’, Father Alan and his two sons, Mark and Richard played for the Club in the 2nd half of the 1980’s and the 1st half of the 1990.

In 1987 Alan won the second Xl batting award and after a season as their vice- captain, before captaining the side in 1989 and 1990.  Both Mark and Richard were talented cricketers who were very aggressive to any bowler who strayed off length and were both playing in the 1st team in 1993 and were picked to play for the Willis Corroon Midland Club Cricket Championship League side against the Shropshire League, and were part of the Sutton Club winning the league that season.

In 1994 both boys scored centauries, Richard with 143 not out against Rugby and Mark was also not out with 125 to his name against Leamington.  In 1995 Mark had a purple patch with 144 runs away at Evesham and was unfortunately run out on 95 against Coventry & NW, and hit 75 against Cannock.  However, both boys left the Midland to follow their career in the London area.

entries.heading: M. Joseph
paras: Mike joined the Club in 1979 and quickly established himself as a quality batsman who has a good correct technic, but his opportunities were limited in the selection of the 1st team so Mike played in the 2nd team and had 5 remarkable seasons scoring over 4,000 runs at an average of 39 runs with an outstanding season in 1982 scoring 1,258 runs.  He scored two centuries, 114 away at Pickwick in 79 and in 1980 he scored 100 runs against Olton.  In the 1980 season Mike featured in a 3rd wicket partnership for the 1st team of 124 at home to Aldridge, scoring 58.

Mike was an excellent after dinner speaker and he entertained members and guests alike when he proposed the toast to the Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club in the Club’s 150th Anniversary Dinner and outshone a professional speaker namely, Henry Blofeld of the BBC Test Match Special.  Mike left the Midland in his banking career, taking with him, as his wife the Umpire’s, (Phil Berry) daughter Judy to live in Amersham.

entries.heading: A. Jones
paras: Andrew in a 3rd team game at Barnt Green in 1990 scored 203 runs not out in an unbroken 2nd wicket partnership of 287 runs with Johnathan Miller who was 100 not out when the captain declared the Sutton innings closed.  He also played a number of games in the 2nd team before trying his hand as a pro-golfer as he played off scratch.

entries.heading: P. Junkin
paras: Paul joined the Club in 1987 and quickly palled up with Andy Luckhurst to become a lethal 1st team bowling attack.  Paul had played for Aston Unity for a number of years before joining a Staffs & Cheshire League club playing as a semi-professional before he came to Sutton.  He had lost some of his extreme pace but maintained his accuracy and opposition batsmen found Paul difficult to score off.  At the start of the 1990 season Paul took 5 Loughborough wickets for 24 runs and a few weeks later away at Evesham he took 5 for 56 against.  In what appeared to be Paul’s last season with the Club in 1995 he captained the two’s

entries.heading: Ian King
paras: In 1984 Sutton were lucky to obtain the services of Ian, who had played County Cricket for both Warwickshire and Essex and League Cricket for a number of local clubs.  Ian, at the age of 52, indicated that he would be available to play only on a Saturday during the 84-season bowling his left arm spin, he was to take 70 wickets for the 2nd team in only 19 games.  His analysis for the season was 287 overs, 64 maidens, conceding 798 runs at an average of 11.4 runs.  His wicket taking by a 2nd Xl side won him the League’s 2nd Xl bowling award.

Some of Ian’s bowling performances are worth recording; Against Leamington he took 8 for 40 runs in 24 overs; against Stratford he took 7 for 17 runs in 11.3 overs; against Wolverhampton Ian took 6 for 17 runs in 14.3 overs;
However, in addition to his success with the ball he achieved a very respectable batting average of 18 innings, 5 not outs, 221 runs and an average of 17.0, and in the field, he held 4 catches.

Apart from his prowess with the bat and ball Ian achieved one other record in the season; he was late for every fixture and even succeeded in going to the wrong ground on one occasion.  This particular occasion caused the captain some problems, as we were in the field, but Ian with no more preparation than a late breakfast, pinched from the tea ladies, was soon bowling away on his normal length.

entries.heading: K.D.W. Lancaster.  Life Member
paras: Ken Lancaster played his early cricket with Burbury CC before they became Lea Marston CC, although he played a considerable number of Seasons with Aston Unity CC before he joined the Sutton Club, which was about 1988, although his best years had been with the Unity during their years in Court Road.  However, Ken quickly became a regular with the 3rd team on both Saturdays and Sundays, although he did have considerable spells in the 2nd team.  In 1990 playing for the 3rd team Ken Lancaster took 6 Solihull wickets for 23 runs.

Playing in the 3rd Xl under the captaincy of Terry Matthews, who also bowled slow off-spin, similar to Ken’s style of bowling meant his opportunities were limited.  However, in 1993 Ken was part of the team that won the Willis Corroon League Champions for 3rd Xl. In the seasons 1997 & 98 Ken was 2nd Xl Sunday Captain & Hawks Captain on Saturdays and relinquished both for the 1999 season only to take on the Fixture Secretaries Position, although he did come back 2001 to captain the Hawks on Saturdays and in 2005 Ken took on the post of General Secretary resigning the Fixture Secretary’s position in 2008. In 2011 Ken was elected President of the Birmingham & District Premier Cricket League and is awarded the Leslie Jones Secretarial Trophy by the Midland Club Cricket Conference, which forced Ken to resign as the Club’s General Secretary because of league commitments.
When the Warwickshire Sunday League was formed in 1984, and within a few years he became their general secretary, a post he held until the League was wound up at the end of the 2016 season.

On the 9th September 1998 Ken had the distinction of playing at Lord’s in the Club’s 150th Anniversary Celebration, which had been delayed 12 months due to the ground development at Lord's to play the MCC side known as the Cross Arrows.  Ken picked up a wicket in a good spell of bowling and going into bat at number 11 to join Jon Miller with the team requiring 10 runs for victory but finishing 2 runs short in a drawn game.

Ken also played in Sutton’s 1998 team against the MCCC side bowling his off-spin economically in a 12 over spell without success only concede 37 runs out of a total of 215 runs for 5 wickets. He was not required to bat.

At the 2017 Annual Dinner, Ken was awarded a Life Membership for his services to the Club over close on 30 years, mainly in an administration capacity both on and off the cricket pitch and is still scoring for the various club teams to day a job he has been doing for 5 seasons.

entries.heading: J. Little
paras: Jimmy first distinguished himself as a wicket keeper who could bat when he was top of the 3rd team batting averages in 1994 when playing only 5 games scored 306 runs at an average of 76.5.  He secured a second spot as their wicket keeper and was the keeper in the 1st team on a relative small number of games in 1996. However, he was in the 1st team side that won the Sutton Coldfield K.O Cup.

entries.heading: Rod Long
paras: Rod joined the Club in 1979, as a 1st team bowler after a very successful couple of seasons with Wishaw C.C. and in his first season headed the bowling averages with 37 wickets at a cost of 16.9 runs per wicket.  In the following season Rod had an outstanding performance of quick to fast bowling against Leamington in 1980 taking 9 wickets for 38 runs in 11.2 overs.  Unable to maintain his accuracy he decided to become a big fish in a small pool returning to play once again for Wishaw Cricket Club.  Incidentally the last occasion a 1st team bowler took 9 wickets was in1962 by Allan Bedggood, a slow bowler, against Leicester Ivanhoe who took 9 for 44 in 15.2 overs; No bowler has taken 9 wickets since Rod’s achievement to date (2017).

entries.heading: Danny Longhorne
paras: Danny joined the Club from Four Oaks & All Saints in 1990; a 1st team batsman who distinguished himself on the May Bank Holiday Monday at Leamington scored 133 not out and followed it with a quick 86 in the final of the Sutton Coldfield C.C. KO competition. Danny with 50 runs shared an opening partnership of 140 runs with Andy Luckhurst 88 against Aston Unity in a Warwickshire Sunday League game later in the season.  We were sorry to see Danny return to his old club but family ties were hard to break.

entries.heading: Andy Luckhust
paras: Andrew was one of the most outstanding all round Midland Club Cricketers in the last quarter of the 21st Century.  Andy joined the Club from Bowdon C.C., a Cheshire league side in 1981 and went straight into the 1st team. During the next 14 seasons he established himself as one of the Midlands best all-rounders.  In 1984 he had a purple patch against some of the Saturday strongest league opponents with 103 not out against Kings Heath, and 5 wickets for 59 against Harborne and 6 for 28 runs against Coventry & NW and at Wolverhampton he bowled unchanged for 30 overs taking 6 for 49 runs. The first time Sutton had won a match against Wolverhampton since 1956. So, it was no surprise that Andy won the 1st XI League’s bowling award.  In 1985 Andy was the Sunday Captain and the team won the Wishaw 6-a-side competition and Sutton’s own KO competition. In 1989 Andy was awarded M.C.C.C. “Cricketer of the Year” and was described in the local press “In his 8 years with the club has developed into a fine opening batsman and is currently enjoying a great campaign with bat and ball”.  In 1990 Andy took on the roll as 1st team captain, a position he held for the 5 seasons, opening the batting and on occasions the bowling. The following season Andy scored 116 runs against Solihull and had an opening partnership with Danny Longhorn of 140 runs against Aston Unity, this was followed by a 101 not out at Coventry & N.W. and with the ball he took 7 for 84 against Stratford, 6 for 50 against Olton and 5 for 37 against Bedworth. During Andy’s captaincy the 1st team won 23 games in the 1990 season. In 1993 the 1st team, under Andy’s captaincy won the Willis Corroon Midland Club Cricket Championship League and he was selected to captain the MCCC side to play in the Inter League Competition against the Shropshire League that included seven 1st team colleagues.

The team of 1993 was considered by many as one of the strongest and most attractive team to play and watch cricket at Sutton.  Incidentally the 3rd Xl also won the 3rd Xl Willis Corroon Midland Club Cricket Championship.
Andy’s last season as 1st team captain was in 1994 when the team won 23 matches.  However, he did captain the 2nd Xl in 1996 before calling it a day.

Andy was certainly an outstanding cricketer over 14 seasons playing 1st team cricket for the Sutton Coldfield Cricket Club, able to bat in any position but was exceptional as an opening batsman and then able to bowl at a lively pace, moving the ball on the most placid playing surfaces.
However, as a Warwickshire Pilgrim he had no success on his first tour with the ball but in his latter tours he performed very well.  He retired at the end of the 1996 season to play golf.
Cartoon by Carol Griffith extract from the 1986 Handbook & Fixture Card

entries.heading: The Maynards, John, Steven & Chris
paras: It is very unusual for a Farther and two sons to play in the same team, well it did happen when Father, John Maynard and Steve, a batsman & leg spinner bowler with the younger brother Chris all played against the Old Blundellians in 1973.  The Old Blundellians were the old boy’s cricket team from Blundell’s School in Tiverton who toured the Midland in August and played against the Sutton Club for around 20 years.
Working backwards in the family, Chris was an outstanding wicketkeeper and competent batsman who played county cricket for Warwickshire and Lancashire.

Steve was never able to obtain a regular 1st team place due to the club having two ex-county leg spinners in Tidy and Gardom in the team and his batting was good but not outstanding.  However, he did turn out for the 1st team on odd occasions when the superstars were unavailable and Steve rarely let the side down, but played most of his cricket in the 2nd team and in 1978 and 79 season he scored 426 and 593 runs respectively, finishing second in the team’s batting averages with 28.3 and 32.9 runs in 1978 and 79 respectively.

John Maynard was a quality batsman playing first in the 2nd team in 1968 to 1973 before establishing a 1st team place.  During his time with the two’s, he regularly scored over 500 runs a season and in the 4 seasons 1970 to 1973 John scored over 2,700 runs with an average of over 32.

Having forced his way into the 1st team in 1974 -75 he scored in the two seasons close on 800 runs at an average of over 27 batting at No.7.  John did figure in a 5th wicket partnership with Chris Barber of 114 runs at Nuneaton with John being not out on 36.  During these two seasons John was not out on 10 occasions out of his 39 innings.   It is interesting to note that in the 1975, his son Chris was playing in the 1st team alongside his father as a wicketkeeper batsman.

John was a sales engineer for a black-country firm who had interests in South Africa and when an opportunity came for John to take a franchise on the companies’ overseas business he immigrated to a new life in South Africa and a few years later Steve joined the family.

entries.heading: J. Miller
paras: Jonathan first caught the eye of senior members of the Club in 1990 when he scored 100 runs not out in an unbroken 2nd wicket partnership of 287 runs with A. Jones 203 not out against Barnt Green.  By 1993 Jon was a regular 1st team player and in 1995 he scored 103 not out at home against Rugby and hit 86 runs against Harborne.  In 1996 Jon teamed up as vice-captain of the 1st team with Michael Dean as captain; posts they both held in the 1997 season and then in 1998 they both switched rolls and carried on in 1999 until Jon relinquished the captaincy at the end of that season to play golf.  During their yeas together they became a very useful bowling attack.

entries.heading: James I. McDowall
paras: James McDowall, born in Sutton Coldfield and played his junior cricket at Rugby School before going up to Cambridge University in 1969 and made 17 first-class appearances, the last of which came against Warwickshire. During his time at Cambridge, he scored a total of 446 runs at an average of 14.86, with a high score of 62 as well as keeping wicket full time in his second year.  This score of 62 was his only half century for the University and that came against Leicestershire in 1969.
He also took 26 catches and was an occasional wicketkeeper where he had a single stumping. He gained a Blue during his time at Cambridge leaving in 1970.

It was also in 1969 that he made his debut for Warwickshire in a first-class match against Somerset in the County Championship at Clarence Park, Weston-super-Mare.  He made eleven further first-class appearances for Warwickshire, the last of which came against Lancashire in the 1973 County Championship.  In his twelve first-class appearances for the county, he scored 365 runs at an average of 20.27, with a high score of 89.  This score was his only half century for Warwickshire and came against Oxford University in 1973.  He also took 24 catches and made 2 stumpings. The presence of first choice wicket-keeper Alan Smith in the Warwickshire side limited his appearances in the first eleven. He left Warwickshire at the end of the 1974 season.

During 1971 and 1972 seasons James managed to play for Sutton, but not as a wicket keeper, he was however a quality batsman opening the innings on many occasions for the 1st team 30 times in 71 and 21 times in 72 scoring 1,146 and 600 runs respectively at an average of 44 and 35.7 before devoting his playing time to the County Club, and later succeeded his father as their treasurer.
In 1971 James scored two centuries for Sutton with a 100 runs at home to Aston Manor and 106 runs at home to Stratford.

entries.heading: G. Moore
paras: Having just left school Gary joined the Club in 1983 and was in the 1st team on merit being a bit quicker than most fast bowlers the team played against in the Midland Cricket Club Championship League.  In a game against K&D., Gary took 5 wickets for 43 runs in a cliffhanger of a game that resulted in the game being drawn and finished the 83 season with 30 wickets and an average of 31.0.

entries.heading: C. Munn
paras: Chris Munn played 1st team cricket in the 1990’s and on his day was a batsman of real quality and in 1990 Chris and Mike Hepburn put on 154 runs for the second wicket with Chris scoring 52 runs.  Mike being 85 not out.  In 1994 Chris scored 101 before being run out at Leamington.  In 1995 he scored 114 not out in the day game against Moseley Ashfield, and then he scored 98 runs in a Warwickshire Sunday League game against Moseley and against Evesham he was out for 92.  In one month, Chris had accumulated nearly 400 runs.

entries.heading: D.P. Murphy
paras: It is believed that Derrick Murphy joined the Club in 1978 and played as a regular player in the 2nd as a seam bowler of a medium pace until he retired in about 1996-97.  In his first two seasons 1978 and again in 1979 he passed the 50-wicket mark; with 58 wickets at an average of 19.5 and in his second season 56 wickets at 15.8 runs per wicket. In 1980 he captained the side for just the one season taking 33 wickets at an average of 27.7.  In 1982 playing for the 1st on a Sunday against Ashby Hastings Derrick took 6 for 67.  However, Derek only played an odd game for the 1st team and in such a game at Aldridge on a 1983 bank holiday, Tuesday when Sutton batting first managing to score 52 runs before being all out.  The Aldridge Xl in their reply were all out for 38 runs with Derrick taking 5 for 8 runs.  The loss of 20 wickets, before tea for less than 100 runs, was not caused by any problem with the playing surface it was just very poor batting and some useful bowling by both teams.  Derrick was a very quiet spoken man although a lecturer for British Gas, his sporting did tend to attract the attention of the ladies.

entries.heading: S. Nicholls
paras: Simon took over the captaincy of the Hawkes in 1995 and held the post for two seasons and in 1996 he took 4 wickets in an over including a hat-trick against Moseley Ashfield before retiring to play golf.

entries.heading: R. Newton
paras: The Author first met Richard in 1967 in the 2nd XL game at Coseley Cricket Club on a Saturday in September when Peter Cadman the Sutton captain loss the toss and was invited to field first.  Much to the delight, and a rare occurrence was to be provided with a new ball, rapping an all.  Richard, our young left arm quick to sharp bowler, bowled the first 5 ball without any response from the opening batsman, so the last ball in the over was extra quick and somewhat short of a length, which woke the batsman up with a fine hook dispatching the ball over the square leg boundary fence for six.  That was the last we saw of the ball, although time was spent looking in the resident’s front garden, but no sign of the ball although there was a telltale streak mark across a freshly painted garage door and a pot of green paint alongside.  No resident was opening the door, so a box of old ball was presented by the Coseley captain with apologies that had been well used with an appearance of chamois leather.  A disappointed Peter Wells bowled the second over from the other end.  Richard played the next season in the 1st team before disappearing from the Club.
